subject: arts
note: Descriptor text: Australian Curriculum v9 (ACARA, CC BY 4.0). Waypoints and prior knowledge: Learning Waypoints. Made by tools/import-curriculum.mjs; do not edit by hand.

descriptors.title: Create works that communicate ideas
descriptors.description: create arts works that communicate ideas
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior knowledge assumed. Students bring physical play, movement, and imaginative storytelling from everyday experience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create arts works — including dance — that communicate ideas drawn from personal or social experience.
elaborations: creating arts works in a range of forms to communicate ideas from lived personal or social experiences
creating works in response to inspiration from sources such as play, imagination, observation, literature, artworks from their cultures and communities
extending and varying known songs, chants or rhymes
manipulating objects, puppets, 2D images and/or available technologies to create or retell stories
repurposing materials and objects such as clothing or packing boxes as starting points for imagining and developing scenes

nodes.label: Ideas as starting points
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify an idea from lived experience or imagination to use as a starting point for movement.
criteria: Student can name or show the idea their movement is communicating
Student produces at least one distinct movement response to a given prompt
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a clear idea-to-movement connection, students produce movement without communicative intent — subsequent choreography and sharing nodes lack the anchor they require.

width.minimum: One lived experience or familiar story used as a prompt for movement exploration.
width.typical: A range of starting points explored — favourite activities, games, animals, or familiar stories — to generate movement ideas.
wider: Use stimuli from multiple modalities — music, objects, tactile materials, or imagery — to generate contrasting movement ideas
Draw on stories and characters from their cultural communities as starting points for movement creation

modes.reason: Help students articulate what their movement is 'about' — the link between an idea and a physical response. Use prompts: 'What does this look like?', 'Show me how that feels in your body'.
More starting-point types (sensory, narrative, observational) build richer imaginative repertoire for movement generation.

nodes.label: Experimenting with movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore and vary movement possibilities — including body shape, level, direction and dynamics — in response to an idea.
criteria: Student demonstrates at least two contrasting movement qualities (e.g. high and low, fast and slow)
Student can vary a movement in response to a teacher prompt (e.g. 'make it bigger', 'move more slowly')

width.minimum: Exploration of one or two movement qualities (e.g. high/low, fast/slow) applied to a single idea.
width.typical: Sustained movement exploration across body parts, levels, locomotor and non-locomotor movement, and contrasting dynamics — e.g. heavy/light, fast/slow, big/small.
wider: Explore movement inspired by tactile qualities of materials (rough, smooth, spikey) — translating sensation into movement
Improvise movement sequences that trace shapes observed in the environment (geometric and organic)

modes.reason: Students need a physical vocabulary of movement options before they can make intentional choices. Time to play with variation across multiple sessions builds this range.

nodes.label: Shaping and sequencing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can organise two or more movement ideas into a simple sequence that communicates an idea to others.
criteria: Student produces a movement sequence with at least two distinct parts
Student can describe or show what their sequence communicates (e.g. 'this is me jumping in puddles')
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to organise movement into a communicable sequence is the foundation of the Presenting strand — students who cannot yet sequence cannot meaningfully share work with audiences.

width.minimum: A simple two-part sequence (start shape → movement → end shape) linked to one idea.
width.typical: A movement sequence with a beginning, middle and end — using improvised movements selected and arranged to communicate an idea, retell a story, or represent a character or experience.
wider: Repurpose objects or costumes as prompts for imagining and developing short movement scenes
Collaborate with a partner to combine and extend individual movement ideas into a shared sequence

modes.reason: Sequencing is the point at which idea (N1) and movement vocabulary (N2) integrate. Support with visual structure prompts: 'What happens first?', 'What do you do next?', 'How do you end?'

descriptors.title: Discover possibilities and develop ideas
descriptors.description: use play, imagination, arts knowledge, processes and/or skills to discover possibilities and develop ideas
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior knowledge assumed. Students bring physical play, movement, and imaginative storytelling from everyday experience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use play, imagination and arts knowledge to discover movement possibilities and develop ideas for arts works.
elaborations: playing with the tactile qualities of a range of materials and exploring how they feel to develop ideas for dance
imagining how characters in a story might dress or move, making still or moving images
identifying shapes, colours and lines in the environment and exploring ways to use these creatively
playing games to develop subject-specific practices; exploring ways that body parts, zones and bases can be moved safely and expressively
responding to emotions while listening to music and using movement to share responses
improvising rhythmic patterns for clapping or stamping or inventing new movements for familiar action songs
exploring speaking and singing voices and discovering ways to use them to communicate ideas and feelings
improvising movements to explain the steps in a process

nodes.label: Using play to discover movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use physical play and imagination to discover new ways of moving their bodies.
criteria: Student initiates new movement in response to a play-based prompt without direct imitation
Student explores at least two different ways of moving in response to the same stimulus
nodes.hinge_reason: If students haven't developed physical play as a generative mode, they will be unable to self-generate movement ideas in the Creating strand — relying instead on imitation only.

width.minimum: Structured play with movement prompts — exploring how body parts, levels, and bases can move safely and expressively.
width.typical: Open-ended movement exploration across multiple sessions: responding to imagery, music, emotions, or environmental features; discovering range across locomotor and non-locomotor movement.
wider: Use scarves, ribbons or other props to discover new movement possibilities and extend spatial awareness
Respond to contrasting music styles and tempos through movement — noticing how emotional response changes movement quality

modes.reason: Play-based movement discovery needs sustained time across varied prompts. Accumulating physical possibilities — different body parts, zones, directions — builds the store students draw on in Creating.

nodes.label: Developing and varying ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a movement idea further — varying, extending, or combining it — through imagination and play.
criteria: Student can vary a movement they have made in at least one way when prompted
Student can show two different versions of the same idea

width.minimum: Taking one movement idea and extending or varying it in at least one way (e.g. doing it faster, bigger, at a different level, with a different body part).
width.typical: Using contrast and playful experimentation to extend movement ideas: changing level, direction, size, speed or body part; inventing new movements for familiar action songs; improvising rhythm patterns; responding to imagery with movement.
wider: Improvise movements that explain a process (e.g. steps in growing a plant), then develop a short sequence from these movements
Collaborate with peers to develop and extend each other's movement ideas through back-and-forth play

modes.reason: Varying ideas across different stimuli types — music, imagery, stories, games — builds transferable imaginative skill. Students who vary ideas in only one context remain dependent on that single prompt type.

descriptors.title: Arts importance for communities
descriptors.description: explore how and why the arts are important for people and communities
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior knowledge assumed. Students bring awareness of arts experiences from family and community life.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how and why the arts — including dance — are important for people and communities.
elaborations: exploring how facial expressions, gestures and other ways of moving communicate emotions and feelings in arts works
identifying and/or learning social or cultural dances that have meaning for people and communities, observing relevant protocols
identifying arts works and experiences in their lives and sharing ideas and feelings about them with peers and teachers
singing songs that are used for celebrations
exploring how illustrations in texts communicate narrative about characters, settings and mood
listening to First Nations Australians talk about the importance of the arts for connecting to People, Culture and Country/Place

nodes.label: Recognising arts in everyday life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify arts works and experiences — including dances and songs — that are present in their own lives and communities.
criteria: Student can name at least one arts experience from their own life
Student can share an idea or feeling about an arts work they have experienced
nodes.hinge_reason: Without recognising arts as present and purposeful in their own lives, students lack a reference point for understanding arts as communicative and culturally meaningful — the conceptual grounding for N2.

width.minimum: Identifying at least one type of arts work or experience from their own life — songs they sing, dances they watch or perform, animations, community events.
width.typical: Identifying a range of arts experiences across multiple forms — songs for celebrations, dances, public art, digital works — and sharing ideas and feelings about these with peers and teachers.
wider: Listen to First Nations Australians talk about the importance of arts for connecting to People, Culture and Country/Place (using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians)
Explore dances or songs from students' cultural communities — identifying what they are used for and who participates

modes.reason: Students from different cultural backgrounds have access to different arts experiences. Sharing across the class builds collective recognition of arts' diversity and omnipresence.

nodes.label: Understanding arts communicate emotion and ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how facial expressions, gestures, movement and voice in arts works communicate emotions and feelings.
criteria: Student can identify an emotion being communicated in a simple arts work
Student can point to at least one feature (face, movement, voice) that communicates that emotion

width.minimum: Identifying how a character or performer in a simple arts work (cartoon, song, dance) communicates an emotion through their face, voice or movement.
width.typical: Exploring how facial expressions, gestures, movement and voice communicate emotions and feelings across a range of arts forms — portraits, cartoons, songs, chants, dances from different times and cultures.
wider: Explore how illustrations and images in picture books communicate mood, character, and narrative without words
Compare how the same emotion (e.g. joy, sadness) is communicated differently across two different arts forms or cultural contexts

modes.reason: Students need language and observational frames to read arts works — prompt with 'How do you know they are happy/sad?', 'What does the dancer do to show that?'. Viewpoints-style questions scaffold the looking.

nodes.label: Arts bring people together
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that arts experiences — including dances, songs and celebrations — bring people together and have meaning for communities.
criteria: Student can name or describe an arts experience that brings people together
Student can say something about why the arts experience is meaningful for the people involved

width.minimum: Identifying at least one arts experience that brings people together — a school song, a celebration dance, a community performance.
width.typical: Identifying social and cultural dances, songs and performances that have meaning for communities — including celebrations, ceremonies and shared cultural practices — and sharing observations about who participates and why.
wider: Learn a social or cultural dance that has meaning for a specific community, observing relevant protocols
Explore First Nations Australian dances used in ceremonies or community events — discussing how they connect people to Culture and Country/Place

modes.reason: Students understand 'community' most concretely when exploring arts practices from communities they recognise — their own family traditions, school events, local events. Broadening context builds genuine understanding.

descriptors.title: Share arts works with audiences
descriptors.description: share their arts works with audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students have created simple movement sequences and arts works communicating personal ideas (AC9ADAFC01). They have some experience of physical play and movement exploration (AC9ADAFD01).
descriptors.endpoint: Students share their arts works — including movement and dance — with audiences.
elaborations: sharing artworks with the class via a gallery or performance walk
performing songs, soundscapes or chants/raps using music skills
taking images of class arts events and creating an image sequence to document the occasion
talking about ideas such as themes, processes, or features of the work
presenting retellings of stories to peers through dramatic play using repurposed objects or puppets
performing movement/dance sequences created for other groups and introducing the work
using digital devices to record arts explorations

nodes.label: Being an audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate as an attentive audience for peers' arts works — watching, noticing, and responding.
criteria: Student watches a peer's work with sustained attention
Student uses at least one positive, specific comment about a peer's work

width.minimum: Participating as audience for at least one class sharing event; using positive language to comment on a peer's work.
width.typical: Participating in class gallery or performance walks; observing peers' works with attention; using positive language to identify features — shapes, movements, patterns — and sharing observations with peers and teachers.
wider: Take and curate digital images of class arts events (with permission), sequencing them to document the occasion
Respond to peers' work through a different arts form — e.g. drawing a response image or creating a sound to accompany a movement

modes.reason: Students need repeated practice as audience members to build observational vocabulary and respectful viewing habits. Multiple sharing events across the year build this repertoire.

nodes.label: Sharing with an audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present a movement sequence or arts work to an audience of peers and/or teachers, communicating their idea through performance.
criteria: Student presents a movement sequence or arts work to at least a small audience of peers
Student can say something about their work when asked — what it is about, or what they enjoyed making
nodes.hinge_reason: Sharing with an audience is the completing act of the creative cycle at Foundation — students who have not experienced presenting their work have not yet closed the loop between making and communicating. This is the foundation for all subsequent Presenting strand standards.

width.minimum: Presenting a movement/dance sequence they have created to the class — with a brief explanation of what their work is about.
width.typical: Performing or presenting arts works — movement sequences, songs, soundscapes, dramatic play — to peers; introducing the work by describing a favourite moment, explaining the idea, or responding to teacher questions about the work.
wider: Use a digital device to record their movement/arts exploration, creating an image sequence or video to share
Perform a movement/dance sequence created collaboratively with a peer or small group, introducing the shared work

modes.reason: Presenting integrates all prior work — idea, movement vocabulary, sequencing — into a communicative act. Frame sharing as purposeful communication: 'What do you want your audience to see?', 'What will you tell them about your work?'

descriptors.title: Create arts works that communicate ideas
descriptors.description: create arts works that communicate ideas
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior Drama curriculum. Students bring imaginative play, storytelling through objects and movement, and early experience using voice, gesture and repurposed materials to express ideas.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create arts works — including dramatic play, scenes and puppetry — that communicate ideas drawn from imagination and experience.
elaborations: creating arts works in a range of forms to communicate ideas from lived personal or social experiences
creating works in response to inspiration from sources such as play, imagination, observation, literature, artworks from their cultures and communities
manipulating objects, puppets, 2D images and/or available technologies to create or retell stories
devising a chant/rap that a character could use to communicate a health or sustainability message
repurposing materials and objects as starting points for imagining and developing scenes and scenarios
considering characters and situations associated with a story and re-imagining them

nodes.label: Ideas from imagination and experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify an idea from play, a story or personal experience to express through making.
criteria: Student can name or show (through action or words) what their drama or artwork is about
Student's making has a recognisable intent — it is not purely random activity
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a communicative intent — even a simple one — students produce activity rather than art-making; the next node (choosing ways to express the idea) has no anchor.

width.minimum: One example: a student names or shows what their dramatic play or object manipulation is about.
width.typical: Students draw on stories, characters or personal experience to identify what they want to make and communicate; they can describe their idea simply to a partner or teacher.
wider: Students explore multiple potential ideas across different starting points (e.g. a story, an object, a place) before choosing one to develop
Students ask 'what if' questions to extend a familiar story into a new scenario

modes.reason: Use teacher-in-role or guided questioning ('What's happening? What happens next?') to help students find and name an idea before they begin making.
Offer a range of imaginative entry points — objects, boxes, puppets, images — so students who don't connect with story-based prompts can engage through material play.

nodes.label: Choosing ways to express the idea
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and use at least one mode (movement, voice, object/puppet, image) to express their idea.
criteria: Student uses at least one mode (voice, movement, object, or image) in a way that communicates their idea to a viewer
Student can explain or show what their chosen mode is doing in the piece

width.minimum: One mode used intentionally: e.g. student uses a puppet to retell a story, or uses movement/voice to show a character.
width.typical: Students experiment with using voice, movement, objects or repurposed materials to express their idea; they try more than one approach and choose one that communicates their intent.
wider: Students combine two modes (e.g. voice and movement, or puppet and voice-over) in the same piece
Students explore how digital devices (e.g. recording voice) can extend how they share an idea

modes.reason: Provide a range of materials, props and modes for students to try; encourage experimentation without locking in a single approach early.

nodes.label: Making and communicating
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a simple arts work — scene, puppetry sequence, or dramatic play — that communicates an identifiable idea.
criteria: Student creates a piece in which an idea is communicated through at least one arts mode
A peer or teacher can identify the idea without needing the student to fully explain it
Student can describe one thing they did to communicate their idea

width.minimum: A short, coherent piece (even 30–60 seconds) in which the idea is legible to another person without full explanation.
width.typical: Students create a scene, puppet sequence, chant, or dramatic play using repurposed materials or props; the piece has a recognisable beginning, moment of action, and ending; a peer or teacher can identify the idea being communicated.
wider: Students create a piece that responds to a specific question or problem ('What message could a character send?', 'What happens in this space?')
Students create a work drawing on stories from their cultural community or family experience
Students use digital capture (photo sequence, voice recording) to document and share their making

modes.reason: This is the integration point — idea, mode and making come together. Teacher role is to scaffold coherence: 'What is this piece about? What do you want someone watching to think or feel?'

descriptors.title: Discover possibilities and develop ideas
descriptors.description: use play, imagination, arts knowledge, processes and/or skills to discover possibilities and develop ideas
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior Drama curriculum. Students bring exploratory play using body, voice and materials; early curiosity about imaginative scenarios.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use play, imagination and available arts skills and materials to discover possibilities and develop ideas for arts-making.
elaborations: playing with the tactile qualities of a range of materials and exploring how they feel to develop ideas
imagining how characters in a story might dress or move, and making still or moving images
playing games to develop subject-specific practices; taking on the point of view of a fictional character
responding to emotions in music and using movement to share their response
exploring their speaking and singing voices and discovering ways to use them to communicate ideas and feelings
improvising movements to explain the steps in a process, then capturing images to document it

nodes.label: Exploring through play and materials
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use play — with materials, voice, or movement — to discover possible ideas or actions.
criteria: Student engages in purposeful exploration with at least one mode (materials, voice, or movement)
Student notices and can name or show something they discovered through play
nodes.hinge_reason: If students are not yet engaging in exploratory play — just watching or randomly handling materials — they have no raw material from which to develop ideas; the 'develop ideas' move collapses.

width.minimum: Student engages in purposeful exploration: trying out a material, voice quality, or movement to see what it might express.
width.typical: Students use a range of materials (rough/smooth textures, objects, clothing items) and modes (voice, movement, gesture) in open-ended exploration; they notice and name something they discover.
wider: Students respond to music or soundscapes through movement, discovering expressive possibilities in their body
Students explore how geometric shapes suggest movement or character — improvising actions that trace or embody a shape

modes.reason: Offer varied entry points: sound, texture, image, movement. Students who don't engage with one mode often connect strongly with another — breadth of invitation is the remedy here.

nodes.label: Developing an idea from exploration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can extend an initial discovery into a developing idea — asking 'what if?' or 'what next?' to push the play further.
criteria: Student makes at least one variation or extension on an initial discovery
Student can describe or show what they were exploring and one thing they tried

width.minimum: Student makes at least one 'what if?' move — e.g. changes a voice quality, adds a movement, or repurposes a material in a new way.
width.typical: Students extend their exploratory play by imagining characters, situations or possibilities ('What would happen if...?'); they try at least two variations and choose one to develop further.
wider: Students use inquiry questions about a story or image ('What is happening? What will happen next?') to generate new imaginative directions
Students document a step in their making process using a digital photo or drawing, creating a simple record of how the idea developed
Students collaborate with a partner to build on each other's ideas in dramatic play

modes.reason: Teacher prompts ('What else could happen?', 'What if your character could fly?') scaffold the move from random play to intentional idea-development.

descriptors.title: Arts importance for communities
descriptors.description: explore how and why the arts are important for people and communities
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior Drama curriculum. Students have personal experience of arts in their lives — songs, stories, performances — but have not yet been prompted to consider why people make and share arts works.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how and why the arts — including drama — are important for people and communities.
elaborations: identifying artworks and experiences in their lives, such as songs, dances, drama, animations, computer games or public art
singing songs used for celebrations such as school songs, anthems, sports teams' songs, birthday songs
exploring how illustrations/images in a text help communicate narrative or information
listening to First Nations Australians talk about the importance of the arts for connecting to people, culture and Country/Place

nodes.label: Noticing arts in life and community
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify arts works they have experienced in their lives and describe what they noticed.
criteria: Student names at least one arts experience from their own life
Student can say something (however simple) about what they noticed or felt
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot yet identify or recall an arts experience, they have no grounded example from which to explore the 'why'; the second node — understanding purpose and meaning — cannot proceed without a concrete referent.

width.minimum: Student names at least one arts experience from their life (song, story, dance, game) and says something about it.
width.typical: Students identify arts works and experiences from school, home and community (songs, animations, dances, drama); they share ideas and feelings about those works with peers and teachers.
wider: Students explore arts from different cultures in their community — including cultural dances, songs or stories — noticing how these carry different meanings for different people

Students engage with First Nations Australians' perspectives on why the arts matter for connecting to people, culture and Country/Place, using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians

modes.reason: Cast the net widely: songs, animations, games, performances at community events all count. Students who don't recognise formal theatre often strongly identify with games or songs — breadth of examples makes this accessible to all.

nodes.label: Why arts matter for people and communities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain a simple reason why an arts work was made or is important to people.
criteria: Student gives at least one reason why an arts work or experience is important to people
Student connects the reason to a specific example from their experience

width.minimum: Student gives one reason for why a particular arts work exists or matters ('it tells a story', 'it's for celebrations', 'it teaches us something').
width.typical: Students discuss why arts works are created and shared — for celebrations, for communication, to express feelings, to teach — and connect these purposes to specific examples they have encountered.
wider: Students explore how drama and storytelling are used in their local First Nations community context to carry cultural knowledge and connection to Country/Place
Students compare why a familiar community arts event (e.g. a school performance, cultural celebration) exists and what it means to the people involved

modes.reason: Use concrete examples and guided questions ('Why do you think people made this?', 'What did it make people feel?') to scaffold simple causal reasoning about purpose.

descriptors.title: Share arts works with audiences
descriptors.description: share their arts works with audiences
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior Drama curriculum. Students have experience of sharing informally in play contexts but have not yet participated in purposeful sharing of arts works with an audience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share their arts works — dramatic play, scenes, puppetry — with an audience, and respond to questions about their work.
elaborations: sharing artworks with the class via a 'gallery' or 'performance walk'
talking about ideas, themes, processes and features of the work
presenting retellings of stories to peers through dramatic play using repurposed objects, toys or puppets
sharing work with teacher and responding to questions about the work
performing movement/dance sequences for other groups and introducing the work
using digital devices to record and curate arts explorations

nodes.label: What sharing means — audience and maker roles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish the role of maker/performer from the role of audience, and understand that sharing involves communication.
criteria: Student can take on both maker and audience roles appropriately in an informal sharing context
Student can name one thing they noticed or liked in a peer's work
nodes.hinge_reason: If students don't yet understand the maker/audience relationship, they cannot engage purposefully with sharing — they perform without awareness of an audience, or cannot attend as an audience member; the sharing event has no communicative dimension.

width.minimum: Student understands that some people make/perform and others watch, and behaves appropriately as both.
width.typical: Students participate in informal sharing contexts (gallery walks, performance walks); they use positive language to comment on peers' works, identifying a feature or difference they noticed.
wider: Students explore different kinds of sharing — live performance, digital recording, gallery display — and discuss what changes for the audience in each mode
Students listen to and respond to an explanation from a peer-maker: 'What is going on in your work? Tell me the story.'

modes.reason: Explicitly name and model the two roles before sharing events; use simple language ('your job as audience is to look and listen, your job as maker is to show your idea').

nodes.label: Sharing and talking about the work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share an arts work with an audience and describe at least one feature or decision in their work when asked.
criteria: Student shares an arts work in an informal setting with at least one other person as audience
Student responds to at least one question about their work, describing a feature or decision they made
Student demonstrates attentive audience behaviour when watching a peer's work

width.minimum: Student shares a piece (however short) with at least one other person watching, and can answer a simple question about it ('What is happening in your work?').
width.typical: Students present their work to peers; they respond to teacher questions about themes, materials, processes or important features of the work; they use positive language about peers' work.
wider: Students create a simple introduction for their work — describing their favourite moment or explaining why they chose a particular movement or object
Students use a digital device to capture their sharing (with permission) and view the recording, noticing what they communicated
Students retell a story through dramatic play to a class audience using repurposed objects or puppets they have made

modes.reason: Sharing integrates all prior making. Teacher scaffolds reflection: 'What did you want your audience to see? What did you enjoy making?'

descriptors.title: Create arts works that communicate ideas
descriptors.description: create arts works that communicate ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students have experience with play and exploration of materials, voice, movement and digital devices in early childhood settings. They can express ideas through drawing, movement and role play but have not yet deliberately used media technologies to communicate ideas to an audience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create arts works using available materials, technologies or tools that communicate a recognisable idea from personal or social experience.
elaborations: creating arts works in a range of forms to communicate ideas from lived personal or social experiences; for example, creating a dance or scenes showing favourite activities such as games; using digital devices to record their peers playing a game and creating a voice-over that describes what's happening; composing a song or chant about a favourite food or activity; drawing a home scene of people and animals

creating works in response to inspiration from sources such as play, imagination, observation, literature, artworks from their cultures and communities or arts knowledge and skill development activities
extending and varying known songs, chants or rhymes; for example, changing words, interpreting without using voice, adding movements/actions or improvising rhythm patterns as accompaniment
manipulating objects, puppets, 2D images and/or available technologies to create or retell stories

devising a chant/rap that a character from an animated series, a text or a fictional hero could use to communicate a health or sustainability message or to learn the steps in a process; recording the chant/rap using an available digital device and sharing live or via a school-managed space such as a learning management system

repurposing materials and objects such as clothing or packing boxes as starting points for imagining and developing scenes and scenarios; for example, using packing boxes to create an imagined environment or vehicle

considering as a class the characters and situations associated with a story and then re-imagining them by asking questions of the story, such as "What's up?", "What happens next?" or "What else might/could happen?" to support the development of their own socio-dramatic or miniature worlds play

nodes.label: Idea to arts form
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a personal or social idea and choose a form (image, sound, movement, story) to communicate it.
criteria: Student can name an idea from their own life or experience they want to communicate
Student can identify at least one form (captured image, voice recording, or object play) that could communicate that idea
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot connect a personal idea to a media form, subsequent making decisions are arbitrary — they cannot make intentional choices about materials, sequencing or communication.

width.minimum: Describe one personal idea and identify one form that could be used to communicate it.
width.typical: Explore multiple forms (captured images, voice recording, movement, puppet play) and explain how each could communicate the same idea differently.
wider: Use digital devices (tablet, camera) to explore how the same idea looks different when captured versus drawn versus acted out
Respond to literature or artworks from own cultural community as a starting point — identifying what idea they want to communicate and why

modes.reason: Expose students to multiple forms early — seeing their own idea communicated across image, sound and movement helps them understand that form is a choice, not a default.

nodes.label: Making and constructing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use available materials or technologies to make an arts work that embodies their idea.
criteria: Student creates an arts work using at least one material or technology
Student can describe what their work communicates or what it is about

width.minimum: Create one arts work (e.g. a sequence of captured images, a voice-over recording, a puppet retelling) using at least one available material or technology.
width.typical: Create arts works across two or more forms or materials — combining images, sounds, objects or digital tools to communicate ideas; manipulate choices (which images to keep, how to sequence events, which sounds to add).
wider: Repurpose everyday materials (boxes, clothing) as environments or characters, and document the creation using a digital device
Devise and record a chant or rap on a digital device that communicates a message or retells a story — sharing via a school-managed platform
Explore claymation or stop-motion animation by manipulating objects and capturing a sequence of images

modes.reason: The making process at Foundation integrates idea, material and tool — support students in connecting their intended communication with the choices they make during construction rather than treating making as separate from meaning.
Vary the making modalities — digital capture, voice, object manipulation, repurposed materials — so students who are ready encounter the full diversity of making contexts available at Foundation.

nodes.label: Communicating to an audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present or share their arts work and explain what idea it communicates.
criteria: Student shares their arts work with at least one other person
Student can articulate what idea their work communicates when asked

width.minimum: Share one arts work with a teacher or small group and respond to 'What is your work about?' with a recognisable connection to their original idea.
width.typical: Share arts works with peers and teacher; describe the idea communicated and what was enjoyable about making it; extend or vary a familiar form (changing words, adding actions) to communicate a new idea.
wider: Share a work created from a health, sustainability or process message — presenting it live or via a school-managed space and explaining why the message matters
Use questions about the story ('What happens next?', 'What else could happen?') to extend and develop the work for a second audience

modes.reason: Sharing and communicating closes the making loop — students connect their original idea to what the audience perceives. This is the integration moment: idea → making → audience response.

descriptors.strand: Media arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Discover possibilities and develop ideas
descriptors.description: use play, imagination, arts knowledge, processes and/or skills to discover possibilities and develop ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students have experience with free play and exploration of materials, voice, movement and basic digital devices. They have not yet deliberately used play as a strategy for discovering creative possibilities in media arts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use play, imagination and arts processes to discover new possibilities and develop ideas for media arts works.
elaborations: playing with the tactile qualities of a range of materials (rough, smooth, spikey, gooey) and exploring how they feel about these qualities to develop ideas for a visual artwork, dance or soundscape
imagining how the characters in a story they are reading might dress or move, and making still or moving images to communicate ideas about the characters
identifying and describing shapes, colours and lines they observe in their environment and exploring ways to use these shapes creatively

playing games to develop subject-specific practices such as pitch, beat and/or rhythm recognition; exploring ways that body parts, zones and bases can be moved safely and expressively; taking on the point of view of a fictional character in dramatic play
responding to the emotions they experience while listening to different pieces of music and using movement to share their response

improvising rhythmic patterns for clapping or stamping, or inventing new movements for familiar action songs, and interpreting these visually using elements of art/design such as shapes, lines and/or colours
exploring their speaking and singing voices and discovering ways they can use their voices/vocalisation to communicate ideas and feelings

improvising movements to explain the steps in a process, and then using a camera to capture a series of images/photographic story that can be displayed in the classroom to remind everybody about the process

nodes.label: Playing to discover
nodes.checkpoint: Students can engage in purposeful play with materials, movement, voice or technology and notice what happens — identifying at least one discovery or surprise.
criteria: Student can describe or demonstrate something they discovered while playing with a material, tool or technology
Student can name at least one way this discovery could be used to communicate an idea
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot engage in purposeful discovery through play, the idea-development strand of this standard collapses — play is the primary mechanism for generating ideas at Foundation level.

width.minimum: Engage with one material, movement quality, or technology in free play — identify one thing they discovered or that surprised them.
width.typical: Explore multiple materials and technologies through play (tactile materials, camera, voice, movement); respond to the emotions or discoveries that arise; describe how different qualities (rough, smooth, loud, quiet) could be used to communicate ideas.
wider: Play with the tactile qualities of materials and use movement, voice or digital tools to embody the qualities discovered — connecting sensory exploration to idea generation
Respond to music through movement — using scarves, drawing or digital capture to document the response and discussing how the music changed what was discovered

modes.reason: Vary the play contexts — tactile materials, digital tools, voice, movement — to ensure students discover possibilities across the full range of media arts modalities available at Foundation.

nodes.label: Imagining possibilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use imagination to extend what they observe or know — asking 'what if?' questions to develop new ideas for arts works.
criteria: Student can use at least one imagining strategy to extend a story, character or situation beyond what was given
Student can describe the new possibility they imagined

width.minimum: Use at least one imagining strategy (asking 'What happens next?', taking the point of view of a character, or imagining an environment) to extend an observed story or situation.
width.typical: Use imagination to explore how characters in stories might look, move or speak; make still or moving images to communicate ideas about characters; ask questions of stories to develop new scenarios; improvise rhythms, movements or melodies and interpret them visually.
wider: Imagine and trial ways to use geometric and organic shapes creatively — collage, movement traces of shapes, or melodies that follow a shape's contour; exploring multiple representations of the same shape
Use a camera to document a process (e.g. mixing colours, building a structure) — sequence and annotate the images as a record of imaginative problem-solving
Explore speaking and singing voices to discover new ways to communicate ideas and feelings — experimenting with pitch, volume, rhythm and tone

modes.reason: Build students' repertoire of imagining strategies — 'What happens next?', character perspective, environment transformation. A wider repertoire means more generative possibilities when making.

nodes.label: Developing and documenting ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can translate discoveries from play and imagination into a developing idea for an arts work — using a tool, material or device to record or represent the idea.
criteria: Student creates or captures something that represents an idea developed through play or imagination
Student can explain the connection between their play/exploration and the developing idea

width.minimum: Use one tool or material to document or represent a developing idea (e.g. capture images that show steps in a process, draw a character imagined during play, record a voice improvisation).
width.typical: Use multiple tools and documentation strategies to develop ideas across sessions — capture image sequences of processes, draw from imaginative play, improvise and record rhythmic patterns; describe how the documentation connects to their original discovery or imaginative exploration.
wider: Improvise movement sequences to explain steps in a process, then use a camera to capture an image story that can be displayed to remind others about the process
Improvise rhythmic patterns and interpret them visually using drawing, collage or digital image-making — cross-modal translation as an idea development strategy

modes.reason: Documenting ideas integrates the play/discovery phase with the making phase — support students in connecting what they found through play to a concrete representation that others can see or hear.

descriptors.title: Arts importance for communities
descriptors.description: explore how and why the arts are important for people and communities
descriptors.knowledge: Students have personal experience of arts events (songs at celebrations, animations, dances) but have not yet consciously reflected on why the arts matter to communities or what role they play.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify arts works and experiences from their lives and explain how they are important for people and communities.
elaborations: exploring how facial expressions, gestures and other ways of moving, and using voice or language, can communicate emotions and feelings in arts works
identifying and/or learning social or cultural dances that have meaning for people and communities, taking care to observe relevant protocols
using dramatic play to explore ideas or understandings they observe or perceive in a text or image

identifying arts works and experiences in their lives, such as songs they sing, dances or drama they watch or perform, animations, computer games or music videos, public art, 2D, 3D or screen-based works they encounter at school or in community settings
singing songs that are used for celebrations, such as school songs, anthems, sports teams' songs, birthday songs
exploring how illustrations/images in a text help to communicate narrative or information about characters or settings and/or mood

listening to First Nations Australians talk about the importance of the arts for connecting to people, culture and Country/Place; for example, using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians

nodes.label: Arts in my life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify at least two types of arts works or experiences from their own life or community (e.g. a song, a dance, a cartoon, a game, public art).
criteria: Student can name at least two different arts works or experiences from their own life
Student can describe where or when they encounter each one
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot identify arts works in their own lives, they have no concrete examples to connect to the 'why arts matter' question — subsequent discussion of community importance has no grounding.

width.minimum: Name and briefly describe two arts experiences from their own life — school-based and community-based (e.g. birthday songs and a TV animation).
width.typical: Identify and describe a range of arts works and experiences encountered at school, home and in the community — songs, dances, animations, computer games, public art, performances; share ideas and feelings about these works with peers and teachers.
wider: Identify arts works encountered in digital and screen contexts (computer games, music videos, animations) and compare how these feel different from live performances or physical artworks
Listen to First Nations Australians talk about the importance of arts for connecting to people, culture and Country/Place — using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians

modes.reason: Ensure students encounter arts examples from multiple contexts — digital/screen, live performance, community celebration, cultural ceremony — so their repertoire of 'what counts as arts' is broad enough to ground later exploration.

nodes.label: How arts communicate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how arts works communicate feelings, ideas or cultural knowledge — using examples they have encountered.
criteria: Student can identify what an arts work is communicating (a feeling, a story, a message)
Student can describe at least one feature of the work that communicates this (a sound, an image, a gesture)

width.minimum: Describe one way an arts work communicates something — e.g. how a character's face shows an emotion, how a song makes them feel, how images in a book tell a story.
width.typical: Explore how facial expressions, gestures, movement, voice and language communicate emotions in arts works; describe how illustrations in books communicate character, setting and mood; identify how songs used at celebrations communicate shared meaning or purpose.
wider: Explore how illustrations and images in picture books or screen texts communicate narrative, character and mood — connecting arts exploration to literacy and building vocabulary for describing how arts communicate
Compare how a favourite song used at a celebration (birthday, sports, school event) communicates differently to the same song heard without context — discussing what the occasion adds to the meaning

modes.reason: Students benefit from explicit scaffolding to move from 'this makes me feel...' to 'this communicates... because...'. Structured questioning (What does this face tell you? How does the music change?) builds the reasoning habit.

nodes.label: Why arts matter to communities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why an arts work matters to a group of people — connecting the work to its community purpose.
criteria: Student can explain why a specific arts work matters to a group of people
Student can connect an arts work to its community or cultural purpose

width.minimum: Explain one reason why a specific arts work matters to a community (e.g. 'We sing the birthday song because it makes everyone feel special on their birthday').
width.typical: Discuss why different arts works are important to different groups — school songs, cultural dances, animations that teach content; identify how arts works connect people and share cultural knowledge; engage with examples of First Nations Australians explaining the importance of arts for culture and Country.
wider: Listen to and discuss stories shared by First Nations Australians about the importance of arts for connecting to people, culture and Country/Place — and compare this to how arts works matter in students' own communities
Identify social or cultural dances that have meaning for people and communities (taking care to observe protocols) — exploring why these dances are performed and what is lost if they are not

modes.reason: This node integrates identification of arts works with understanding of their community function — connect students' concrete examples from Node 1 to the 'why it matters' question.

descriptors.title: Share arts works with audiences
descriptors.description: share their arts works with audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students have experience sharing work informally with teachers during play or activity time, but have not yet engaged in deliberate presentation to an audience — where the relationship between maker and viewer is conscious and considered.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share arts works with an audience and engage with that audience's responses.
elaborations: sharing their artworks with the class via a "gallery" or "performance walk"
performing songs, soundscapes or chants/raps, using music skills they have learnt and practised
taking images of class arts events (with permission from the people involved), creating an image sequence to document the occasion, and adding sound
talking about ideas such as themes, processes used to make the work, or features of the work such as patterns, pathways or lines
presenting retellings of stories to peers; for example, through dramatic play using repurposed objects, toys or puppets they have made
sharing their work with their teacher and responding to questions such as "What is going on in your work?", "Tell me the story of what is happening?", "What did you enjoy about making this work?"
performing movement/dance sequences they have created for other groups in their class
using digital devices to record their arts explorations; for example, curating (selecting, ordering) a sequence of digital images (photos) to show the steps in a process

nodes.label: Preparing to share
nodes.checkpoint: Students can prepare a work to share — selecting what to present and thinking about who will see or hear it.
criteria: Student can identify what work they will share and who their audience is
Student has made at least one preparation choice (what to include, how to introduce it)

width.minimum: Choose one arts work to share and identify the audience (teacher, small group, or class).
width.typical: Select and sequence arts work for sharing; practise presenting a performance or retelling; use digital devices to curate or document work before sharing; prepare an introduction or description of the work.
wider: Curate (select and order) a sequence of digital images to document steps in an arts process — adding commentary about what each step communicates or what was discovered
Practise a performance (song, soundscape, story retelling) using skills learnt, such as matching starting pitch or staying in time with a group

modes.reason: The curation and selection step is often skipped at Foundation — students benefit from deliberate practice in choosing what to present, as this builds the habit of audience awareness that underpins all future presenting work.

nodes.label: Presenting to an audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share an arts work with an audience and explain what it communicates or how it was made.
criteria: Student shares their arts work with at least one other person or group
Student responds to at least one question about their work with a recognisable connection to the work's ideas or process
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot present a work and engage with an audience's response at Foundation, the feedback loop between making and audience that underlies all subsequent arts learning does not form.

width.minimum: Share one arts work with a teacher or small group; respond to at least one question (e.g. 'What is going on in your work?') with a description connected to the work.
width.typical: Present arts works to peers in gallery, performance or digital formats; use positive language to describe own and others' works; explain themes, processes or features when asked; talk about what was enjoyed during making.
wider: Participate in a class gallery or performance walk — comment on peers' works using observational language (similarities, differences, use of materials, patterns, pathways, lines)
Present a story retelling to another class or group (through dramatic play, puppets or digital capture) — introduce the work and describe favourite moments
Present a performance of a song, soundscape or chant/rap — introduce it and explain the choices made during the creation

modes.reason: Vary the presentation contexts — gallery walk, live performance, digital sharing, small group retelling — so students encounter multiple audience types and relationships, not only teacher-directed sharing.

nodes.label: Responding to audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can engage with an audience's response to their work — listening to feedback and reflecting on what others noticed or felt.
criteria: Student can engage with at least one audience response (question or comment) about their work
Student can describe at least one thing the audience noticed or responded to

width.minimum: Listen to at least one comment or question from an audience about their work and respond to it — either elaborating, agreeing or explaining further.
width.typical: Engage with audience responses in gallery, performance or sharing contexts; use positive language when commenting on others' work; reflect on what features of their work others noticed; describe what they enjoyed about making and sharing the work.
wider: Use digital documentation (photos or video of the sharing event) to revisit and reflect on the audience response — describing what the audience noticed and what was surprising
Participate in a gallery walk as both maker and audience member — practising both presenting and responding with constructive, observational language

modes.reason: Responding to audience closes the presenting cycle — connecting making, presenting and the feedback loop. Support students in treating audience response as information about communication, not just approval or disapproval.

descriptors.title: Create works that communicate ideas
descriptors.description: create arts works that communicate ideas
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior arts learning assumed. Students bring play, curiosity and informal experience with voice, movement and sound from early childhood. This is their first formal encounter with creating arts works within a school context.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create arts works in at least one form that communicate ideas from personal experience, using deliberate choices about how the work will look, sound or feel.
elaborations: creating arts works in a range of forms to communicate ideas from lived personal or social experiences; for example, composing a song or chant about a favourite food or activity
creating works in response to inspiration from sources such as play, imagination, observation, literature, artworks from their cultures and communities
extending and varying known songs, chants or rhymes; for example, changing words, interpreting without using voice, adding movements/actions or improvising rhythm patterns as accompaniment
manipulating objects, puppets, 2D images and/or available technologies to create or retell stories
devising a chant/rap to communicate a health or sustainability message; recording using an available digital device
repurposing materials and objects as starting points for imagining and developing scenes and scenarios

nodes.label: Ideas from experience as starting points
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a personal experience or idea as the starting point for an arts work and describe what they want to communicate.
criteria: Can name one personal experience or idea they want to communicate in their arts work
Can describe (in any form — drawing, speaking, gesturing) what they want the work to show or express
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify a personal idea or intent before making will produce work without communicative purpose. The next phase — making deliberate choices in a form — requires a starting intention. Without it, students move through the activity without the central act of the descriptor being engaged.

width.minimum: Identify one personal experience (e.g. a favourite activity or a feeling) and describe what they want to show or express.
width.typical: Draw on personal or social experiences, play, imagination or observation as starting points; name what they want to communicate — e.g. 'I want to show how running feels' or 'I want to tell the story of my pet.'
wider: Draw on literature, artworks or stories from their culture as starting points — compare how their idea connects to or differs from the source
Use dramatic play scenarios as starting points for both musical and visual ideas — ask 'What could the sound of this story be?'

modes.reason: Use questioning to help students articulate their starting idea before they begin making — 'What do you want to show?', 'Who is this for?', 'What should people feel when they see/hear it?' This scaffolds the intent-setting that the rest of the making depends on.

nodes.label: Choosing an arts form
nodes.checkpoint: Students can choose an arts form (voice/music, movement, drawing, dramatic play) that suits the idea they want to communicate.
criteria: Attempts to create in at least one arts form with a recognisable connection to their intended idea
Can say something about why they chose that form or what it shows about their idea

width.minimum: Attempt to create in at least one arts form (e.g. a chant, a drawing, or a movement sequence) with a connection to their intended idea.
width.typical: Try communicating an idea across two or more arts forms; notice how each form communicates differently — e.g. a chant communicates rhythm and energy while a drawing communicates visual detail.
wider: Compare how the same idea (e.g. 'the ocean') could be communicated through voice/sound vs movement vs image — make a choice and explain it
Use digital devices (e.g. camera or recording app) to capture and compare attempts in different forms

modes.reason: Students need exposure to the full range of arts forms available to them before they can make informed choices. Ensuring students have tried voice/sound, movement and image-making contexts builds the repertoire from which genuine choice becomes possible.

nodes.label: Making deliberate choices in the work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make at least one deliberate decision during the making process (e.g. changing a word, adding a movement, choosing a sound) and connect it to their communicative intent.
criteria: Makes at least one deliberate decision during the making process (not just following a template)
Can describe the decision and connect it in some way to what they wanted to communicate
nodes.hinge_reason: Deliberate choice-making — however simple — is the difference between executing an activity and making an arts work. If students do not practise connecting decisions to intent at Foundation, the later demands of composition and performance (which require iterative decision-making) begin without this foundational habit established.

width.minimum: Make one deliberate change or decision during the making process; describe why they made it.
width.typical: Extend and vary known songs, chants or rhymes through deliberate choices (changing words, adding movements, improvising accompaniments); use play and experimentation to try options and select preferred ones.
wider: Use an available digital device to record work in progress, listen back and make a decision about what to change or keep
Devise a chant or rap with a specific message in mind — make deliberate decisions about rhythm and words to carry the message

modes.reason: Pause during making to ask simple reflective questions: 'Why did you put that there?', 'What would happen if you changed it?', 'Does it still show your idea?' These questions build the habit of connecting decisions to intent.

nodes.label: Completing and sharing a work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can complete a simple arts work that communicates an intended idea and share it with peers or teacher.
criteria: Produces a completed arts work (in any form) that communicates a recognisable idea
Can talk about what the work is meant to show or express when asked

width.minimum: Complete an arts work (in any form) that has a recognisable communicative intent; share it with at least one other person.
width.typical: Complete arts works across two or more forms; share them via a gallery walk, informal performance, or digital capture; respond to questions about the work such as 'What is happening in your work?' or 'What did you want to show?'
wider: Create a multi-form work (e.g. a chant combined with a drawing) that communicates one idea across two forms simultaneously
Use a digital device to record and share a composed chant or soundscape — curate a simple image sequence to accompany it

modes.reason: This node is where intent, form choice and deliberate decisions come together in a finished, sharable work. The teaching investment is in supporting students to see their work as complete and communicating — not just as an activity they did.

descriptors.title: Discover possibilities and develop ideas
descriptors.description: use play, imagination, arts knowledge, processes and/or skills to discover possibilities and develop ideas
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior arts learning assumed. Students bring informal experience with play, voice and movement from early childhood. This is their first formal encounter with arts skill-development in a school context.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use play, imagination and at least one arts process or skill to discover possibilities and develop ideas across at least one arts form.
elaborations: playing with the tactile qualities of a range of materials and exploring how they feel to develop ideas for a soundscape or visual artwork
playing games to develop subject-specific practices such as pitch, beat and/or rhythm recognition
responding to the emotions they experience while listening to different pieces of music and using movement to share their response
improvising rhythmic patterns for clapping or stamping and interpreting these visually using elements of art/design such as shapes, lines and/or colours
exploring their speaking and singing voices and discovering ways they can use their voices/vocalisation to communicate ideas and feelings
improvising movements to explain the steps in a process, then using a camera to capture a series of images or a photographic story

nodes.label: Exploring through play
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use play as a genuine tool for discovering musical or arts possibilities — trying things out without a fixed endpoint.
criteria: Engages in open-ended play involving sound, voice or movement without requiring a predetermined outcome
Can name one thing they discovered or tried during play
nodes.hinge_reason: If students treat arts activities as instruction-following rather than play-based exploration, they miss the imaginative generativity that underpins the descriptor. Later skill development (including improvisation and composition) depends on students being comfortable with exploratory, non-predetermined making. A class that bypasses play at Foundation arrives at composition without the habits of experimentation it requires.

width.minimum: Engage in at least one open-ended play activity involving sound, voice or movement; identify one discovery or surprise from the play.
width.typical: Use play to explore tactile qualities, voice possibilities, movement options and rhythm patterns across multiple contexts; describe what they discovered and how it might be used in an arts work.
wider: Explore how tactile qualities of materials (rough, smooth, spikey) can be translated into sound or voice — e.g. 'This rough texture sounds like...'
Use dramatic play scenarios to generate musical or movement ideas — ask 'What would the sound of this place/character be?'

modes.reason: Explicitly frame play as productive: 'We're going to try things and see what happens — there's no wrong answer here.' Debrief after play by asking 'What did you discover?' to help students articulate that play generates usable ideas.

nodes.label: Exploring voice and sound
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore their speaking and singing voices and a range of sound sources to discover ways of communicating ideas and feelings.
criteria: Demonstrates at least two distinct ways their voice can sound (e.g. high/low, fast/slow, smooth/rough)
Can connect one vocal quality to an emotion or idea (e.g. 'my quiet voice sounds like someone sleeping')

width.minimum: Explore at least two ways their voice can sound differently (e.g. loud/soft, high/low, smooth/rough); connect one vocal quality to an idea or feeling.
width.typical: Explore speaking voice, singing voice and vocalisation across multiple activities — responding to music through movement, improvising rhythmic clapping patterns, discovering how voice changes in response to different emotions or situations.
wider: Explore sounds from found and environmental objects alongside voice — compare how different sound sources can express similar ideas
Use a camera or recording device to capture voice explorations and listen back — identify discoveries worth keeping

modes.reason: Voice exploration is cumulative — the wider the range of vocal qualities students have tried, the richer their subsequent compositional and performance options. Prioritise breadth of vocal experimentation over accuracy at this stage.

nodes.label: Responding to and interpreting music
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond to music they hear through movement, image-making or vocalisation, and describe one feeling or idea the music gave them.
criteria: Responds to music through at least one mode (movement, image, voice or words)
Can articulate one feeling or idea the music communicated

width.minimum: Listen to a piece of music and respond in one way (e.g. movement, drawing, describing a feeling); share one thing the music made them think or feel.
width.typical: Respond to diverse pieces of music through movement (scarves, gestures), visual image-making (crayons, paint) and voice; describe emotional responses and connect them to features of the music such as tempo or loudness.
wider: Compare responses to two contrasting pieces of music (e.g. fast/loud vs slow/quiet) — discuss what made them different
Use body and voice to embody a character from a story, responding to background music — change response as the music changes

modes.reason: Listening response is richer when students encounter a variety of music — different tempos, moods, cultural origins. Broader exposure builds the listening vocabulary that supports musical decision-making in later composition and performance.

nodes.label: Developing and extending an idea
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a discovered possibility to develop a musical or arts idea — taking one thing they found through play and doing something intentional with it.
criteria: Takes a discovery from play and uses it deliberately in a subsequent arts activity
Can describe the connection between their earlier exploration and what they are now doing intentionally

width.minimum: Take one discovery from play or exploration (a vocal quality, a rhythm, a movement) and use it deliberately in a simple arts activity.
width.typical: Use discoveries from play to develop ideas across multiple forms — improvising new movements for action songs and interpreting them visually; using a discovered rhythm pattern as the basis for a chant; taking a vocal quality and using it to represent a character.
wider: Improvise rhythmic clapping patterns and then represent them visually using shapes and lines — make explicit connections between the sound and the image
Use improvised movement to explain the steps in a process, then capture it as a photographic story with sound commentary

modes.reason: This node integrates play, exploration and skill development into an intentional arts act. The teaching investment is in helping students see the connection: 'You discovered that earlier — now you're using it deliberately.'

descriptors.title: Arts importance for communities
descriptors.description: explore how and why the arts are important for people and communities
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior arts learning assumed. Students bring personal experience of music, song, stories and community celebrations from their family and cultural contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how and why the arts are important for people and communities, and share their own observations and responses.
elaborations: exploring how facial expressions, gestures and other ways of moving, and using voice or language, can communicate emotions and feelings in arts works
identifying and/or learning social or cultural dances that have meaning for people and communities, taking care to observe relevant protocols
identifying arts works and experiences in their lives, such as songs they sing, dances or drama they watch or perform, animations, computer games or music videos
singing songs that are used for celebrations, such as school songs, anthems, sports teams' songs, birthday songs
listening to First Nations Australians talk about the importance of the arts for connecting to People, Culture and Country/Place

nodes.label: Arts in daily life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify arts works and experiences in their own life and describe why they matter to them.
criteria: Can name at least one arts experience from their own life
Can describe why that experience is enjoyable or meaningful to them

width.minimum: Name at least one arts experience from their daily life (e.g. a song they sing, a dance they know, a game with music) and say something about why it is meaningful or enjoyable.
width.typical: Identify arts works and experiences across multiple contexts — songs, dances, drama, animations, games, public art; share preferences and responses; connect personal arts experiences to what they mean for themselves and their family or community.
wider: Compile a class list of songs everyone knows — notice which songs are shared across the class and which are specific to certain families or cultures
Explore how music is used in celebrations the students know (birthday songs, school songs, sporting anthems) and compare their purposes

modes.reason: Students' awareness of arts in their lives varies enormously at Foundation. Broadening the contexts in which they notice arts (home, community, screen, ceremony) builds the experiential base for understanding why arts matter.

nodes.label: How arts communicate emotions and ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how an arts work (e.g. a song, a dance or a drawing) communicates an emotion or idea.
criteria: Can identify one emotion or idea communicated by an arts work
Can describe (simply) one feature of the work that communicates that emotion or idea
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that arts works communicate — that they are intentional acts of meaning-making — is the conceptual foundation for all exploring and responding work in subsequent years. Students who do not grasp this at Foundation approach arts engagement as passive entertainment rather than communication, which limits their capacity to analyse and respond to music in later bands.

width.minimum: Observe one arts work (e.g. a song, a portrait, a dance) and identify one emotion or idea it communicates.
width.typical: Explore how facial expressions, gestures, voice and movement communicate emotions across different arts forms; listen to songs and discuss how the music makes them feel and why; explore how illustrations in picture books communicate mood and character.
wider: Compare how two different songs communicate the same emotion (e.g. joy) using different elements of music — what makes each feel joyful?
Explore how images in a picture book and the music in a song work together or differently to tell the same kind of story

modes.reason: Use guided questioning after listening or watching: 'How did that make you feel?', 'What do you think the singer/dancer/artist wanted to show?', 'How did they do that?' This builds the habit of reading arts works as communications, not just experiences.

nodes.label: Arts as important for communities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe at least one way that an arts work is important for a community — beyond personal enjoyment.
criteria: Can describe one way an arts work is important to a community (e.g. it brings people together, it celebrates something, it tells a story about who we are)
Can give at least one example from a community context beyond their own personal experience

width.minimum: Identify one way an arts work (e.g. a ceremony song, a school anthem, a community celebration) is important to a group of people, not just to themselves personally.
width.typical: Sing songs used for celebrations and discuss why they are used; explore how arts experiences are shared in their school community; listen to First Nations Australians talk about the importance of the arts for connecting to People, Culture and Country/Place.
wider: Investigate how a local cultural event (e.g. a school concert, a community festival) uses music — discuss what it does for the people who participate
Listen to First Nations Australians discuss the role of music and arts in connecting to Country/Place — compare this to how music is used in the students' own community

modes.reason: The concept that arts matter to communities (not just individuals) benefits from encountering multiple community contexts — school, family, cultural, ceremonial. Each new context adds evidence for why the arts have collective importance.

descriptors.title: Share arts works with audiences
descriptors.description: share their arts works with audiences
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior arts learning assumed. Students bring informal experience with showing things to others (e.g. showing a drawing to a parent). Formal experience of sharing arts works with an audience is new.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share their arts works with an audience, introduce what the work is about, and respond to questions or comments about it.
elaborations: sharing their artworks with the class via a 'gallery' or 'performance walk'
performing songs, soundscapes or chants/raps, using music skills they have learnt and practised
taking images of class arts events, creating an image sequence to document the occasion, and adding sound
talking about ideas such as themes, processes used to make the work, or features of the work
presenting retellings of stories to peers through dramatic play using repurposed objects, toys or puppets
using digital devices to record their arts explorations; curating a sequence of digital images to show the steps in a process

nodes.label: What it means to have an audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand that sharing arts works involves an audience with a role to play — watching, listening and responding.
criteria: Participates appropriately as an audience member (watching/listening during the performance)
Can make at least one specific positive comment about another student's work
