nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that performance involves an audience relationship — not just doing something in front of people — is foundational to all presenting and performing work. Students who see sharing as 'showing and sitting down' do not develop the intentional communication of later performance work. This concept underpins AC9AMU2P01's requirements around staging, introduction and post-performance discussion.

width.minimum: Participate as an audience member during a peer sharing: listen or watch quietly, then make one positive comment about what they noticed.
width.typical: Experience both roles — performer/sharer and audience member; practise using positive language to comment on others' works; understand that the audience's role is to engage with and respond to the work, not just to watch.
wider: Discuss the difference between being an audience at a school performance vs watching a cartoon at home — what does the performer/artist need from each?
Practise responding to an arts work with specific observations (e.g. 'I noticed the chant got faster') rather than only general praise

modes.reason: Explicitly teach the audience role before sharing events: 'When you are the audience, your job is to...' Debrief after sharing: 'What was it like to perform? What was it like to watch?' Build language for responding to arts works.

nodes.label: Introducing and sharing a work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can introduce their arts work to an audience by naming one feature of it, then perform or display it.
criteria: Introduces their arts work with at least one identifying statement before or after sharing
Can respond to one question about their work from the teacher or a peer

width.minimum: Before or after sharing, say one thing about their arts work (e.g. 'This is a chant about running' or 'I made this to show my dog').
width.typical: Introduce works by naming the theme, process or a favourite part; share arts works in at least two formats (e.g. a gallery walk and a performance); respond to teacher questions such as 'What is going on in your work?'
wider: Introduce a performance by telling the audience what you want them to listen for or feel — practise this as a structured sentence before the performance
Take turns as a 'gallery guide' — stand next to their displayed work and explain it to visiting classmates

modes.reason: Students need experience sharing works in multiple formats (gallery, performance, digital) so they develop a repertoire of sharing modes. Each format teaches slightly different performance skills — standing and speaking differs from performing a song differs from pointing to a displayed work.

nodes.label: Performing with music skills
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform a song, soundscape or chant using at least one practised music skill (e.g. matching starting pitch, staying in time with the group, following a simple graphic score).
criteria: Performs a song or chant as part of a group with some awareness of at least one music convention
Attempts to match the group's timing or dynamic level during the performance

width.minimum: Perform a song or chant with the group, demonstrating awareness of at least one music convention (e.g. staying in time, or using singing voice rather than speaking voice).
width.typical: Perform songs, soundscapes or chants using practised skills — matching pitch, staying in time, following an agreed plan or graphic score; use a digital device to document the performance via images or recording.
wider: Follow a graphic score when performing a soundscape — practise reading the score in rehearsal and apply it in performance
Curate a sequence of digital images from a class arts event and add voice narration or soundscape as commentary

modes.reason: Music performance skills at Foundation (staying in time, matching pitch, following an agreed plan) require repeated practice in low-stakes contexts before students can apply them reliably in a shared performance. Fluency here underpins the more deliberate performance decisions required at Y1-2.

descriptors.title: Create artworks that communicate ideas
descriptors.description: create arts works that communicate ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students have no formal prior arts education assumed. They bring play-based experience with materials, mark-making and imaginative representation from early childhood contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create artworks in one or more forms that communicate an idea drawn from personal experience, imagination or observation.

nodes.label: Materials and imagination as starting points
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a material or imaginative prompt as a starting point for making — exploring what happens when they manipulate materials or act out ideas.
criteria: Uses at least one material or imaginative prompt intentionally to begin making
Can say or show what their work is about
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot connect materials or imagination to a communicative intent will make without purpose — subsequent nodes requiring communicative choice are blocked.

width.minimum: Use one material or imaginative prompt to begin making something; say what the work is about.
width.typical: Use play, materials and imagination across several contexts to develop starting points for artworks; explore how different materials (paint, clay, collage, digital) produce different effects.
wider: Use repurposed objects (packing boxes, clothing) as starting points for imagining environments or characters — extend the imaginative world through making
Use a digital device to capture the making process — photograph or film steps as part of the artwork itself

modes.reason: Students need experience across a range of materials and imaginative prompts to discover which spark genuine communicative intent. No single material works for everyone at this stage.

nodes.label: Making with communicative intent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make a deliberate choice in their artwork — choosing what to include, how to arrange it, or what material to use — because of what they want to communicate.
criteria: Makes at least one deliberate choice about what to include or how to arrange the artwork
Explains the choice in terms of what the work is meant to show or communicate

width.minimum: Make one deliberate choice (what to put in, what colour, what shape) and explain why it helps communicate the idea.
width.typical: Make multiple deliberate choices across materials, arrangement and content; explain choices in terms of what the artwork is communicating.
wider: Respond to First Nations Australian visual arts or designs encountered through culturally authoritative resources — explore how specific choices (colour, symbol, pattern) communicate meaning
Create a work in response to another arts form (music, dance) — make choices about what visual elements express the feeling or story

modes.reason: Young students often make without reflecting on why. Simple scaffolding — 'What does your artwork show? Why did you choose that?' — builds the habit of connecting choice to intent.

nodes.label: Completing and communicating
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create an artwork in one or more forms that communicates an idea from personal experience, imagination or observation.
criteria: Creates a substantially complete artwork in at least one form
Communicates an idea from personal experience, imagination or observation — can explain what the work is about

width.minimum: Create one finished (or substantially complete) artwork and explain what idea it communicates.
width.typical: Create artworks in multiple forms (drawing, 3D, digital, collage) that communicate ideas from personal experience, imagination or observation; make choices that serve the communicative intent.
wider: Create a series of small works responding to a single idea in different forms — compare what each form can and cannot communicate
Use digital tools alongside analog materials to create a work — document the process and reflect on how each medium contributed

modes.reason: This node brings together material exploration and communicative intent. Students coordinate what they want to say with how to say it — the making and the meaning are unified.

descriptors.strand: Visual arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Discover possibilities and develop ideas
descriptors.description: use play, imagination, arts knowledge, processes and/or skills to discover possibilities and develop ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students bring informal play experience with materials and imaginative scenarios. No formal arts processes or skills assumed.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use play, imagination and emerging arts knowledge to discover possibilities and develop ideas for artworks.

nodes.label: Noticing and describing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can notice and describe visual or tactile qualities in materials and their environment — naming what they observe (rough, smooth, round, jagged; colours, shapes, lines).
criteria: Names at least two visual or tactile qualities of a material or environmental feature
Makes a connection between a quality and how it might be used in an artwork or creative activity
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot name or attend to visual and tactile qualities cannot use them purposefully in developing ideas — the observational foundation for all subsequent making is missing.

width.minimum: Describe at least two qualities of a material or environment feature observed.
width.typical: Identify and describe shapes, colours, lines and textures in materials and the environment; make connections between observed qualities and possible uses in artworks.
wider: Explore how natural and human-made materials feel and look differently — collect, sort and name qualities across a range of materials
Use a digital camera or device to capture lines, shapes and colours found in the school environment — describe what you found

modes.reason: Students need a vocabulary of qualities they can notice and name. Repeated exposure across many materials builds the observational repertoire that fuels idea development.

nodes.label: Playing and experimenting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use play, trial and imagination to discover new possibilities with materials, movement or voice — noticing what happens when they try something and building on it.
criteria: Tries at least two different ways of using a material or process
Describes at least one discovery — something that surprised them or that they want to use again

width.minimum: Try at least two ways of using a material or process; describe what was discovered.
width.typical: Use play, games and imagination to experiment with materials, movement and voice across multiple forms; identify what worked, what surprised and what could be used in future artworks.
wider: Respond to music by making visual marks — use crayons, paint or other media to express what the music makes you feel or see
Improvise movements or vocalisation to represent a tactile quality (rough, smooth, bouncy) — then translate the same idea into a visual form

modes.reason: Play-based discovery depends on variety of stimulus. Students who only experiment in one medium or context develop narrow ideas. More material and sensory contexts produce richer possibilities.

nodes.label: Developing ideas from play
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use something discovered through play or imagination as the starting point for developing an idea for an artwork.
criteria: Uses a discovery from play or experimentation as the basis for an artwork idea
Can explain what they want to make and what gave them the idea

width.minimum: Take one discovery from play or experimentation and use it as the starting point for an artwork idea.
width.typical: Use play, experimentation and emerging arts knowledge across multiple forms to develop ideas for artworks; ask 'what if?' questions to push ideas further; document discoveries informally.
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians connect visual arts, story and place — use resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians to see how ideas are developed into artworks
Use a camera to capture the steps in a play-based discovery as a photographic story — share the story and explain the idea it developed

modes.reason: This node connects noticing and experimenting into the idea-development process. Students bring together what they have observed, tried and imagined to generate an artwork idea.

descriptors.title: Arts importance for communities
descriptors.description: explore how and why the arts are important for people and communities
descriptors.knowledge: Students bring lived experience of arts in daily life (songs, drawings, stories, celebrations) but have not yet been invited to reflect on why arts matter to communities.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify examples of arts in their lives and communities and share ideas about why arts are important for people and communities.

nodes.label: Identifying arts in daily life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify arts works and experiences in their own lives — naming songs, artworks, dances, animations or performances they know.
criteria: Names at least one arts work or experience from their own life
Can categorise it as visual art, music, dance, drama or digital
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify arts in their own lives have no foundation from which to reason about why arts matter — the subsequent conceptual move (importance) requires concrete examples to anchor it.

width.minimum: Name at least one arts work or experience from their own life (a song, a drawing, a dance).
width.typical: Identify arts works and experiences across multiple forms (visual, music, dance, drama, digital) encountered at school, at home and in community settings.
wider: Identify arts works from different cultural celebrations (school songs, ceremonial dances, birthday traditions) — compare which forms appear in different communities
Use dramatic play to explore a text or image — act out 'what is happening?' and 'what will happen next?' to understand how arts communicate story

modes.reason: Students need a sufficient inventory of examples before they can generalise about why arts matter. Broadening the range of recognised arts forms ensures the concept applies beyond a single familiar type.

nodes.label: Why arts matter to people
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share an idea about why an arts work or experience is important — connecting it to feelings, celebrations, stories or communication.
criteria: Shares at least one reason why an arts work matters to them or their community
Connects the reason to feelings, celebrations, stories or communication (not just 'I like it')

width.minimum: Share one idea about why a specific arts work matters to them or their community (e.g. it makes people happy, it tells a story, it is used in celebrations).
width.typical: Explore how arts works communicate emotions, stories and cultural meanings; discuss why different arts forms matter to different people and communities.
wider: Listen to First Nations Australians talk about the importance of arts for connecting to people, culture and Country/Place — using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians
Explore how illustrations in a picture book communicate narrative and mood — discuss how the visual choices help the story and why that matters to readers

modes.reason: Students' initial reasons why arts matter are usually personal ('I like it'). Encountering arts that matter to different communities — especially First Nations voices — broadens understanding beyond personal preference.

nodes.label: Arts in communities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how and why arts are important for people and communities — identifying examples and explaining their importance in terms of shared meaning, celebration or connection.
criteria: Identifies at least one example of arts important to a community (not just an individual)
Explains why the arts work or event matters to that community

width.minimum: Identify one example of arts that is shared by or important to a community (not just an individual) and explain why.
width.typical: Explore arts works and events that are important to communities — songs, public art, cultural celebrations, shared stories; discuss the role arts play in bringing people together and communicating shared values.
wider: Investigate arts works that serve specific community functions (school songs, sports team anthems, ceremonial dances) — compare different communities' arts traditions
Explore how facial expressions, gesture and visual imagery communicate feelings across cultures — discuss how this shared function makes arts important everywhere

modes.reason: Students bring together their personal examples and their understanding of why arts matter to arrive at the broader claim: arts are important for communities, not just individuals.

descriptors.title: Share arts works with audiences
descriptors.description: share their arts works with audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students have no formal sharing or presenting experience assumed. They bring familiarity with informal show-and-tell and play-based sharing with peers.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share artworks with an audience and explain something about the work — its ideas, processes or features.

nodes.label: What audiences do
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify what it means to be an audience — that others look at, listen to or watch arts works, and that the audience receives something from the work.
criteria: Participates as an audience member for a peer's work
Shares at least one observation about the work
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have no concept of an audience share work without communicative intent — they cannot make meaningful choices about how to present or explain their work.

width.minimum: Participate as an audience member for a peer's work; share one thing noticed or felt.
width.typical: Participate as audience and maker in informal sharing contexts; identify features of artworks when looking at peers' work (similarities, differences, use of materials, visual elements).
wider: Walk around a class gallery and use positive language to comment on specific features of peers' works (line, colour, shape, materials)
Watch a performance or sharing of a different arts form — describe what the audience does and what the experience is like

modes.reason: The audience role needs to be experienced from both sides — as receiver and as presenter. Students who have only made, without experiencing what it is to receive, lack the perspective needed for intentional sharing.

nodes.label: Sharing with explanation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share an artwork with an audience and say something about it — what it shows, what they used to make it, or what they enjoyed.
criteria: Shares at least one artwork with an audience
Says at least one thing about the work — what it shows, what it is made from, or what was enjoyable

width.minimum: Share one artwork and say one thing about it — what it shows, what it is made from, or what was enjoyable about making it.
width.typical: Share artworks in multiple informal settings; talk about ideas, processes, materials and features; respond to teacher questions; present to small groups and to the class.
wider: Use a digital device to document an artwork or making process — curate a short sequence of images with added commentary expressing feelings and understandings
Present a retelling of a story using objects, puppets or repurposed materials — respond to audience questions about the story and the choices made

modes.reason: Sharing becomes more intentional when students experience multiple contexts (gallery walk, one-to-one with teacher, group presentation) — each context demands slightly different communication and builds versatility.

descriptors.title: Choreograph dance sequences
descriptors.description: use the elements of dance to choreograph dance sequences
descriptors.knowledge: Students have created arts works communicating ideas and used play and imagination to discover movement possibilities (Foundation). They can sequence simple movement ideas and present them to peers.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use the elements of dance to choreograph dance sequences.
elaborations: using improvised movements to create a dance sequence that represents a weather event, or shows how they might take care of a place that is important to them
using music they have created as inspiration for a dance
devising a starting shape, a way of moving to another place, and combining ideas with a partner
using ideas from exploration of balance, posture, and body part movement to create a dance sequence
using patterns of locomotor movements, sharing these with a partner, and working collaboratively to combine and extend
using own words and learnt dance terminology and recognising constructive feedback

nodes.label: Elements of dance as tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and intentionally use at least two elements of dance (e.g. space, time, dynamics) as tools for shaping movement.
criteria: Student can name at least two elements of dance
Student can demonstrate a movement choice that deliberately uses one named element (e.g. 'I'm going low — that's level')
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a working vocabulary of dance elements as intentional tools, students cannot make deliberate choreographic choices in N2-N3. They will move without compositional awareness.

width.minimum: Using one or two elements (e.g. level and direction) deliberately in movement — can name the element being used.
width.typical: Exploring and naming how space (level, direction, size), time (speed, rhythm), and dynamics (heavy/light, sharp/smooth) shape movement; using these elements intentionally in short movement improvisations.
wider: Use music created by students themselves (rhythmic patterns, clapping) as a prompt — applying time and dynamics elements in response
Explore how maintaining balance, manipulating posture, or isolating specific body parts are themselves expressive element choices

modes.reason: Students need vocabulary and labelling before they can use elements as tools. Name elements in the moment during play: 'You just changed your level — that's a space choice.' Use Viewpoints-style questioning to build metacognitive awareness.

nodes.label: Improvising and selecting movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can improvise movement using the elements of dance and select movements they want to use in a sequence.
criteria: Student generates multiple movement possibilities in an improvisation (does not stop at the first idea)
Student can identify which movements they want to keep and use in their sequence

width.minimum: Improvising a movement sequence in response to a stimulus; selecting two or more movements to keep and sequence.
width.typical: Using improvisation to generate a range of movement possibilities in response to stimuli (weather, music, stories, environments); selecting, sharing and learning movements with a partner; combining ideas to extend sequences.
wider: Improvise locomotor sequences (travelling movements) and teach these to a partner — combining and extending into a collaborative sequence
Use imagery (floating like a cloud, stomping like a giant) as stimulus — selecting movements that best represent the image

modes.reason: Improvisation requires a physical and imaginative repertoire. Students who have encountered many different stimuli types and movement contexts will generate richer ideas during improvisation.

nodes.label: Choreographing and refining a sequence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can choreograph a dance sequence with a beginning, middle and end, using the elements of dance, and can reflect on and refine it using peer/teacher feedback.
criteria: Student produces a dance sequence with a beginning, middle and end
Student can identify at least two element choices in their sequence
Student can describe what their sequence communicates and incorporate at least one piece of feedback
nodes.hinge_reason: Completing a choreographed sequence — with intentional element use and reflective refinement — is the prerequisite for all subsequent Creating strand work. Students who have not produced a whole sequence lack the foundational production experience.

width.minimum: A choreographed sequence with clear start and end; at least two identifiable element choices; can describe what the sequence is communicating.
width.typical: A dance sequence that represents an idea (weather, place, story, music) using multiple element choices; devised starting shape, locomotor movement through space, and ending position; combined with a partner or group to extend the sequence; feedback sought and used to refine.
wider: Choreograph a sequence that communicates care for a place that is important to the student — using element choices to express relationship and responsibility
Devise a collaborative sequence where each person's contribution is identifiable — using contrast and connection between individual parts

modes.reason: Choreographing integrates element knowledge (N1) with improvised material (N2) into a structured, communicative whole. Scaffold with structural prompts: 'How will it begin?', 'How do you move through the space?', 'How does it end?'

descriptors.title: Move safely and expressively
descriptors.description: experiment with ways to move safely and expressively using fundamental movement skills and the elements of dance
descriptors.knowledge: Students have used play and imagination to discover movement possibilities at Foundation. They can vary movement in simple ways and are building awareness of their body in space.
descriptors.endpoint: Students experiment with ways to move safely and expressively using fundamental movement skills and the elements of dance.
elaborations: developing awareness of and taking responsibility for safe dance practice
using improvisation to explore movement possibilities in response to stimuli
using Viewpoints to ask questions and identify movement possibilities
exploring fundamental movements safely to develop ideas based on familiar situations
moving around open and crowded spaces safely; identifying distance between self and others; using props; reflecting on safe and unsafe movement

nodes.label: Safe dance awareness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe and practise safe dance — being aware of self and others in the space, moving with care, and taking responsibility for their own physical wellbeing.
criteria: Student consistently maintains awareness of others in the dance space during movement activities
Student can describe at least one safe dance practice (e.g. checking space around them, landing softly)
nodes.hinge_reason: Safe dance awareness is a prerequisite for all physical engagement in dance. Students who do not internalise spatial awareness and body care cannot participate safely in subsequent technical or expressive movement work.

width.minimum: Consistent demonstration of spatial awareness and care for self and others during movement activities in a defined space.
width.typical: Developing responsibility for safe dance practice: awareness of self and others in the space; recognising the boundaries of the dance space; understanding body care (hydration, rest); moving safely in open and crowded spaces; using props such as scarves without endangering others.
wider: Reflect explicitly on moments of safe and unsafe movement — discussing what made movement feel safe or risky and identifying strategies
Practise safe movement in varied spatial configurations — small groups, scattered, lines — building adaptable spatial awareness

modes.reason: Safe practice must become habitual — not a checklist that requires conscious effort. Repeated practice across many sessions builds the automatic awareness and responsibility that safety in dance requires.

nodes.label: Fundamental movement exploration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore fundamental locomotor and non-locomotor movements expressively — varying level, direction, size and quality in response to prompts.
criteria: Student demonstrates at least four fundamental locomotor movements
Student can vary a movement in at least two ways (e.g. change level AND change speed) when prompted

width.minimum: Practising at least four fundamental movements (e.g. running, jumping, rolling, skipping) — varying one element (e.g. level or speed) in each.
width.typical: Exploring fundamental locomotor movements (running, skipping, rolling, jumping, walking backwards, sideways movements) and non-locomotor movements; using improvisation to explore movement possibilities in response to stimuli (imagery, music, stories); making movements bigger, smaller, faster, slower, higher, lower.
wider: Explore movement inspired by familiar natural phenomena — falling like a leaf, gliding like a bird, rolling like a log — attending to dynamics and control
Improvise movements in response to Viewpoints questions: 'What levels are you using?', 'Can you use a different body part?', 'What direction could you travel?'

modes.reason: Students need broad physical repertoire — many movement types across many variations — before they can make expressive choices. Movement variety must be built before it can be deployed intentionally.

nodes.label: Expressive movement with elements
nodes.checkpoint: Students can move expressively using fundamental skills and elements of dance — communicating ideas or feelings through movement quality.
criteria: Student uses movement quality (not just movement type) to communicate an idea — evident from observer's perspective
Student can identify what they are communicating through their movement

width.minimum: One movement sequence using at least two elements to express an idea or feeling — student can explain what they are communicating.
width.typical: Using improvisation and element awareness to communicate expressively: contrasting dynamics (stamping heavily vs tip-toeing lightly), using movement qualities to express ideas (slow sinking = melting, sharp jerky = robot); applying Viewpoints questions to improve expressive clarity.
wider: Explore how the same idea (e.g. a weather event) can be expressed through contrasting element combinations — comparing expressive effect
Use Viewpoints questions to evaluate own expressive choices: 'How are you communicating your ideas?', 'What other body parts could you use?'

modes.reason: Expressive movement integrates safe body use (N1), physical vocabulary (N2), and element awareness (from C strand) into intentional communication. Connect back explicitly: 'You're moving safely AND communicating — that's expressive dance.'

descriptors.title: Dance across cultures and contexts
descriptors.description: explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and/or other contexts experience dance
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored how arts are important for communities at Foundation. They recognise that arts experiences — including dances — bring people together and carry cultural meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and/or other contexts experience dance.
elaborations: identifying features of dances that communicate cultural knowledge such as stories, traditions or ceremonies
using Viewpoints to ask questions about dances experienced
recognising and describing patterns of movement using own words and learnt terminology
identifying similarities and differences in dances by sharing, viewing and learning dances from families and communities
identifying how dance can show what feelings people have about places, people or experiences

nodes.label: Observing and describing dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can observe a dance and describe its features — movements, music, costume — using their own words and some dance terminology.
criteria: Student can describe at least two features of a dance they have observed (e.g. movements, music, costume)
Student uses at least one learnt dance term correctly in describing what they see
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to observe and describe dance features is the foundation for cultural and contextual understanding — without it, students cannot engage meaningfully with where, why and how dance occurs.

width.minimum: Observing at least one dance from a culture or context different from their own; describing what they notice using their own words.
width.typical: Observing and describing multiple dances using Viewpoints questions ('What movements?', 'What music?', 'What are they wearing?', 'What are they communicating?'); recognising and describing movement patterns; using a mix of own words and learnt terminology.
wider: View and compare two dances from different cultural contexts — identifying similarities and differences in movement, costume, music and setting
Share dances familiar from home and family, and compare with dances shared by peers — building a collective picture of dance diversity in the class community

modes.reason: Viewpoints questioning scaffolds observation into description. Students need a lens for looking — provide structured prompts before asking open responses. Build vocabulary incrementally: movements → music → costume → purpose.

nodes.label: Where, why and how people dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that people dance for different reasons in different places and contexts — and that dance can communicate feelings, knowledge and cultural identity.
criteria: Student can identify at least two different purposes for dance (e.g. celebration, storytelling, ceremony)
Student can explain that dance can communicate feelings about places, people or experiences

width.minimum: Identifying at least two different contexts in which people dance (e.g. celebration, ceremony, entertainment) and one reason why dance is used in each.
width.typical: Exploring where, why and how dance is experienced: identifying cultural purposes (stories, traditions, ceremonies), recognising similarities and differences across dances, identifying how dance communicates feelings about places, people and experiences.
wider: Explore dances experienced with students' own families and communities — comparing purposes and traditions with dances experienced by peers
Investigate how dance communicates feelings about specific places or environments — connecting to students' own sense of belonging to place

modes.reason: Understanding that dance has many purposes and contexts requires encountering genuine diversity — not just acknowledging it exists. More cultural and contextual examples = richer understanding of dance's role in human life.

descriptors.title: First Nations dance
descriptors.description: explore examples of dance choreographed and/or performed by First Nations Australians
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored how the arts are important for communities at Foundation, including listening to First Nations Australians talk about arts and connection to Country/Place. They can observe and describe dance features (AC9ADA2E01).
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore examples of dance choreographed and/or performed by First Nations Australians.
elaborations: exploring when, where, how and why First Nations Australians use dance during celebrations and significant occasions
observing how the elements of dance are used in First Nations Australian choreography and/or performance
identifying where dance occurs in First Nations Australians' cultural expressions and noting audience protocols
learning about First Nations Australians' interpretations of the night sky and co-creating movements with cultural authority holders

nodes.label: When and why First Nations Australians dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify when and why First Nations Australians use dance — including connections to significant occasions, ceremonies and community events.
criteria: Student can name at least one occasion when First Nations Australians use dance
Student can explain one reason why dance is important in that context

width.minimum: Identifying at least one occasion when First Nations Australians use dance (e.g. NAIDOC Week, ceremonies) and a reason why.
width.typical: Exploring when, where, how and why First Nations Australians use dance to share cultural knowledge — including celebrations such as NAIDOC Week, National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children's Day, Reconciliation Week, Sorry Day; identifying dance in First Nations cultural expressions at school, in community, and in state/national events.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians use dance in specific significant events — noticing how performers and audiences observe protocols and respect Elders and knowledge holders

Explore First Nations Australians' interpretations of the night sky — working with community members who have cultural authority to co-create movements representing shapes and patterns visible at different times of year

modes.reason: Understanding the range of occasions and purposes requires exposure to multiple examples — single-example exposure risks tokenism. Use resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians.

nodes.label: Observing elements in First Nations dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can observe how elements of dance are used in choreography and/or performance by First Nations Australians.
criteria: Student can identify at least one element of dance used in a First Nations Australian dance example
Student engages with First Nations dance examples with respect and attentiveness
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot yet apply element observation to First Nations dance will engage only at a surface cultural level — missing the connection between element choices and cultural meaning that underpins respectful engagement in later bands.

width.minimum: Observing one example of First Nations Australian dance and describing at least one element of dance used (e.g. movement type, level, relationship).
width.typical: Observing examples of First Nations Australian dance using learnt element vocabulary; noticing how movements, relationships, space and time are used; exploring movements with representatives of the First Nations Australian community or via resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians.
wider: Co-create movements with a First Nations Australian community member who has cultural authority — exploring how specific movements represent cultural knowledge
Compare element use in two examples of First Nations Australian dance from different communities or occasions

modes.reason: Apply the same Viewpoints questions used in E01 — 'What movements do you see?', 'What levels?', 'What relationships between dancers?' — to First Nations dance examples. Familiarity with the observational frame transfers across contexts.

descriptors.title: Share dance in informal settings
descriptors.description: share dance sequences in informal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students have shared arts works with audiences at Foundation. They can present a movement sequence and describe what it communicates. They are building choreography skills using dance elements (AC9ADA2C01).
descriptors.endpoint: Students share dance sequences in informal settings.
elaborations: presenting a learned sequence or performing dances learnt to peers and teachers
performing a dance co-created with a First Nations Australian person with cultural authority, following ICIP protocols
expressing ideas through movement — contrasting dynamics, movement qualities communicating ideas
using Viewpoints to develop questions when responding to dances to reflect on choreography and performance

nodes.label: Communicating ideas through movement to an audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share a dance sequence to peers and/or teachers, using movement to express an idea, feeling or intention.
criteria: Student presents a dance sequence to a small audience in an informal setting
Student uses at least one intentional expressive quality in their performance (visible to observer)

width.minimum: Presenting a choreographed or learned sequence to peers in an informal setting — with at least one deliberate expressive choice (e.g. stamping heavily to express strength).
width.typical: Performing and sharing dance sequences in informal class settings: presenting learned sequences, performing co-created dances, using expressive movement qualities (heavy/light, sharp/smooth) to communicate ideas; introducing the work with a brief explanation.
wider: Perform a dance co-created with a First Nations Australian person who has cultural authority — following protocols for Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property
Perform a dance for an audience beyond the class (another class, a school event) — adapting performance presence for a larger or different audience

modes.reason: Students build performance confidence through repeated opportunities to present. Multiple informal sharing experiences across the year develop presence, spatial awareness and communicative intent in performance.

nodes.label: Reflecting on choreography and performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on their own and others' dance performances using Viewpoints questions — and use reflections to develop ideas.
criteria: Student can respond to a Viewpoints question about their own performance with at least one specific observation
Student can receive a piece of constructive feedback without dismissing it
nodes.hinge_reason: Reflective capacity — connecting what was intended with what was communicated — is the bridge between performing and refining. Without this, students cannot use performance as a learning loop. This is foundational for the reflective practices required in Y3-4 and beyond.

width.minimum: Responding to at least one Viewpoints question about their own or a peer's performance — connecting observation to choreographic intent.
width.typical: Using Viewpoints questions to reflect on what the dance communicated ('What did this dance make you think about?', 'Did the movements remind you of anything?', 'How did you communicate your idea?'); identifying what worked and what might change; recognising and accepting constructive feedback.
wider: Compare how two different performances of the same sequence communicate the idea differently — discussing element choices that change the effect
Use reflection to set a goal for a future performance — identifying one aspect to develop

modes.reason: Reflection requires a scaffold — students this age need specific, framed questions rather than open prompts ('What worked?'). Viewpoints questions provide accessible entry points. Model the thinking: 'I noticed you stamped heavily — what were you trying to show?'

descriptors.title: Create fictional situations
descriptors.description: create and co-create fictional situations based on imagination and/or experience
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create arts works that communicate ideas using play, movement, voice and repurposed materials (Foundation). They can draw an idea from imagination or experience and use at least one mode to express it.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and co-create fictional situations — through dramatic play, process drama, puppetry or movement — based on imagination and/or experience.
elaborations: using puppets to create new stories, including stories that communicate understanding of existing stories or personal experiences
using learning from explorations of First Nations Australians' drama to devise drama communicating connection to place
using costume items and props to share character information in Readers' Theatre
identifying situations from stories, films, fantasy, history or personal experience to explore through dramatic play
contributing ideas within whole group or small group improvisations including teacher-in-role
communicating non-verbally using facial expressions and movements to explore role and situation in mime
accepting or developing the pretence situation established by others

nodes.label: Accepting and proposing the pretence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can enter a fictional situation created by others and contribute to it — accepting the 'as if' and adding ideas or actions within it.
criteria: Student participates in a dramatic play scenario, accepting the fictional situation established by the group
Student contributes at least one idea or action that extends the fictional world
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot accept the pretence — cannot sustain the 'as if' — co-creation collapses into activity rather than drama; creating original fictional situations (the next move) depends on this collaborative foundation.

width.minimum: Student participates in an established dramatic play scenario, staying in role or accepting the pretence set by a teacher or peer.
width.typical: Students take turns offering and accepting ideas in improvised drama; they stay in role when participating and suggest relevant roles, situations or props to extend the fictional world.
wider: Students use inquiry questions to propose new situations within the drama ('What else might happen? What if I was there?')
Students co-create a dramatic play space using unstructured materials and everyday clothing items to establish a fictional world

modes.reason: Sustained engagement in the pretence builds through repeated practice in short, clear scenarios; students need regular opportunities to practise entering and extending fictional worlds before they generate original ones.

nodes.label: Drawing on imagination and experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a situation from their own imagination, a story, or personal experience to explore through drama.
criteria: Student can name or describe a situation they want to explore in drama, drawing on imagination or experience
Student can explain (however simply) where the idea came from

width.minimum: Student names or shows a situation they want to explore — drawn from a story, film, history, fantasy or personal experience.
width.typical: Students brainstorm and discuss situations from experiences (stories, films, games, personal moments) and use these ideas to initiate improvised drama; they consider what roles and situations might be explored.
wider: Students use puppets they have made from repurposed materials to create new stories that communicate their understanding of existing stories or personal experiences
Students use learning from First Nations Australians' drama that communicates connection to Country/Place to devise drama communicating their own connection to a place in their community

modes.reason: Offer varied starting points — familiar stories, personal experiences, fantasy, community events — to help students who struggle to generate ideas from one prompt find a richer entry point.

nodes.label: Creating and co-creating fictional situations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create and co-create fictional situations, using non-verbal and verbal communication to establish role and situation with others.
criteria: Student creates or co-creates a fictional situation in collaboration with at least one other person
Student uses non-verbal communication (facial expression, movement, gesture) within the drama
Student can describe the role or situation they were exploring

width.minimum: Student participates in creating a fictional situation with at least one other person, contributing roles or scenarios and communicating within the drama.
width.typical: Students contribute ideas and actions within whole-group or small-group improvisations; they communicate non-verbally through facial expressions and movement; they use costume items, props or materials to establish roles and situations; they accept and build on others' contributions.
wider: Students participate in Readers' Theatre, using costume items and props to share information about their character while 'in role'
Students co-create dramatic play with teacher-in-role, responding to the teacher's contributions and extending the fictional world
Students devise short scenes communicating their feelings about a place or how they care for their community, drawing on exploration of First Nations Australians' drama about Country/Place

modes.reason: Co-creation integrates the pretence-acceptance and idea-sourcing moves — students must simultaneously contribute, accept, and maintain the fictional world. Teacher scaffolds with process drama strategies and teacher-in-role.

descriptors.title: Elements of drama in play
descriptors.description: use the elements of drama and imagination in dramatic play and/or process drama
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use play and imagination to discover possibilities and develop ideas (Foundation). They can engage in purposeful exploration of materials, voice and movement.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use the elements of drama — role, place, situation, language and movement — and imagination in dramatic play and/or process drama.
elaborations: exploring a situation through dramatic play using familiar props
understanding and employing appropriate drama terminology
taking part in purposeful dramatic play focusing on creating roles and situations
taking turns offering and accepting ideas, and staying in role during improvised drama
brainstorming and discussing situations from experiences and using these ideas to improvise drama

nodes.label: Understanding the elements of drama
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name and recognise the basic elements of drama — role, place, situation, language, movement — in drama they experience and create.
criteria: Student correctly uses at least two drama element terms when discussing drama
Student can identify an element of drama (e.g. role, place) in a drama they have participated in or observed
nodes.hinge_reason: If students lack element vocabulary and conceptual awareness, they cannot intentionally use elements in their drama-making — subsequent nodes about taking roles and developing situations lack a shared language.

width.minimum: Student can use at least two drama element terms appropriately when describing their own or others' drama.
width.typical: Students understand and use appropriate drama terminology (role, place, situation, language, movement, dramatic play, process drama, pretending, audience, theatre, performance, actors) when discussing drama they have made and/or experienced.
wider: Students explore how elements combine differently in different forms — comparing dramatic play to a class performance — and name what changes
Students use props from familiar contexts (empty containers, clothing, toys) to explore how physical objects create or signal role and place

modes.reason: Explicitly introduce each element with concrete examples from drama students have just experienced; use questioning ('What role were you playing? What was the place?') to make the elements visible.

nodes.label: Taking on role in dramatic play
nodes.checkpoint: Students can take on a role purposefully in dramatic play or process drama, developing ideas through that role.
criteria: Student takes on a named or implied role and sustains it for the duration of a short dramatic play sequence
Student makes at least one decision or contribution from within the role

width.minimum: Student takes on a specific role in dramatic play and makes decisions from within that role.
width.typical: Students take on roles in dramatic play focusing on creating situations; they stay in role when participating in improvised drama; they develop ideas from texts (children's literature, images) into character and situation.
wider: Students explore a range of role types — from characters in familiar stories to imagined roles in invented scenarios — and consider how different roles produce different perspectives
Students participate in process drama with teacher-in-role, accepting and responding to the teacher's character within the fictional world

modes.reason: Staying in role requires repeated practice; students need multiple short experiences of role-taking before they can sustain it through a more complex dramatic sequence.

nodes.label: Using elements to develop dramatic situations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use elements of drama — particularly role, place, situation and movement — intentionally to develop and sustain a dramatic situation.
criteria: Student uses at least two elements of drama intentionally in a dramatic play or process drama sequence
Student can describe which elements they were using and what they were trying to show

width.minimum: Student uses at least two elements intentionally within a sustained dramatic play or process drama sequence.
width.typical: Students use language, movement and role to develop situations in dramatic play; they use facial expressions and body to show role and situation; they brainstorm and discuss situations and improvise drama that develops those ideas.
wider: Students explore how manipulating one element (e.g. changing the place, adding a new character) transforms the dramatic situation and what it communicates
Students use movement-based drama or mime to show role and situation without words, exploring how movement communicates meaning independently of language

modes.reason: This node is where element knowledge and role-taking come together into purposeful drama-making. Support students to make intentional choices about which elements to use and how.

descriptors.title: Drama across cultures and contexts
descriptors.description: explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and/or other contexts experience drama
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify arts works in their lives and explain a simple reason why the arts are important for people and communities (Foundation). They have not yet explored drama specifically across different cultures and contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and other contexts experience drama.
elaborations: identifying where they might experience drama in their lives and community
recognising how drama can show feelings and ideas people have about the world
asking questions about drama they experience
considering how drama communicates cultural knowledge in their own communities

nodes.label: Where drama happens in life and community
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify places and occasions where drama is experienced — at school, in the community, and beyond.
criteria: Student names at least two different contexts where drama is experienced (e.g. at school, at a community event, on screen)
Student asks or responds to at least one question about where or why drama is made
nodes.hinge_reason: If students only understand drama as a school classroom activity, they cannot engage with the 'across cultures and contexts' scope of the descriptor; understanding that drama exists widely is the foundation for the 'why' inquiry.

width.minimum: Student identifies at least one context where drama is experienced beyond their classroom (a school performance, a community event, a screen-based drama).
width.typical: Students share experiences of attending drama performances or participating in drama at school and in their community; they discuss where and why drama is made and experienced.
wider: Students explore drama contexts from another culture or region (e.g. shadow puppetry, Asian performance traditions, community storytelling theatre) and compare with familiar drama
Students consider how drama communicates cultural knowledge in their own communities through stories, traditions and shared experience

modes.reason: Deliberately expand students' awareness of drama contexts — community theatre, cultural ceremonies, puppetry, screen drama — before narrowing to 'why' questions.

nodes.label: How and why drama communicates — across cultures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how drama communicates feelings and ideas, and identify that different communities and cultures use drama for different purposes.
criteria: Student explains at least one reason why people in a given context make and experience drama
Student identifies that drama can communicate different things for different cultures or communities

width.minimum: Student can explain one reason why people in a specific context make and experience drama.
width.typical: Students recognise how drama shows feelings and ideas people have about the world; they ask and discuss questions ('How and why are these people making drama?', 'What is the drama about?'); they explore how drama communicates cultural knowledge in their own and other communities.
wider: Students investigate how drama communicates stories from a country or region in Asia, exploring what that drama is about and why it matters to that community
Students compare two different drama contexts — one familiar and one from another culture — and identify similarities and differences in purpose and form

modes.reason: Use guiding questions ('What is the drama about?', 'How do you think the people making it feel?', 'Why would a community share this story?') to scaffold simple causal and cultural reasoning.

descriptors.title: First Nations drama
descriptors.description: explore examples of drama created and/or performed by First Nations Australians
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored the arts as important for people and communities (Foundation). They are developing awareness that drama is used across different cultures and contexts (AC9ADR2E01). No specific prior knowledge of First Nations drama is assumed.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore examples of drama created and/or performed by First Nations Australians, attending to how elements of drama communicate connection to culture and Country/Place.
elaborations: exploring when, where, how and why First Nations Australians use drama during cultural celebrations
exploring First Nations Australians' use of drama to express connection to and responsibility for Country/Place
observing how elements such as place, language and movement are used in First Nations cultural expressions
exploring ways of communicating knowledge through stories from their region
co-creating a Welcome to Country or Acknowledgement of Country with cultural authority

nodes.label: When, where and why First Nations Australians use drama
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify occasions when First Nations Australians use drama and explain why drama is important in those contexts.
criteria: Student names at least one occasion or context when First Nations Australians use drama
Student gives a simple reason why drama is important in that context
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding why First Nations Australians use drama — its cultural purpose, not just its existence — students observe drama as spectacle rather than as a living cultural practice; the second node about elements and meaning cannot proceed meaningfully.

width.minimum: Student identifies at least one occasion (e.g. NAIDOC Week, Sorry Day, Reconciliation Week, community storytelling) when First Nations Australians use drama and gives a simple reason for it.
width.typical: Students explore when, where, how and why First Nations Australians use drama to share knowledge about their cultures; they investigate drama associated with cultural celebrations and significant occasions using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians.
wider: Students explore how First Nations Australians use drama to express connection to and responsibility for Country/Place — including communicating knowledge about local seasons and sustaining ways of life
Students engage directly or via co-created resources with stories that communicate knowledge of the environment in their region through drama

modes.reason: Use resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians to ensure cultural authority; offer varied contexts (celebration, storytelling, ceremony) so students encounter the breadth of purpose.

nodes.label: How elements of drama communicate in First Nations contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can observe and describe how elements of drama — place, language, movement — are used in First Nations Australians' cultural expressions they have experienced.
criteria: Student observes and names at least one element of drama used in a First Nations cultural drama example
Student describes what that element communicates or expresses in that context

width.minimum: Student describes one way an element of drama (e.g. movement, language) is used in a First Nations drama example they have observed.
width.typical: Students observe how elements of drama such as place, language and movement are used in First Nations Australians' cultural expressions; they describe what they notice; they explore how drama communicates knowledge through stories in their region using direct engagement or co-created resources.
wider: Students co-create (as appropriate, with cultural authority and guidance) a Welcome to Country or Acknowledgement of Country to perform before their drama class
Students explore how First Nations drama communicates ways of caring for the land, sea, sky or waterways, connecting drama to environmental knowledge

modes.reason: Guide students to name specific elements they observe ('What do you notice about the movement?', 'What is happening with language and voice here?') to make element-level observation explicit.

descriptors.title: Share drama in informal settings
descriptors.description: share their drama in informal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can share arts works with audiences and respond to questions about their work (Foundation). They have been developing skills in dramatic play, process drama and simple performance within class contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share their drama in informal settings, communicating to an audience and reflecting on what the drama made them think or feel.
elaborations: retelling a familiar story through acting and sharing with an audience
performing sequences of frozen images linked by transitions to communicate key scenes
reflecting using questions about what they want audiences to think, what the drama made them think about, and what they liked and why

nodes.label: What the audience should experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify what they want their audience to think about or feel when watching their drama.
criteria: Student names at least one thing they want the audience to think about or feel when watching
Student can connect one performance decision (e.g. 'I used a loud voice because...') to an intended effect
nodes.hinge_reason: If students have no awareness of the audience — no sense that sharing involves communicating something — the performance event is purely expressive without communicative intent; this distinction is what makes 'sharing drama' different from 'doing drama'.

width.minimum: Student can respond to the question 'What do you want your audience to think about your drama?' with at least one idea.
width.typical: Students consider their personal responses to drama experiences and think about audience perspective; they can describe what they want the audience to notice or feel; they connect their drama-making decisions to an intended audience effect.
wider: Students consider the difference between what they intended and what the audience actually experienced, using simple reflection after sharing
Students explore how different performance choices (facial expression, movement, voice) might produce different effects on an audience

modes.reason: Explicitly prompt audience-awareness before sharing: 'Before we share — what do you want people watching to think or feel?' This question is the hinge-prevention move.

nodes.label: Performing and reflecting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform their drama in an informal setting and reflect on the experience as performer and as audience member.
criteria: Student performs their drama in an informal setting to at least one audience member
Student responds to at least one reflection question about what the drama made them think or feel
Student identifies at least one thing they liked in their own or a peer's drama and says why

width.minimum: Student performs their drama to an audience (even a partner) and responds to at least one reflection question afterwards.
width.typical: Students retell a familiar story or share a drama through acting in an informal setting; they perform sequences (including frozen images or transitions) to communicate key scenes; they reflect using questions about what they liked, what the drama made them think about, and how they felt making and watching it.
wider: Students perform a drama based on a community story, family experience or exploration of First Nations Australians' connection to place, sharing with their class
Students use digital recording to capture and watch back their performance, noticing what communicated well

modes.reason: Performance and reflection integrate all prior skills. Post-performance discussion ('What did you like best? Why? What did this drama make you think about?') scaffolds the reflective habit that builds over the later bands.

descriptors.title: Construct representations
descriptors.description: use media languages and media technologies to construct representations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create arts works that communicate a recognisable idea and share them informally. They have explored media technologies through play. They have not yet deliberately applied media languages (shot types, composition) or production choices to construct representations with communicative intent.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use media languages and media technologies to construct representations that communicate identifiable ideas or stories.
elaborations: creating a story through a series of captioned or voice-over images or direct to camera footage; exploring composition through character creation using images, sounds, and/or animation; for example, claymation
selecting and editing images, sound and text to re-create the characters in well-known stories or songs, using Viewpoints to develop questions when making decisions about composition
capturing and sequencing images and text to create a media arts work, such as a comic book that retells familiar or traditional stories
producing and presenting a media arts work for a particular purpose; for example, creating an advertisement that recommends appropriate behaviour when using cameras
using features such as shot types in media arts works; for example, identifying long-shots, mid-shots and close-ups; discussing what the shots tell the audience about the story

nodes.label: Media languages — what they are and why they matter
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify at least two media language features (e.g. shot types: long, mid, close-up) and explain what each communicates to an audience.
criteria: Student can identify at least two shot types (long, mid, close-up) in a media work
Student can explain what each shot type communicates to the audience
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding media language features (shot types, composition) is the conceptual foundation for all subsequent production decisions — without it, construction choices are arbitrary and cannot be evaluated or improved.

width.minimum: Identify long-shot, mid-shot and close-up in an example media work and describe what each tells the audience about the story.
width.typical: Identify and describe a range of media language features in existing works (shot types, composition, sequencing, captions, voice-over); discuss what different choices communicate; use Viewpoints questions to frame observations.
wider: Investigate how shot type changes what the audience knows and feels about characters — comparing the same scene shot as a long-shot vs a close-up and discussing what is gained or lost
Explore how media languages in advertising (e.g. a camera-safety advertisement) differ from narrative storytelling — identifying the purpose and how language choices serve it

modes.reason: Students need explicit scaffolding to move from observing shot types to understanding why they communicate differently. Use structured questions: 'What does a close-up tell us that a long-shot doesn't?'

nodes.label: Constructing with media technologies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a media technology to capture, sequence or edit media elements — making at least one deliberate compositional decision.
criteria: Student uses a media technology to capture or create at least three media elements
Student makes at least one deliberate composition decision (selection, sequencing, or captioning) and can explain the reason for it

width.minimum: Use a digital device to capture and sequence at least three images or sounds, making at least one deliberate choice (which image to keep, how to order them, what caption to add).
width.typical: Capture and sequence images and text to create a media arts work (comic book, captioned sequence, voice-over story); select, edit and delete elements based on purpose; apply shot type decisions during capture; combine visual and audio elements.
wider: Explore claymation or simple animation by creating a character using images and/or sounds — making deliberate composition decisions at each stage and reflecting on what each choice communicates

Experiment with retelling a school day story using a digital camera to capture still or moving images and adding appropriate captions — reviewing and selecting the best images with Viewpoints questions: 'What images will I keep or delete?'

modes.reason: The mechanics of capture, sequencing and selection require practice — students who rush through production without deliberate selection and review produce accidental rather than intentional representations.

nodes.label: Representations communicate ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a complete representation — a media arts work that communicates an identifiable story or idea to an audience.
criteria: Student produces a media arts work that communicates an identifiable story or idea
Student can describe at least one media language choice they made and why they made it

width.minimum: Produce one media arts work (e.g. captioned image story, voice-over sequence, simple animation) that communicates a recognisable story or idea and present it to an audience.
width.typical: Produce media arts works across two or more forms for specific purposes (advertisement, story retelling, character creation); apply learned media language features (shot types, captions, sound) deliberately; reflect on whether the representation communicates the intended idea.
wider: Create an advertisement that recommends appropriate behaviour when using cameras — applying shot type decisions and discussing how the representation serves the persuasive purpose

Produce a media arts work that re-creates characters from a well-known story or song using selected and edited images, sound and text; reflect on how the re-creation communicates differently to the original

modes.reason: This node integrates media language knowledge with production skills — the work produced here is the evidence that both are operating together. Ensure students connect their language choices to their communicative intent.

descriptors.strand: Media arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Use media technologies responsibly
descriptors.description: explore ways of using media technologies responsibly to capture and organise images, sounds, text and/or interactive elements
descriptors.knowledge: Students have used digital devices for play and idea exploration. They can capture images or sounds informally. They have not yet explicitly considered responsible use, or deliberately combined visual and audio elements to communicate.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore ways of using media technologies responsibly to capture and organise images, sounds, text and/or interactive elements.
elaborations: exploring ways to use digital tools to capture moving image; for example, using a digital device to capture and manipulate short videos, add sound effects or voice-overs, and considering how best to combine the visual and audio elements to communicate ideas or a narrative
exploring how sound can be used to communicate ideas; for example, creating sound effects using found objects or sound recording technology to integrate with a picture book story
experimenting with images; for example, retelling the story of a school day using a digital camera to capture still or moving images and adding appropriate captions

experimenting with ways that media artists communicate with audiences by combining text, symbols and images; for example, combining headlines, subtitles and digital images to communicate ideas or emotions

using Viewpoints to develop questions as they experiment with media technologies, such as, "What happens if I take a photo up close to the object, and how does it change as I move further away?", "How can I change the meaning of this image by adding different text headings?"

nodes.label: Responsible use of media technologies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify at least one principle of responsible media technology use and apply it when capturing media elements.
criteria: Student can identify at least one responsible use principle for media technology
Student applies that principle when capturing or sharing media in class activities
nodes.hinge_reason: Responsible use principles are a prerequisite for all public sharing of student work — if not established here, subsequent presenting and sharing activities lack the ethical grounding that ACARA requires.

width.minimum: Identify one responsible use principle (e.g. asking permission before taking photos of people) and apply it during a media capture activity.
width.typical: Discuss and apply responsible use principles when capturing images, sounds and text — including permission to use images of people, care with cultural material, and safe online sharing; connect responsible use to real situations (school excursion photos, class news bulletin).
wider: Develop a class set of rules for using and creating images, sounds and text in media arts works — consulting relevant people (teachers, cultural knowledge holders) and online safety resources, and presenting the rules to the class
Explore what permission means in different contexts (individual permission vs permission for cultural material belonging to a group) through specific case examples

modes.reason: Use structured scenarios to build reasoning about responsible use — 'Is it OK to take this photo? What do we need to do first?' This develops transferable principles rather than rules memorised for a single context.

nodes.label: Capturing and organising media elements
nodes.checkpoint: Students can capture and organise images, sounds and/or text using a digital device — making deliberate choices about what to capture and how to combine elements.
criteria: Student captures at least two types of media elements using a digital device
Student organises the elements to communicate an identifiable idea, and can describe one choice they made during organisation

width.minimum: Use a digital device to capture at least two types of media elements (e.g. still image and voice-over, or moving image and caption) and organise them to communicate an idea.
width.typical: Capture, organise and combine images, sound and text across multiple tasks; experiment with how different combinations change meaning; review and select media elements based on communicative purpose; apply Viewpoints questions during capture and review.
wider: Explore how sound communicates ideas by creating sound effects using found objects and integrating them with a picture book or image sequence — experimenting with what changes when different sounds are combined with the same images

Experiment with combining text, symbols and images to communicate emotions or ideas — for example, creating headlines with digital images and comparing how different text changes the meaning of the image

modes.reason: Build students' repertoire of capture and combination skills across media types (image, sound, text, moving image) — a broader repertoire means more choices available in later production work.

nodes.label: Experimenting to change meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can experiment with how changes to media elements (different text, different sound, different framing) change what a work communicates.
criteria: Student makes at least one deliberate change to a media element (text, sound, or framing)
Student can describe how the change affects what the work communicates

width.minimum: Change at least one element in a media work (e.g. add different text headings to the same image, or move closer/further from a subject) and describe how the change affects meaning.
width.typical: Systematically experiment with changes to images, sound and text to discover how each change affects meaning; use Viewpoints questions to guide experimentation ('What happens if I take a photo up close?', 'How can I change the meaning of this image by adding different text?'); document discoveries.
wider: Investigate how moving closer to or further from a subject changes the meaning of the captured image — applying Viewpoints questions systematically across a series of distance experiments and comparing results
Explore how adding a voice-over to existing video changes what it communicates — recording multiple different voice-overs for the same footage and comparing the audience experience of each

modes.reason: Experimentation to change meaning integrates capture skills with media language understanding — students connect the 'how to do it' (capture) with the 'why it works' (language) by observing the effect of their own changes.

descriptors.title: Media arts across cultures and contexts
descriptors.description: explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and/or other contexts experience media arts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify arts works in their own lives and explain why they matter to people. They have not yet explored media arts works across different cultures or communities, or considered the roles and responsibilities of media artists.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and/or other contexts experience media arts, and describe the role of media artists and what permissions mean.
elaborations: identifying where they might experience media arts works in their lives and communities; for example, considering how media arts works communicate cultural knowledge and the purpose of a range of media types

using Viewpoints to ask questions about societies and cultures; for example, "What story is this media arts work telling me/us?", "Who made this media arts work?", "Where is this media arts work from?"
discussing the roles of media artists and what permission means; for example, deciding on a class set of rules for using and creating images, sounds and text in media arts works
considering how media arts works communicate and celebrate cultural knowledge in their own communities; for example, through podcasts or animated children's shows

nodes.label: Media arts across contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify where they encounter media arts works in their lives and communities — naming types of media and contexts.
criteria: Student can identify at least two types of media arts works from their own life
Student can describe where and when they encounter each type
