nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot identify the range of media contexts they inhabit, the 'across cultures and communities' exploration has no concrete grounding — subsequent questions about purpose and meaning have no examples to work from.

width.minimum: Identify at least two different types of media arts works encountered in their own life and explain where and when they experience each.
width.typical: Identify a range of media types and contexts (podcasts, animated shows, advertisements, games, news) encountered in school, home and community settings; describe the purpose of each type; ask Viewpoints questions: 'What story is this work telling?', 'Who made this?', 'Where is it from?'
wider: Compare media arts works encountered at home vs at school vs in the community — investigating how different contexts produce different types of media and different audience experiences
Investigate how media arts works in different cultural contexts (e.g. animated shows from different countries) communicate cultural knowledge and community values

modes.reason: Vary the media contexts encountered — podcasts, animated shows, advertisements, games, news — so students develop a broad understanding of what counts as media arts, not just the forms most familiar to them.

nodes.label: Purpose and cultural knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why a media arts work was made and how it communicates cultural knowledge — connecting purpose to content and form.
criteria: Student can identify who made a media arts work and what community it comes from
Student can describe what cultural knowledge or story the work communicates

width.minimum: Choose one media arts work and explain: who made it, what community it comes from, and what cultural knowledge or story it communicates.
width.typical: Explore media arts works from different cultural contexts and communities; use Viewpoints questions to investigate purpose and cultural knowledge ('Who made this work?', 'What story is it telling?', 'Where is it from?'); discuss how media arts works celebrate cultural knowledge in their own and other communities.
wider: Investigate how media arts works in students' own community communicate and celebrate cultural knowledge — for example, through podcasts, animated children's shows, or community news bulletins
Compare how the same cultural event (e.g. a community celebration) might be communicated differently through different media forms — discussing what each form can and cannot communicate

modes.reason: Use Viewpoints questions explicitly as a structured inquiry frame — 'Who?', 'Where?', 'What story?' — to build transferable critical viewing skills.

nodes.label: Roles and responsibilities of media artists
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the role of media artists and explain what permission means in relation to using and sharing images, sounds and text.
criteria: Student can describe at least one role a media artist plays
Student can explain what permission means in at least one media context (e.g. taking photos of people, using someone else's music)

width.minimum: Describe at least one role a media artist plays (e.g. photographer, animator, filmmaker) and explain one permission consideration for using images or sounds created by others.
width.typical: Discuss the roles of media artists across different types of media; develop class rules for using and creating images, sounds and text; apply permission principles to their own creation and sharing activities; understand that some cultural material belongs to a group rather than an individual.
wider: Develop a class set of rules for using and creating images, sounds and text in media arts — drawing on media artist role examples and permission principles to ground each rule in a real scenario

Investigate a specific case of permission in context: obtaining permission to share a class story as a news bulletin, understanding that permission from individuals and from cultural groups may be different

modes.reason: Connecting media artist roles to permission responsibilities integrates the 'what people do' with the 'what they owe' — support students in seeing permission as an ethical dimension of the media artist's role, not a separate compliance requirement.

descriptors.title: First Nations media arts
descriptors.description: explore examples of media arts produced and/or distributed by First Nations Australians
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify media arts works and explain how they communicate cultural knowledge. They may have encountered First Nations Australian arts works in Foundation but have not yet specifically explored media arts produced and/or distributed by First Nations Australians.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore examples of media arts produced and/or distributed by First Nations Australians, identifying how visual, audio and/or interactive elements communicate cultural knowledge.
elaborations: exploring when, where, how and why First Nations Australians use media arts works to share knowledge about their cultures; for example, during celebrations such as National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children's Day, NAIDOC Week, Reconciliation Week or the acknowledgement of significant occasions including Sorry Day

exploring children's television programs, cartoons/animations and child-focused print media, such as an advertisement encouraging people to adopt a healthy lifestyle, created and distributed by First Nations Australians

observing how visual, audio and/or interactive elements are used in media arts works created by First Nations Australians; for example, exploring colours, symbols and patterns used in media arts works with representatives of the First Nations Australian community or through resources that are created or co-created by First Nations Australians
exploring media arts works created and/or co-created by First Nations Australians that communicate cultural narratives

nodes.label: First Nations media arts works
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify at least one media arts work produced and/or distributed by First Nations Australians and describe its form and context.
criteria: Student can identify at least one media arts work produced by First Nations Australians
Student can describe the form of the work and one context in which it is shared
nodes.hinge_reason: Without encounter with actual First Nations Australian media arts works, subsequent exploration of visual, audio and cultural elements has no concrete material to work from.

width.minimum: Explore one First Nations Australian media arts work (e.g. a children's television program, animation, or podcast) and describe: what form it is in, who made it, and when or where it is shared.
width.typical: Explore a range of First Nations Australian media arts works across forms (television programs, cartoons/animations, print media, podcasts, advertisements); describe the forms, makers and distribution contexts; discuss when and why these works are created (celebrations, NAIDOC Week, Sorry Day, Reconciliation Week, everyday cultural sharing).
wider: Explore First Nations Australian media arts works created for specific occasions (NAIDOC Week, National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children's Day, Sorry Day, Reconciliation Week) — discussing how the occasion shapes the work's purpose and audience
Compare two First Nations Australian media arts works in different forms (e.g. an animated show and a podcast) — describing how each form is used to communicate cultural knowledge

modes.reason: Use resources created or co-created by First Nations Australian communities — expose students to multiple forms (animation, podcast, print media) rather than a single example, to develop understanding of the breadth of First Nations Australian media practice.

nodes.label: Elements and cultural communication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify at least one visual, audio or interactive element in a First Nations Australian media arts work and describe what cultural knowledge it communicates.
criteria: Student can identify at least one visual, audio or interactive element in a First Nations Australian media arts work
Student can describe what cultural knowledge that element communicates (using community resources or accredited materials to ground the description)

width.minimum: Identify one element (colour, symbol, pattern, sound, or image) in a First Nations Australian media arts work and describe what it communicates about culture, identity or story.
width.typical: Observe and describe how visual, audio and/or interactive elements (colours, symbols, patterns, sounds, voices, language) are used in First Nations Australian media arts works to communicate cultural knowledge; work with community representatives or accredited resources to understand the significance of specific elements.
wider: Investigate how colours, symbols and patterns are used in First Nations Australian media arts works — working with community representatives or accessing resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians to understand their cultural significance

Explore media arts works created by First Nations Australians that communicate cultural narratives — comparing how the same story or knowledge is communicated through different media elements in different works

modes.reason: Students need explicit scaffolding to connect observable elements (colour, symbol, sound) to cultural meaning — this requires guided inquiry with community resources or accredited materials, not independent interpretation.

descriptors.title: Share media arts in informal settings
descriptors.description: share media arts works with audiences in informal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can share arts works informally and respond to audience questions. They have not yet shared specifically media arts works in ways that require permission, protocol consideration, or audience relationship thinking.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share media arts works with audiences in informal settings, applying permission principles and considering audience relationships.
elaborations: collecting and sharing class stories and presenting them in the form of a class news bulletin, with permission of the people involved and observing relevant protocols
presenting a media arts work they have made to the class, a small group or their teacher, and explaining how they made it and what they enjoyed about making it
considering relationships that peers may have with their work when creating, rehearsing and recording a radio play, and seeking permission to share it with another class

exploring what permission means; for example, consulting relevant people such as cultural knowledge holders or using online safety resources, and deciding on a class set of rules for using and creating images, sounds and text in media arts works

nodes.label: Permission and protocols for sharing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and apply at least one permission consideration before sharing a media arts work.
criteria: Student can identify at least one permission requirement before sharing a media work
Student applies that permission principle in at least one class sharing activity
nodes.hinge_reason: Permission principles are the non-negotiable precondition for any public sharing — without this, sharing activities cannot proceed ethically, and the habit is foundational to all future media arts practice.

width.minimum: Identify one permission requirement before sharing a media work (e.g. asking peers before using their images) and apply it in a class sharing context.
width.typical: Apply permission principles across sharing contexts — obtaining individual permission for photographs, understanding that cultural material may belong to a group rather than an individual; consult relevant people or online safety resources; develop class rules for sharing.
wider: Develop a class set of rules for using and creating images, sounds and text in media arts works — presenting the rules to the class and explaining the reasoning behind each rule with a real scenario

Explore the difference between individual permission and permission for cultural material belonging to a collective group — using a specific scenario (e.g. a class news bulletin) to ground the distinction

modes.reason: Use real scenarios to build reasoning about permission — 'Before we share this photo of Jake, what do we need to do? Why?' Scenario-based reasoning transfers better than abstract rule recitation.

nodes.label: Presenting in informal settings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share a media arts work with an audience in an informal setting — presenting the work and explaining how it was made or what they enjoyed.
criteria: Student presents a media arts work to an audience in an informal setting
Student explains how the work was made or what they enjoyed about making it

width.minimum: Present one media arts work to a class, small group or teacher — explain how it was made and at least one thing they enjoyed about making it.
width.typical: Present media arts works in informal settings (class, small group, another class); explain making process and enjoyment; collect and share class stories as a news bulletin; create and record a radio play for another class audience; document and seek permission for sharing.
wider: Collect and share class stories as a class news bulletin — applying permission protocols, acknowledging individual and cultural permissions, and presenting the bulletin in a live or recorded format

Create, rehearse and record a radio play in a small group — practising the full creation-to-sharing workflow, seeking permission to share with another class, and reflecting on what it felt like to have a real audience

Present a media arts work to a real community audience beyond the classroom (another class, assembly, school intranet) — considering how the larger audience changes how the work is prepared and presented

modes.reason: Vary the informal sharing contexts — small group, whole class, another class, recorded distribution — so students develop experience of different audience types and begin to understand how audience shapes presentation choices.

descriptors.title: Select and combine elements of music
descriptors.description: select and combine elements of music when composing and practising music for performance
descriptors.knowledge: Students have created arts works that communicate ideas (AC9AMUFC01) and made deliberate choices during making. They have explored voice, body percussion and sound sources through play (AC9AMUFD01). They have no formal vocabulary for elements of music and have not yet deliberately selected or combined musical elements.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and combine elements of music when composing and practising music, using at least two elements deliberately to create expressive or communicative effects.
elaborations: contributing to decisions about how to interpret the elements of music, such as tempo, dynamics and/or articulation when performing songs, chants, rhymes or instrumental music
improvising and making decisions about how to combine sounds to create compositions; for example, combining pitch and rhythm patterns, improvising melodies and drone accompaniments
using voices and body percussion to create music that features contrasting examples of elements of music, such as sound/silence, fast/slow, long/short, high/low, loud/soft
improvising patterns of body movement, such as clapping or stamping, to create accompaniments for songs
practising a repertoire of songs, chants and rhymes focusing on using elements of music such as tempo, dynamics or articulation to create expressive effects
using signs and symbols to notate or document patterns or soundscapes and/or using an available device to record work in progress
practising music using accessible technologies; for example, using recordings to make decisions about dynamics or tempo
writing lyrics for a chant/rap and improvising to develop rhythmic patterns they can use to perform the lyrics

nodes.label: What elements of music are
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name and demonstrate at least three elements of music (e.g. tempo, dynamics, pitch, rhythm) and identify them when listening.
criteria: Can name at least three elements of music when prompted
Can identify each named element when listening to a musical example (e.g. points to the fast/slow change)
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot name and identify elements of music as distinct variables, they cannot make deliberate selections. All subsequent composing and practising decisions in this standard depend on students having a shared vocabulary for elements. Without it, directions like 'vary the tempo here' or 'what element could you change?' are inaccessible.

width.minimum: Identify at least three named elements of music in a piece of music heard; demonstrate each by making a sound or movement that represents it.
width.typical: Name and demonstrate elements including tempo (fast/slow), dynamics (loud/soft), pitch (high/low), duration (long/short), and identify them in a range of musical examples (songs, chants, instrumental music).
wider: Listen to contrasting pieces and identify which elements change and which stay the same — e.g. 'The tempo slowed down but the dynamics stayed loud'
Explore elements through body percussion — create sounds that demonstrate fast/slow, loud/soft, high/low using only body and voice

modes.reason: Build element vocabulary through naming + demonstrating + listening in combination. Games like echo clapping (rhythm), call-and-response pitch matching, and move-with-the-beat activities build the aural recognition that makes vocabulary meaningful rather than just memorised labels.

nodes.label: Combining elements to create effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can combine two or more elements of music deliberately to create a specific expressive effect (e.g. fast and loud to create excitement, slow and soft to create calm).
criteria: Creates a composition or section that deliberately combines at least two named elements
Can describe the expressive effect they intended when combining those elements
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to combine elements deliberately — not just vary one at a time — is the composing move this standard requires. Without it, students' compositions are single-element variations rather than multi-element creations. This cascades to AC9AMU4C01 which requires manipulating elements (plural) to communicate ideas.

width.minimum: Combine two elements of music (e.g. tempo + dynamics) to create a composition or section with a described effect.
width.typical: Combine multiple elements across different composition types — e.g. combining pitch and rhythm in a melody, combining dynamics and articulation in a song performance, using contrasting sections (fast/loud then slow/quiet) to create expressive structure; improvise with voices and body percussion.
wider: Create a composition with at least two clearly contrasting sections (e.g. sound/silence, fast/slow) and describe the expressive effect of each
Improvise a melody with a drone accompaniment — experiment with combining pitch patterns and decide which combinations sound best together

modes.reason: Combination decisions are easier to make when students have encountered many examples of how combinations create different effects. Listening to contrasting pieces and analysing which elements are combined helps students build a mental library of effect-combination relationships.

nodes.label: Selecting elements for a purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make deliberate decisions about which elements to use in a composition or performance to achieve a specific communicative or expressive intention.
criteria: Selects at least two elements for a composition or performance and states a reason for each
Can explain how the selected elements serve the intended communicative or expressive purpose

width.minimum: Choose which elements to include in a composition or performance and state a reason connected to what they want the music to communicate.
width.typical: Make and justify element selections across multiple composition and performance contexts — e.g. deciding to use a slow tempo for a lullaby, choosing to use loud dynamics for an exciting section, selecting particular instruments based on their tone colour; practise a repertoire of songs using elements such as tempo, dynamics or articulation for expressive effect.
wider: Write lyrics for a chant/rap and select rhythmic patterns that match the mood or message of the lyrics — explain the connection
Use accessible technologies (recording device) to listen back to a composition and make decisions about which elements to change to better achieve the intended effect

modes.reason: Selection decisions require students to reason from intent to choice: 'What do you want this music to feel like? Which elements could help create that feeling?' Structured prompting — before composing — builds the habit of selecting with purpose rather than selecting by default.

nodes.label: Documenting and practising
nodes.checkpoint: Students can notate or record a composition using signs, symbols or a recording device, and use this documentation to practise and refine the work.
criteria: Documents a composition in at least one form (drawing, symbols, recording)
Uses the documentation during practice to maintain or refine the composition

width.minimum: Use at least one form of documentation (signs, symbols, drawing or recording) to capture a composition; use it during practice to maintain consistency.
width.typical: Use signs and symbols, graphic notation or available devices to document compositions; use recordings to listen back and make decisions about what to change; practise a repertoire of songs using documentation to support accuracy and refinement.
wider: Create a graphic score that represents a soundscape — use it as a performance guide and refine it based on what worked in rehearsal
Record a composition in progress, listen back, and make one documented change — compare the before and after recordings

modes.reason: Documentation enables practice — without it, compositions exist only in the moment and cannot be refined. The consolidation investment here is in making documentation habitual and functional: students should automatically reach for a recording device or notation tool as part of their composing process.

descriptors.title: Develop listening and performance skills
descriptors.description: develop listening skills and skills for singing and playing instruments
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored their speaking and singing voices through play (AC9AMUFD01) and discovered ways voice can communicate ideas. They have not yet formally practised listening skills for specific musical purposes, ensemble blending, or instrumental technique.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop listening skills for specific musical purposes and demonstrate developing skills for singing and playing instruments across a range of sound sources.
elaborations: experimenting with their speaking and singing voices/vocalisation to create a range of expressive effects
playing music games or taking part in skill-development activities to develop skills for listening, composing and performing
improvising on pitch and rhythm patterns to develop skills relevant to different elements of music; for example, echo clapping, calling and response singing
participating in singing games/activities that involve pitch awareness or matching pitch
developing listening skills for specific purposes, such as listening to count-ins, to become confident about tempo
exploring and improvising ways to create and vary sounds using a range of sound sources, such as voice, classroom instruments, found/environmental objects or digital instruments
developing understanding of what matching pitch means; for example, by using a digital tuner
practising techniques for singing songs and playing classroom instruments

nodes.label: Listening for specific purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can listen to music for at least one specific purpose (e.g. to identify tempo, match pitch, follow a count-in, or stay with the group's dynamic level).
criteria: Demonstrates listening for at least one specific purpose (e.g. follows a count-in, identifies a dynamic change, matches a starting pitch)
Can describe one thing they listened for and what they noticed
nodes.hinge_reason: Purposeful listening is the foundation of all ensemble and performance skill development. Students who listen passively during music activities cannot develop the pitch-matching, ensemble blending and tempo-awareness skills the descriptor requires. This cascades to AC9AMU4D01 which requires manipulating elements in response to listening.

width.minimum: Listen for one specific musical purpose in a structured activity (e.g. stay silent during rests, follow a count-in, identify when the music gets louder).
width.typical: Develop listening skills across multiple specific purposes — listening to count-ins for tempo confidence, listening to blend with others when singing in a group, listening to identify dynamics or articulation and replicating them; participate in active listening activities (moving with the beat, clapping rhythmic ideas).
wider: Participate in ensemble singing with a focus on hearing whether own voice is blending with others — practise adjusting volume in response to listening
Play musical games (e.g. call-and-response) that require listening to a specific feature and replicating it — increase the complexity of the feature over time

modes.reason: Before each listening activity, name the specific purpose: 'This time, listen for when the music changes tempo.' After the activity, ask: 'What did you notice?' Build the habit of directed listening with explicit pre-briefing and reflective debriefing.

nodes.label: Exploring and varying sound sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how sounds from a range of sources (voice, classroom instruments, found objects, digital instruments) can be varied using elements of music.
criteria: Explores at least two different sound sources
Demonstrates at least one variation of a musical element on each source explored

width.minimum: Explore at least two different sound sources; demonstrate one way each can be varied (e.g. played louder/softer, faster/slower, or with a different technique).
width.typical: Explore and improvise ways to create and vary sounds across multiple source types — voice/vocalisation, classroom instruments, found/environmental objects and digital instruments; ask and answer questions such as 'Which way of playing sounds best?' and 'What is the way I want it to sound?'
wider: Compare how the same element (e.g. dynamics) is varied differently on different instruments — what techniques are used on a drum vs a xylophone vs voice?
Explore found and environmental objects as instruments — investigate the range of sounds each can produce and how elements like articulation and tone colour vary

modes.reason: A rich repertoire of sound source experiences builds the tonal imagination that underpins composition and performance decisions. Students who have only explored one or two instruments default to those instruments in composition; broader exploration opens up more deliberate choices.

nodes.label: Pitch awareness and matching
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate developing pitch awareness — attempting to match a given pitch or adjust their singing toward a target pitch.
criteria: Attempts to match a given pitch when singing
Shows some adjustment when aware their pitch is different from the target

width.minimum: Attempt to match a given pitch when singing; describe whether their attempt was close or different.
width.typical: Participate in pitch-matching activities (e.g. echo singing, call-and-response) and gradually adjust pitch to match a partner or group; use a digital tuner or other feedback tool to develop understanding of what pitch-matching means; practise pitch awareness in singing games.
wider: Use a digital tuner to see pitch visualised — sing toward a target pitch and observe the feedback
Play echo singing games across a range of intervals — practise adjusting pitch and noticing how large vs small adjustments feel and sound

modes.reason: Pitch matching develops through repeated, low-stakes practice with clear feedback. Students need many opportunities to try, hear the result and adjust. Consolidation here means repeated pitch-matching activities across different musical games and singing contexts, not formal assessment.

nodes.label: Singing and playing technique
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate basic technique for singing songs and playing classroom instruments with developing control.
criteria: Demonstrates at least one correct technique for singing (e.g. using singing voice, not speaking voice)
Demonstrates at least one correct technique for a classroom instrument (e.g. holding beaters in a way that produces clear sound)

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least one specific technique for singing (e.g. using singing voice, breathing) and one for a classroom instrument (e.g. holding beaters correctly, producing a clean sound).
width.typical: Practise techniques for singing songs and playing classroom instruments across a range of repertoire — using singing voice with appropriate breath support, holding and playing instruments in ways that produce clear sound, developing accuracy and control in rhythm and pitch.
wider: Focus on a specific technique improvement across several rehearsals — compare a recording from week one with week three and describe what changed
Practise a technique (e.g. beater hold) in isolation, then apply it in a group performance — reflect on whether the technique held under performance conditions

modes.reason: Technique at Y1-2 requires repetition to become automatic. The consolidation investment is in returning to the same technique across multiple songs and activities so that correct hold, breath or vocal placement becomes habitual rather than effortful.

descriptors.title: Music across cultures and contexts
descriptors.description: explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and/or other contexts experience music
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored how arts are important for people and communities (AC9AMUFE01) and can identify arts works in their own life. They have not yet formally explored music across diverse cultural or community contexts, or considered the different roles people play in relation to music.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and other contexts experience music, and share observations about music preferences and purposes.
elaborations: listening to and talking about music that features instruments and/or voices from diverse contexts and cultures, and sharing observations about the music
exploring ways that people in their local community are making and experiencing music
identifying opportunities for engaging with music in their daily life by being a composer, performer or audience
discussing where, how and why they and their peers or family members experience music, and their music preferences
practising active listening skills; for example, moving with the beat and clapping rhythmic ideas

nodes.label: Where and how people experience music
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify multiple places and ways people experience music — including as performer, composer and audience.
criteria: Can name at least two different contexts in which people experience music
Can identify at least one role a person plays in relation to music (beyond audience)

width.minimum: Identify at least two different contexts in which people experience music (e.g. at home, at a concert, in a game, in a ceremony).
width.typical: Explore the full range of contexts in which people experience music — at home, in performance spaces, in public spaces, via streaming, in games and screen-based products, in ceremonies; identify different roles (singer, songwriter, composer, instrumentalist, sound engineer, digital producer, audience member).
wider: Map the places and roles of musicians in the school and local community — create a class list of who the musicians are and what they do
Investigate how music is used in screen-based products (games, cartoons, e-books) — ask 'How is the music telling me what to feel?' and 'Who made this music?'

modes.reason: Students' awareness of music contexts is limited to their personal experience at Y1-2. Broadening the contexts they are aware of (ceremonial, digital, community, screen-based) builds the foundation for understanding why music is created for specific purposes and audiences.

nodes.label: Music from diverse cultures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can listen to music from at least one culture or community different from their own and share observations about instruments, voices and purpose.
criteria: Listens to music from at least one unfamiliar cultural context
Can identify at least one instrument or voice and describe one feature of the music (e.g. 'it uses a drum and sounds fast')

width.minimum: Listen to music from one culturally diverse context; identify at least one instrument or voice used and describe one feature of the music.
width.typical: Listen to music from multiple culturally diverse contexts; identify instruments and voices; describe the purpose the music was composed for (e.g. dance, ceremony, celebration, storytelling); share personal responses to the music.
wider: Compare two pieces from different cultural contexts created for similar purposes (e.g. two different celebration songs) — what is similar and what is different?
Explore music from a cultural group represented in the class or local community — share what community members know about the music's purpose and context

modes.reason: The range of cultural music contexts encountered at Y1-2 determines the breadth of students' understanding of why and how people make music. Each new cultural context adds evidence for the diversity of musical purpose and practice.

nodes.label: Personal music preferences and experiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss their own music preferences and compare them with peers and family members, linking preferences to where and how music is experienced.
criteria: Can share a music preference and give at least one reason
Can connect their preference to a context in which they experience that music (e.g. 'I listen to it at home', 'my family plays it at celebrations')

width.minimum: Share one music preference (a type of music, a song, or a context they like music in) and give a reason.
width.typical: Discuss music preferences with peers and family; identify what music they encounter daily and in what contexts; compile or imagine a playlist that combines favourites from different people or generations; practise active listening (moving with the beat, clapping rhythmic ideas).
wider: Compile a family or community playlist combining music from different generations — discuss what each piece means to the people who love it
Investigate how music preferences relate to cultural identity — interview a family member about music important to them and share findings with the class

modes.reason: This node integrates context awareness with personal response — students connect what they know about how music works in different contexts to their own experience of music. The teaching investment is in making the connection between 'music happens in many contexts' and 'I encounter music in specific contexts for specific reasons.'

descriptors.title: First Nations Australian music
descriptors.description: explore examples of music composed and/or performed by First Nations Australians
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored how arts are important for communities (AC9AMUFE01) including listening to First Nations Australians talk about arts and Country/Place. They have explored music from diverse cultural contexts (AC9AMU2E01). This is their first focused exploration of music specifically by First Nations Australian composers and performers.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore examples of music composed and/or performed by First Nations Australians across diverse styles, asking questions about instruments, voices, cultural messages and connections to Country/Place.
elaborations: identifying where and how they can experience music composed and/or performed by First Nations Australians, such as via mainstream music platforms, music for ceremonies, or state and national events
exploring the diverse music styles represented in music composed and performed by First Nations Australians
exploring how the elements of music are used to create specific effects in screen-based or theatrical works that communicate First Nations Australian cultural knowledge

nodes.label: Where First Nations Australian music is heard
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify at least two contexts in which they can experience music composed or performed by First Nations Australians.
criteria: Can name at least two contexts where First Nations Australian music can be experienced
Can identify at least one First Nations Australian musician, group or musical context they have encountered

width.minimum: Name at least two contexts where they could hear First Nations Australian music (e.g. mainstream streaming, school ceremony, local festival, television).
width.typical: Identify and explore multiple contexts — mainstream music platforms, live performance, music for school or community ceremonies, state and national events, local festivals, choirs and orchestras, Welcome to Country and cultural openings.
wider: Access First Nations Australian music through different platform types (streaming service, live performance or community event, television) and compare how each context shapes the listening experience
Identify a local First Nations Australian musician or group and find out where their music can be experienced

modes.reason: Students often assume First Nations Australian music is only encountered in ceremonial or historical contexts. Broadening awareness to include mainstream media, contemporary performance and everyday community life challenges this assumption and opens up ongoing engagement.

nodes.label: Listening to diverse First Nations Australian music styles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can listen to examples of First Nations Australian music across diverse styles and identify instruments, voices and features of the music.
criteria: Can identify at least one instrument or voice in a First Nations Australian music example
Can describe at least one feature of the music (e.g. tempo, mood, instrumentation) and ask at least one question about it
nodes.hinge_reason: The quality of listening engagement here determines whether students engage with First Nations Australian music as genuine music-making or as cultural background. If students do not develop attentive, observational listening skills in this standard, they cannot access the more analytical exploration of cultural knowledge and connection to Country/Place in AC9AMU4E02.

width.minimum: Listen to at least one example of First Nations Australian music; identify one instrument or voice and describe one feature of the music.
width.typical: Listen to First Nations Australian music across diverse styles (mainstream media, local festival, choir/orchestra, ceremonial); identify instruments and voices; ask questions such as 'What instruments can I hear?', 'How is this music similar or different to other music I listen to?', 'How is this music communicating a message about Country/Place?'
wider: Compare two examples of First Nations Australian music from different styles or contexts — describe what is similar and what is different in the instruments, voices and feeling of each
Focus on one example and listen multiple times for different things — first for instruments, then for mood, then for what message the music might be communicating

modes.reason: Use explicit listening frames before and after each listening experience: 'We're going to listen for instruments first — put up your hand when you hear something you recognise.' After listening: 'What did you hear? What was surprising? What questions do you have?' Build observation habits rather than passive reception.

nodes.label: Music communicating messages about Country/Place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how First Nations Australian music communicates messages about Country/Place, asking questions about how musical elements are used to carry those messages.
criteria: Can identify how at least one element of music (e.g. tempo, dynamics) is being used in a First Nations Australian piece to create a specific effect
Can ask or respond to a question about how the music communicates a message or feeling about Country/Place

width.minimum: Listen to one piece of First Nations Australian music connected to Country/Place; identify one way the music might be communicating a message or feeling about a place.
width.typical: Explore screen-based or theatrical works that communicate First Nations Australian cultural knowledge — view animations or cartoons retelling traditional stories; use questions to explore how texture, melody, tempo and dynamics are used to represent characters, mood and narrative; ask 'How is this music telling me about this story/place?'
wider: Watch an animation or cartoon that retells a First Nations Australian story and focus on how the music changes when the setting or character changes — map the musical choices to the narrative
Use Viewpoints questions to analyse how specific elements of music (texture, tempo, dynamics, melody) are used to communicate specific aspects of a First Nations Australian story or place

modes.reason: The connection between music and cultural message is not self-evident to Y1-2 students. Guided Viewpoints questioning ('How is the music telling you about this character/place/moment?') builds the analytical framework that underpins deeper engagement with First Nations Australian cultural knowledge through music in subsequent bands.

descriptors.title: Perform music in informal settings
descriptors.description: sing and play music in informal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can share arts works with audiences (AC9AMUFP01), understand the audience relationship, and have practised basic music performance skills (staying in time, using singing voice). They have not yet performed with formal introductions, staging decisions or post-performance reflection.
descriptors.endpoint: Students sing and play music in informal settings, following agreed performance decisions, introducing performances to audiences, and contributing to post-performance discussion.
elaborations: singing songs, performing chants/raps or playing instrumental music they have learnt or composed for an audience of peers and teachers
following agreed decisions about how the music should sound; for example, using singing voice rather than speaking voice
making decisions about how/where to sit/stand in a performance space
introducing a performance by writing text for a slide that shares information about the music with the audience
listening intentionally and respectfully during performances
contributing to post-performance discussions

nodes.label: Following agreed performance decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can follow agreed decisions about how music should sound during a performance (e.g. using singing voice, performing at the agreed tempo, holding instruments correctly).
criteria: Follows at least two agreed performance decisions during a group performance
Can identify whether they met the agreed decisions when reflecting after the performance
nodes.hinge_reason: Following agreed decisions is the foundational collective skill of ensemble performance. Students who cannot subordinate personal impulse to group agreement cannot function in ensemble contexts, which underpins all performance work in Y3-4 and beyond. This is also where performance as a social and communicative act — not just individual music-making — is first established.

width.minimum: Follow at least two agreed performance decisions (e.g. use singing voice AND perform at the agreed tempo) in a group performance.
width.typical: Follow a full set of agreed performance decisions across singing and instrumental music — using correct voice type, agreed tempo, agreed dynamics, correct instrument hold; begin to self-monitor whether they are meeting the agreed decisions during performance.
wider: Discuss which performance decisions are most important for the audience experience — prioritise and explain choices
Practise a section of a performance specifically focused on one agreed decision, then perform the whole piece and evaluate whether the decision was maintained

modes.reason: Agreed performance decisions need to be established early in rehearsal and reinforced repeatedly before performance. Consolidation here means using rehearsal time to practise the specific decisions — stop, name the decision, try it again — rather than running through the piece from start to finish.

nodes.label: Staging and presentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make and justify at least one decision about how to position themselves in a performance space.
criteria: Can give at least one reason for a staging choice (related to seeing cues, hearing others, or audience visibility)
Contributes to a staging decision in a group performance

width.minimum: Identify at least one reason why where they stand/sit during a performance matters (e.g. to see the conductor, to hear others, for the audience to see them).
width.typical: Contribute to decisions about how/where to sit/stand in a performance space — consider whether curved or straight rows allow them to see cues, whether standing or sitting affects their ability to perform accurately; try different options and discuss which works better.
wider: Try two different staging arrangements for the same performance and compare: which made it easier to see cues? Which looked better for the audience?
Discuss how the size and shape of a performance space (classroom vs hall vs outdoors) changes staging decisions

modes.reason: Staging decisions are a concrete, discussable case of performance planning. Use guided questions: 'Can you see the teacher/conductor from there?', 'Can the audience see you?', 'Can you hear the other performers?' This builds the habit of thinking about performance holistically rather than just about the music itself.

nodes.label: Introducing a performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can introduce a performance by sharing information about the music — including at least the title and one piece of contextual information (e.g. who composed it, when or why it was created).
criteria: Contributes to or delivers an introduction that includes the title and at least one piece of contextual information
Can explain why introducing a performance is useful for the audience

width.minimum: Introduce a performance with at least a title and one piece of contextual information about the music.
width.typical: Write or contribute to a spoken or visual introduction to a performance sharing: title, composer, and where/when/why the music was composed; deliver or display the introduction before or during the performance.
wider: Create a projected slide introduction for a performance — include title, composer, context, and one personal reflection from the performers
Introduce a performance by connecting the music to its cultural context — share one thing about where this music comes from and why it matters

modes.reason: Introducing a performance is a significant step from Foundation sharing — it requires students to frame their work in context for an audience. Support with sentence starters and a simple introduction template: 'The name of our piece is... It was composed by... We chose it because...'

nodes.label: Respectful listening and post-performance discussion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can listen intentionally and respectfully during others' performances and contribute to a post-performance discussion.
criteria: Listens attentively during a peer performance without disrupting
Contributes at least one specific comment or question to a post-performance discussion

width.minimum: Listen respectfully during one peer performance; contribute at least one comment or question to a post-performance discussion.
width.typical: Listen intentionally during performances, participating where invited (e.g. clapping along, joining in singing); contribute to post-performance discussions by sharing what they noticed, what worked well, or asking questions of the performers.
wider: Ask a specific question of performers after a performance — e.g. 'How did you get your instrument to make that sound?' or 'How long did you practise that?'
Compare two performances of the same piece (e.g. a rehearsal recording vs the final performance) and describe what changed

modes.reason: Post-performance discussion integrates all previous performance work — following decisions, staging, introduction — with the audience relationship established at Foundation. Students who can articulate what they noticed connect performance as communication to their own listening experience.

descriptors.title: Use visual conventions and materials to create artworks
descriptors.description: use visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials to create artworks
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create artworks that communicate ideas using materials and play (AC9AVAFC01). They have begun making deliberate choices about what to include and why. They have not yet used visual conventions deliberately or selected processes to serve specific communicative intentions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials to create artworks, making deliberate choices about how these elements work together.

nodes.label: What visual conventions are
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and name basic visual conventions — line, shape, colour, texture — and recognise how they are used in artworks.
criteria: Names at least two visual conventions correctly
Identifies those conventions in at least one artwork or environmental example
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot name and recognise visual conventions cannot use them deliberately in making — the vocabulary enables the intentionality that all subsequent creating nodes require.

width.minimum: Name at least two visual conventions (e.g. line, colour, shape, texture) and identify them in an artwork or the environment.
width.typical: Identify and name a range of visual conventions (line, shape, colour, texture, pattern, space) in artworks, the environment and their own making; distinguish between open lines and closed shapes.
wider: Observe how visual conventions are used in artworks and designs by First Nations Australians — identify colours, symbols and patterns with guidance from culturally authoritative resources
Go on a 'line hunt' — photograph or sketch different types of lines in the school environment and categorise them

modes.reason: Visual convention vocabulary needs to accumulate across many encounters in making, looking and environment. Students who have seen conventions named in only one or two contexts develop fragile recognition.

nodes.label: Experimenting with materials and processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can experiment with a range of materials and visual arts processes to discover what effects are possible.
criteria: Experiments with at least two different materials or processes
Describes at least one effect discovered — what the material or process can do

width.minimum: Try at least two materials or processes; describe one effect discovered.
width.typical: Experiment with a range of materials and processes (mark-making, printing, layering, 3D construction, digital tools); explore accidental and intentional effects; reflect on what each material can do.
wider: Explore layering as a visual technique — build a surface using pastels, then watercolour, ink and wax; identify how each layer changes the work
Combine digital and analog tools in one experiment — use a drawing app alongside traditional media and compare what each can do

modes.reason: Students who experiment with only one or two materials develop limited material vocabulary. A wider range of processes (printing, layering, 3D, digital) reveals that different materials serve different communicative purposes.

nodes.label: Using conventions and materials to create
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and use visual conventions, processes and materials deliberately to create an artwork.
criteria: Creates an artwork using at least one named visual convention deliberately
Can explain why they chose a particular material, process or convention for this work

width.minimum: Create an artwork that uses at least one named visual convention and one chosen process or material deliberately.
width.typical: Create artworks using combinations of visual conventions, processes and materials; make and explain choices about how these elements serve the work's communicative intent; include both analog and digital options.
wider: Create an artwork that combines digital and analog art-making — respond with colour, line and shape to music to communicate how the music makes you feel
Use 3D construction methods to represent an idea from another learning area — select materials (modelling clay, found objects) based on what the work needs to communicate
Create a collagraph or relief print — select textures and materials deliberately to produce a specific visual effect

modes.reason: Students bring together their understanding of conventions and their material experimentation to create with deliberate intent. The coordinating move — choosing elements because they serve the work — is the integration point.

descriptors.strand: Visual arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Experiment and play with visual conventions and materials
descriptors.description: experiment and play with visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use play and imagination to discover possibilities with materials (AC9AVAFD01). They have begun noticing visual qualities and developing ideas through experimentation. They have not yet deliberately experimented with visual conventions as named elements.
descriptors.endpoint: Students experiment and play with visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials, reflecting on what they discover.

nodes.label: Playing within limits
nodes.checkpoint: Students can work with constraints on materials or processes to focus experimentation and notice what the material can do.
criteria: Engages with at least one material or process constraint
Describes at least one discovery — what worked, what failed, or what could be used again

width.minimum: Work with one material or process constraint (e.g. only one colour, only folding and tearing) and describe what was discovered.
width.typical: Play with a range of constrained experiments (limited materials, limited tools, limited time, silent working); describe discoveries and failures; identify what could be used in a future artwork.
wider: Work in small groups to make something from a surprise bag of everyday materials — compare what different groups discovered about the same materials
Set a timed challenge to find as many ways as possible to create lines using a wide range of materials — compare results and discuss what each option is good for

modes.reason: Constrained play focuses attention on what materials actually do rather than defaulting to familiar habits. Different constraint types (colour, tool, process) reveal different material properties.

nodes.label: Reflecting on experimentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use questions (Viewpoints-style) to reflect on their arts experiences — naming what was challenging, what was discovered and what failures led to something new.
criteria: Responds to at least one reflection question about an experiment with specific content
Identifies something specific that was challenging, discovered or produced from failure
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reflect on their experiments cannot convert discoveries into purposeful future making — the reflective habit is the mechanism that links experimentation to growing artistic practice.

width.minimum: Answer at least one reflection question about an experiment: what was challenging, what was discovered, or what failed and what came from the failure.
width.typical: Use Viewpoints questions to reflect on multiple experiments; document reflections through annotation, arrows or statements; connect discoveries to potential future artworks.
wider: Create a sound or voice file that accompanies a visual experiment — talk through the thinking and learning as a 'work-in-progress' presentation
Examine artworks and identify a 'layer + layer + layer' structure — experiment with the same layering approach and annotate how each layer changed the work

modes.reason: Reflection at this level is not intuitive — students need question scaffolds ('What was challenging?', 'What failed and what came from it?') to surface the thinking. Without the scaffold, reflection stays at 'I liked it/didn't like it'.

nodes.label: Using arts language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use visual arts language when describing and documenting their experiments — naming conventions, processes and effects.
criteria: Uses at least two visual arts terms accurately when describing an experiment or artwork
Applies at least one term to their own work in a way that shows they understand what it names

width.minimum: Use at least two visual arts terms (e.g. line, shape, texture, colour, layering) when describing an experiment or artwork.
width.typical: Use visual arts language accurately across multiple experiments; annotate visual experiments with short statements and arrows; identify open lines, closed shapes, layering and other conventions in their own work.
wider: Explore visual conventions in artworks by First Nations Australians — use visual arts language to describe what is observed with guidance from culturally authoritative resources
Identify the difference between open lines and closed shapes across a range of media — digitally fill selected areas using collaged closed shapes to form silhouettes

modes.reason: Accurate use of visual arts language requires repeated use across contexts until it becomes fluent. Students who use terms inconsistently or only when prompted need consolidation practice across many examples.

descriptors.title: Visual arts across cultures and contexts
descriptors.description: explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and/or other contexts experience visual arts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify arts in their own lives and explain why arts matter to communities (AC9AVAFE01). They have begun to recognise that arts serve functions beyond personal enjoyment. They have not yet investigated specific artists, their practices or arts across different cultural contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and other contexts experience visual arts, and share observations and questions about artworks and artists.

nodes.label: Looking at artworks — asking questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can look carefully at an artwork and share observations and questions about it — what they see, what they think it means, and what they want to know.
criteria: Shares at least one observation about an artwork (what they see)
Asks at least one genuine question about the artwork or artist
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot ask genuine questions about artworks treat looking as passive — they have no mechanism for investigating how or why arts are made across cultures, which blocks the descriptor's 'explore' demand.

width.minimum: Look at one artwork and share at least one observation and one question.
width.typical: Examine a range of artworks and develop Viewpoints questions — 'What is the story?', 'What do I recognise?', 'What materials might have been used?'; share observations and questions with peers.
wider: Examine artworks that represent subject matter from other learning areas (living creatures, celebrations, environments) — identify similarities and differences across cultural contexts
Explore artworks from a local, state or national collection — use Viewpoints questions to investigate what the work might be saying and why it was made

modes.reason: Questioning is not intuitive at this level — students need question scaffolds (Viewpoints prompts) to move from surface observation to genuine inquiry. Without scaffolds, looking stays at 'I like/don't like it'.

nodes.label: Investigating artists and their practices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate an artist and their practice — where they work, what materials and techniques they use, and when and why they made an artwork.
criteria: Identifies the artist, approximate time/place, and at least one material or technique for an artwork
Shares one idea about why the artist might have made the work

width.minimum: Identify who made an artwork, when or where it was made, and one material or technique used.
width.typical: Investigate a range of living Australian artists using Viewpoints questions; explore their practices, materials and techniques; discuss what motivated the work.
wider: Explore artworks by living Australian artists from a diverse range of backgrounds — compare how different artists communicate similar subject matter
Investigate an artist whose practice responds to place or environment — connect this to your own understanding of places that matter to you

modes.reason: Students who investigate only one artist type develop narrow assumptions about what 'an artist' is. A diverse range of living Australian artists (in age, background, location, medium) builds richer understanding.

nodes.label: Exploring visual arts across cultures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how and why people across different cultures and communities experience and make visual arts — identifying similarities and differences in purpose, context and visual conventions.
criteria: Explores artworks from at least two different cultures or communities
Identifies at least one similarity and one difference between them in terms of purpose, context or visual conventions

width.minimum: Compare two artworks from different cultures or communities; identify one similarity and one difference.
width.typical: Explore artworks from a range of cultures, communities and contexts; use Viewpoints questions to investigate where, why and how arts are experienced; connect to subject matter from other learning areas.
wider: Explore when, where, how and why First Nations Australians use visual arts, crafts and designs to share cultural knowledge — investigate artworks connected to NAIDOC Week, Reconciliation Week or similar occasions using culturally authoritative resources
Compare how artists from different cultural contexts represent similar subject matter (e.g. living things, celebrations) — discuss how cultural context shapes what is emphasised

modes.reason: The descriptor explicitly requires 'cultures, communities and/or other contexts' — students who explore only one cultural context cannot meet the descriptor's scope. First Nations contexts are an especially important extension direction.

descriptors.title: First Nations visual arts
descriptors.description: explore examples of visual arts created by First Nations Australians
descriptors.knowledge: Students have begun to explore arts across cultures and communities (AC9AVA2E01). They have some awareness that arts serve different purposes in different communities. They have not yet specifically explored First Nations Australian visual arts or the concept of Country/Place in art-making.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore examples of visual arts created by First Nations Australians, identifying how these artworks communicate connection to Country/Place and cultural identity.

nodes.label: Country/Place in First Nations visual arts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that many First Nations Australian artworks feature Country/Place as central — connecting where we are to who we are.
criteria: Identifies at least one way a First Nations Australian artwork represents or communicates place
Explains why place might be important to the artist or their community
nodes.hinge_reason: The Country/Place concept is foundational to understanding First Nations Australian visual arts at this level — without it, students interpret these artworks through a generic 'landscape' lens that misses the cultural function.

width.minimum: Look at one First Nations Australian artwork and identify one way it represents or communicates place.
width.typical: Explore artworks by First Nations Australian artists that feature places as central; discuss what the artworks communicate about why place is part of identity; engage with artists' own voices through culturally authoritative resources.
wider: Listen to First Nations Australian artists describe the importance of Country/Place to their art-making — using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians
Explore artworks that represent First Nations Australians' interpretations of the night sky — discuss how different times of year and different perspectives shape the sky as subject matter

modes.reason: The concept that place is part of identity is culturally unfamiliar for many students. Explicit discussion with prompts ('Why might where you are be part of who you are?') is needed before students can engage with the artworks meaningfully.

nodes.label: Visual conventions in First Nations arts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can observe specific visual conventions (colours, symbols, patterns) used in First Nations Australian artworks and connect them to cultural meaning.
criteria: Identifies at least one visual convention in a First Nations Australian artwork
Shares one observation about what the convention might mean or communicate

width.minimum: Identify at least one visual convention (colour, symbol or pattern) in a First Nations Australian artwork and share one observation about why it might be used.
width.typical: Observe how visual conventions are used in a range of First Nations Australian artworks; discuss colours, symbols and patterns with guidance from culturally authoritative resources or community representatives; connect conventions to cultural meanings.
wider: Co-create symbols and designs to represent patterns visible in the night sky at different times of year — do this with First Nations Australians who have cultural authority
Explore First Nations Australian cultural expressions in community settings and at national events — identify how artists observe protocols and respect Elders or knowledge holders

modes.reason: Students need to engage with a range of First Nations Australian visual arts rather than a single example to develop genuine understanding — diverse artists, regions and forms prevent the misconception that all First Nations art looks the same.

nodes.label: First Nations arts in community and national life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify where First Nations Australian cultural expressions appear in their lives and communities, and recognise that artists follow cultural protocols.
criteria: Identifies at least one place or occasion where First Nations Australian cultural expressions appear
Shows awareness that artists follow cultural protocols and that these are meaningful

width.minimum: Identify at least one place or occasion where First Nations Australian cultural expressions are present (in community, at national events, at school).
width.typical: Explore how First Nations Australian cultural expressions appear in community and national life; notice ways that artists observe protocols and respect Elders; connect these observations to the earlier understanding of arts as important for communities.
wider: Explore artworks connected to significant occasions (NAIDOC Week, Reconciliation Week, Sorry Day) — investigate how these artworks serve community and cultural purposes
Use Viewpoints questions to co-create an inquiry about a First Nations Australian artist and their practice — investigate what the work teaches about their community and Country

modes.reason: Students bring together their understanding of Country/Place, visual conventions and cultural community functions to see First Nations visual arts as a living, ongoing practice — not a historical artefact.

descriptors.title: Share artworks in informal settings
descriptors.description: share artworks and/or visual arts practice in informal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can share artworks with an audience and say something about the work (AC9AVAFP01). They have basic experience of informal sharing with peers and the teacher. They have not yet made deliberate decisions about audience, context or presentation format.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share artworks and/or visual arts practice in informal settings, making choices about audience and ways to share.

nodes.label: Deciding how and with whom to share
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different ways and audiences for sharing artworks — from sharing with a friend to sharing with the whole class or online with families.
criteria: Identifies at least two different ways or audiences for sharing an artwork
Makes a choice and gives a reason for it

width.minimum: Identify at least two different ways or audiences for sharing an artwork and choose one.
width.typical: Identify a range of sharing options (class, small group, school LMS, teacher, family); choose an appropriate audience and format for a specific artwork; explain the choice.
wider: Post an artwork or work-in-progress on the school learning management system with a short explanation — consider what families can understand about the work from the image and text
Decide whether to share a finished work or a work-in-progress, and explain what sharing at each stage communicates to the audience

modes.reason: Students at this level default to 'show everyone' without considering what different sharing contexts involve. Structured prompts ('Who would understand this work best? What do you want people to know about it?') build deliberate decision-making.

nodes.label: Sharing and explaining
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share an artwork or visual arts practice in an informal setting and explain what they like, what they made or what the work communicates.
criteria: Shares at least one artwork in an informal setting
Explains at least one thing — what they like, what the work shows, or how they made it

width.minimum: Share one artwork in an informal setting and explain one thing — what they like, what it shows, or how they made it.
width.typical: Share artworks and visual arts practice in multiple informal settings; explain choices, ideas and processes; respond to questions; participate in peer activities that involve explaining and interpreting works.
wider: Dramatise the making of a work — use gesture and movement to communicate the creative process for an audience, then select the most successful section and frame it for display
Participate in a peer activity where everyday-object artworks are matched to their objects — explain how you interpreted the visual personification choices made

modes.reason: Different sharing formats demand different explanatory moves. The dramatised presentation, the gallery-walk, and the work-in-progress review each require students to communicate in distinct ways — a range of formats builds versatile presentational capability.

descriptors.title: Choreograph to communicate ideas
descriptors.description: use the elements of dance to choreograph dance that communicates ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use elements of dance to choreograph dance sequences (Y1-2). They have produced sequences with beginning, middle and end, made deliberate element choices, and used feedback to refine their work.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use the elements of dance to choreograph dance that communicates ideas, perspectives and/or meaning.
elaborations: improvising using movements from a dance they have learnt and using elements to develop sequences based on original movements
using Viewpoints to frame questions about choreography being developed
creating dance sequences by combining fundamental locomotor and non-locomotor movements at various levels and directions
using learning from First Nations Australians' connection to Country/Place to devise dance communicating their own connection

nodes.label: Choreographic intent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and articulate a clear choreographic intent — the idea, perspective or meaning their dance will communicate.
criteria: Student can articulate what idea, feeling or perspective their dance communicates before or during the choreographic process
Student can explain how at least one element choice serves their communicative intent
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a clear intent, choreographic choices become arbitrary — students select movements for visual interest rather than communicative purpose. Intent is what transforms movement arrangement into dance that communicates meaning.

width.minimum: Articulating one intended meaning or idea for a dance before beginning choreography — using Viewpoints questions to frame the intent.
width.typical: Using Viewpoints questions to clarify choreographic intent: 'How will the dance begin/end?', 'What shapes will we make?', 'How can we connect these parts?'; planning structure (beginning, middle, end) around a chosen idea, perspective or connection to Country/Place.
wider: Use learning from dances that communicate First Nations Australians' connection to Country/Place to frame intent — devising a dance communicating students' own connection to and responsibility for a place in their community
Investigate how dances from different cultural celebrations communicate specific ideas — using this research to frame and enrich their own choreographic intent

modes.reason: Articulating intent requires rehearsal — students often discover what they want to say through movement rather than before it. Use Viewpoints questions iteratively: before, during and after choreography. Journal or verbal planning tools help crystallise intent.

nodes.label: Generating and extending movement material
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generate movement material using improvisation and known movements, extending and varying sequences using choreographic exploration.
criteria: Student can generate at least three movement variations from one starting movement (varying level, direction, dynamics, body part, or timing)
Student demonstrates use of both locomotor and non-locomotor movements in generated material

width.minimum: Improvising from at least one known movement type; generating two or more extension variations (e.g. at different levels, in different directions, with different dynamics).
width.typical: Improvising using locomotor and non-locomotor movements; exploring known movements to find alternative versions; using contrast and repetition to generate new material; combining running and sliding, bending and stretching; using a variety of levels and directions.
wider: Use cultural stories as stimulus — developing movements to represent different aspects of a story (character walk, mood, setting)
Explore how the same movement changes meaning when performed at different levels, with different dynamics, or in different spatial relationships with a partner

modes.reason: Students need material to work with before they can structure it. Prioritise movement generation across multiple sessions and stimuli before expecting students to select, combine and arrange.

nodes.label: Structuring and combining into whole dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select, combine and structure movement material into a dance that communicates their intended meaning — using choreographic decisions to shape the whole.
criteria: Student produces a dance with a clear beginning, middle and end
Student can explain how their structural choices (how it begins, how it ends) serve the communicative intent
Student can identify at least one change they made in response to feedback
nodes.hinge_reason: Producing a complete structured dance — not just movement material — is the capability milestone of this standard. Students who cannot yet structure and combine at this level will lack the compositional experience to engage with choreographic devices (Y5-6 C strand) and more complex structural forms.

width.minimum: A structured dance with clear beginning, middle and end; at least two deliberate element choices serving the communicative intent; combined with a partner or group.
width.typical: Selecting and combining locomotor and non-locomotor movements into sequences; structuring into a dance with beginning-middle-end; combining with a partner or group to extend; using Viewpoints to evaluate and refine structural choices; following protocols where content draws on First Nations knowledge.
wider: Choreograph a dance that communicates connection to and responsibility for a specific place in their community — with element choices that reflect emotional relationship to place
Extend the dance by layering a second structural device (e.g. canon, contrast section, call-and-response) to deepen the communication of meaning

modes.reason: Structuring integrates intent (N1) with generated material (N2) into a communicative whole. Scaffold with explicit structure prompts and repeated partner/group sharing — hearing 'what did you think my dance was about?' calibrates intent-execution alignment.

descriptors.title: Practise safe and expressive movement
descriptors.description: experiment with and practise skills for moving safely and expressively using fundamental movement skills and the elements of dance
descriptors.knowledge: Students can move safely and expressively using fundamental movement skills and elements of dance (Y1-2). They have established spatial awareness and can use movement quality to communicate ideas.
descriptors.endpoint: Students experiment with and practise skills for moving safely and expressively using fundamental movement skills and the elements of dance.
elaborations: exploring known movements to find alternative ways of performing them at different levels, directions, sizes, body parts
using contrast and repetition to explore and generate new movement in response to stimuli
exploring how elements of dance can be used to communicate ideas from cultural stories
developing the habit of always using safe dance practice including warm-up and cool-down
developing body awareness and refining technical skills in response to teacher feedback

nodes.label: Safe practice as habit
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate safe dance practice as a consistent habit — including warm-up and cool-down, and surface/footwear awareness.
criteria: Student independently initiates warm-up before dance activity
Student makes at least one independent safe practice decision during a session (e.g. adjusts footwear, identifies space)
