nodes.hinge_reason: Safe practice at this band involves students taking increased personal responsibility — not just following instructions. This self-regulatory habit is necessary before students can engage with more complex technical demands (balance, coordination, accuracy) without injury risk.

width.minimum: Independently warming up before dance activity and cooling down after; removing socks on slippery surfaces; demonstrating spatial awareness consistently across sessions.
width.typical: Developing the habit of safe dance practice: warming up before complex movement patterns; cooling/calming down afterwards; adapting to surface conditions; maintaining spatial awareness and body control as complexity increases.
wider: Lead a warm-up sequence for a small group — making decisions about what to include and why
Reflect explicitly on how warm-up changes movement capacity — comparing quality of movement before and after

modes.reason: Safe practice must be fully habitual before technical complexity increases. Consistent reinforcement across sessions — not one-off instruction — builds the automatic self-regulation this requires.

nodes.label: Technical skills — body control and accuracy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can refine technical movement skills — body control, accuracy, alignment, strength, balance and coordination — in fundamental movements.
criteria: Student demonstrates improved body control or accuracy in a target movement following teacher feedback
Student can perform a fundamental movement with attention to at least two technical qualities (e.g. alignment and balance)

width.minimum: Demonstrating body control and accuracy in at least two fundamental movement types in response to teacher feedback.
width.typical: Developing body awareness and refining technical skills in fundamental movements: control, accuracy, alignment, strength, balance, coordination; exploring known movements to find alternative ways of performing them (waving at different levels, with different body parts, bigger/smaller); using contrast and repetition to explore and generate new movement.
wider: Focus sustained technical practice on one complex movement type (e.g. rolling, jumping and landing, balance sequences) — refining quality across multiple attempts
Explore how the same technical skill (e.g. balance) can be used expressively — comparing technical execution with expressive intent

modes.reason: Technical precision requires repeated practice with feedback. Set specific technical targets and return to them across sessions — accuracy, alignment and balance are skills that improve with deliberate repetition, not one-off exposure.

nodes.label: Using elements to communicate ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the elements of dance deliberately to communicate ideas — connecting physical skill to expressive intent.
criteria: Student uses at least two elements intentionally in movement — can explain the expressive purpose of each choice
An observer can identify what idea the student is communicating from their movement quality

width.minimum: Using at least two elements intentionally in a movement sequence to communicate a specific idea.
width.typical: Exploring how elements of dance communicate ideas: using elements to develop locomotor and non-locomotor movements representing aspects of a story (character walks, emotions, moods of a place); making deliberate element choices to express ideas clearly.
wider: Explore how cultural stories can be shared through dance — using element choices to represent different aspects of a specific cultural narrative
Compare how changing one element (e.g. switching from slow to sharp dynamics) changes what an idea communicates — developing selective expressive awareness

modes.reason: Communicative movement integrates technical skill (N2) with element awareness and intent. This is where physical capacity becomes expressive capacity — connect technical work explicitly to expressive purpose.

descriptors.title: Dance across cultures, times and places
descriptors.description: explore where, why and how dance is choreographed and/or performed across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify where, why and how people experience dance across cultures and communities (Y1-2). They can observe and describe dance features using learnt terminology.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore where, why and how dance is choreographed and/or performed across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts.
elaborations: identifying meaning and describing purposes that dance is created for across a range of cultures
learning dances created for different purposes such as entertainment, dance crazes
using Viewpoints to ask questions about similarities, where dances are performed

nodes.label: Purposes and meanings of dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe different purposes for which dance is choreographed and performed across cultures and times.
criteria: Student can describe at least two different purposes for which dance is created and performed
Student can identify at least one dance from a cultural context different from their own and explain its purpose

width.minimum: Identifying at least two different purposes for dance from at least two different cultural or temporal contexts.
width.typical: Identifying meaning and purposes across a range of dances: cultural celebration, narrative storytelling, entertainment, ceremony; exploring dances from local community and/or countries in Asia; noting dances created for entertainment ('dance crazes', widely known dances).
wider: Investigate a dance craze or widely known dance — tracing its origin, spread, and transformation across different cultural contexts
Explore dances from a country or region in Asia — identifying their cultural purpose, the occasions on which they are performed, and what they communicate

modes.reason: Understanding purposes requires genuine range — single-context exposure produces single-context understanding. Ensure dances encountered span multiple purposes (not all celebrations, not all entertainment).

nodes.label: Comparing dance across contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare dances from different cultures, times or places — identifying similarities and differences and asking questions about what they observe.
criteria: Student can identify at least one similarity and one difference between two dances from different cultural or temporal contexts
Student generates at least one question about what they have observed in a dance from an unfamiliar context

width.minimum: Comparing two dances from different cultural or temporal contexts — identifying at least one similarity and one difference.
width.typical: Using Viewpoints questions ('Are the movements similar to movements in dances you know?', 'Where are these dances performed?') to explore and compare dances across cultures, times and places; identifying movement similarities and differences; connecting observations to context.
wider: Investigate how a dance tradition has changed over time — exploring how context, purpose or materials have evolved while the dance persists
Explore dances from two countries in Asia and compare how they reflect cultural values, stories or occasions

modes.reason: Comparison requires a frame — use Viewpoints questions to structure observation before students attempt to compare. Name what they are looking for: movements, music, costume, setting, purpose, audience relationship.

descriptors.title: First Nations dance and country/place
descriptors.description: explore how First Nations Australians use dance to communicate their connection to and responsibility for Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored examples of dance choreographed and/or performed by First Nations Australians (Y1-2). They can observe element use in First Nations dance and know that First Nations Australians use dance on significant cultural occasions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how First Nations Australians use dance to communicate their connection to and responsibility for Country/Place.
elaborations: collecting and sharing information about dances for festivals or ceremonies; reflecting on how they communicate knowledge about Country/Place
exploring how First Nations Australians use dance to express connection to and responsibility for Country/Place including seasonal knowledge
exploring screen-based storytelling to maintain unique ways of life
observing how elements are used in dances communicating connection to Country/Place
exploring movements in dances with community representatives or co-created resources

nodes.label: Connection and responsibility through dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how First Nations Australians use dance to express connection to and responsibility for Country/Place, culture and people.
criteria: Student can explain what 'connection to Country/Place' means in the context of First Nations Australian dance
Student can describe how at least one specific dance communicates this connection
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a genuine conceptual grasp of connection and responsibility as expressed through dance, students cannot move beyond surface observation. This understanding is the foundation for the more analytical engagement required in Y5-6 (revitalising cultures) and Y7-8 (ICIP rights).

width.minimum: Describing at least one way in which a First Nations Australian dance communicates connection to or responsibility for Country/Place — using a specific example.
width.typical: Exploring how First Nations Australians use dance to express connection to and responsibility for Country/Place: communicating knowledge about local seasons, wind, water, fire, sustainable practices; exploring dances with representatives of First Nations Australian communities or via resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians.
wider: Collect and share information about dances performed by First Nations Australians at festivals or ceremonies — reflecting on how these dances communicate knowledge about Country/Place
Explore screen-based storytelling used by First Nations Australians to maintain unique ways of life — comparing with dance forms used for similar purposes

modes.reason: Connection and responsibility are concepts that require explicit unpacking — they are not self-evident from observation alone. Use guided discussion and resources created by First Nations Australians to build conceptual understanding before asking students to describe it.
Exploring multiple examples of how different First Nations communities use dance to express their relationship to Country/Place prevents conflation of all First Nations Australian cultures.

nodes.label: Elements communicating Country/Place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how specific element choices in First Nations Australian dance communicate knowledge about Country/Place.
criteria: Student can identify at least one element choice in a First Nations Australian dance and explain what it communicates about Country/Place
Student engages with First Nations dance content with respect — uses appropriate terminology and follows any protocols introduced

width.minimum: Identifying at least one element of dance used in a First Nations Australian dance and explaining how it communicates something about Country/Place.
width.typical: Observing how elements of dance (movement, space, time, dynamics) are used in dances choreographed and performed by First Nations Australians to communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place — e.g. how movements represent wind, water, fire, or seasonal knowledge; exploring movements with community representatives or through co-created resources.
wider: Compare element use across two First Nations Australian dances from different communities — identifying how different environmental or seasonal knowledge is communicated through different element choices
Explore cultural accounts of Country/Place through dance with community representation — noticing how specific movement types carry specific knowledge

modes.reason: Reading element use as culturally meaningful — not just aesthetically interesting — requires a specific observational frame. Scaffold with focused questions: 'What in the movement shows us something about this place?', 'What do you think this movement represents?'

descriptors.title: Practise and perform informally
descriptors.description: practise and perform dances in informal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students have shared dance sequences in informal settings (Y1-2). They can present with expressive intent and reflect on performances using Viewpoints questions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students practise and perform dances in informal settings.
elaborations: using expressive skills such as projection and focus to communicate to an audience
presenting dance using screen-based technologies or online platforms
being an attentive audience member during class performances and providing constructive feedback
sharing meaning and intended purposes using own words, images, learnt terminology, movement or drawing

nodes.label: Expressive skills in performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use expressive skills — projection and focus — to communicate dance ideas to an audience.
criteria: Student demonstrates projection or focus in their performance — visible to an observer
Student can name the expressive skill they are using and describe what it involves

width.minimum: Demonstrating at least one expressive skill (projection or focus) in a performance — student can name and describe what they are doing.
width.typical: Using expressive skills of projection and focus in informal performances: looking out and up to communicate joy; extending movements outwards; maintaining focus to communicate intention; practising these skills across multiple performances.
wider: Practise the same sequence with deliberate variation in expressive skill (e.g. with and without projection) — comparing what changes in the audience's experience
View recordings of own performances to identify where expressive skills are strong and where they could be developed

modes.reason: Expressive performance skills require repeated practice across many performance opportunities. Single performances don't build the consistency and confidence that genuine performance presence requires.

nodes.label: Presenting and reflecting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present a dance to an audience, communicate its meaning and purpose, and be an attentive audience member for peers' work.
criteria: Student performs a dance in an informal class setting using at least one expressive skill
Student can share the meaning or intended purpose of their dance using words, images or movement
Student provides at least one constructive, specific comment on a peer's performance
nodes.hinge_reason: Presenting and reflecting as a complete loop — performing, communicating intent, receiving feedback, reflecting — is the capability milestone of this standard. Students who have not closed this loop lack the reflective performance practice needed for the more formal and technically demanding presenting contexts of Y5-6.

width.minimum: Performing one dance to the class; sharing the meaning and intended purpose in a class debrief; being attentive and providing at least one constructive feedback comment.
width.typical: Performing in informal class settings; using screen-based technologies or online platforms to present where appropriate; sharing meaning and purpose (own words, images, learnt terminology, movement, drawing); being an attentive audience and providing constructive feedback to peers.
wider: Present a dance on a digital platform (e.g. school learning management system) — adapting the introduction for a remote or asynchronous audience
Receive peer feedback on a performance and use it to make one specific revision — documenting the change and its effect

modes.reason: Presenting integrates expressive skills (N1) with communicative intent and audience awareness. Debrief discussions are critical — 'What did you think my dance was about?' directly connects performance and reception.

descriptors.title: Improvise and devise drama
descriptors.description: improvise and/or devise and shape drama using the elements of drama to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create and co-create fictional situations using elements of drama in dramatic play and process drama (Y1-2). They can take on roles, contribute ideas, and communicate non-verbally within a group improvisation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students improvise and/or devise and shape drama using elements of drama to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning.
elaborations: using learning from First Nations Australians' drama to devise drama communicating connection to place
creating drama by exploring roles and situations in a 'miniature world'
improvising drama to explore issues, using empathy to take on roles and 'stand in the shoes' of another
devising dialogue for a previously 'wordless story'
using elements of drama and principles of story to shape improvisations
working in groups to devise sections of drama and combining them using play-building
communicating Acknowledgement of Country before a performance

nodes.label: Identifying dramatic potential
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a situation, issue or story worth exploring through drama and name what ideas or perspectives it raises.
criteria: Student names a situation or perspective they want to explore through their drama
Student can explain what ideas or feelings their drama is trying to communicate
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot identify what a drama might be about — cannot articulate the idea, perspective or meaning they want to explore — shaping and devising collapses into random action; the purpose-driven crafting in subsequent nodes depends on this.

width.minimum: Student identifies one scenario or situation from a given starting point (story, image, issue) and names what they want to explore through drama.
width.typical: Students create drama by exploring and experiencing roles and situations they initiate and develop; they consider how empathy assists them to take on roles and 'stand in the shoes' of another; they explore roles in a 'miniature world' or from everyday interactions.
wider: Students improvise drama exploring situations from another time or place, imagining themselves as participants in an event
Students devise dialogue for a previously 'wordless story' or dramatic action for a story known only through spoken/audio sources
Students devise drama communicating their connection to a place in their community, drawing on First Nations Australians' drama about Country/Place as a starting point

modes.reason: Use guiding questions ('What is this story really about?', 'What do you want an audience to think or feel?', 'Whose perspective are you exploring?') before improvisation begins.
Offer varied stimulus material — images, texts, community contexts, historical moments — to ensure students with different entry points can each find genuine dramatic potential.

nodes.label: Using elements to shape improvised drama
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use elements of drama — time, place, role, language, movement — to shape improvisations and give them meaning and structure.
criteria: Student makes at least one deliberate element-based choice when shaping improvised drama
Student can name the element they used and what effect it had on the drama

width.minimum: Student makes at least one deliberate choice about how to use an element (e.g. changing place, pace, or character relationship) to shape the drama.
width.typical: Students use elements of drama and principles of story (establishing time, place, roles and characters) to shape improvisations; they experiment with voice (loudness, pace, pitch) and movement to create roles and situations; they explore heightening tension through language and spatial awareness.
wider: Students experiment with ways to connect short scenes (rhythmic patterns, transition phrases, movement sequences)
Students explore how developing spatial awareness — distance, proximity, stillness — can manipulate tension in dramatic action

modes.reason: Students need a growing repertoire of element-based choices to draw on; provide frequent short improvisation tasks that each focus on one element, building command of the full kit.

nodes.label: Devising and presenting drama with communicative intent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can work collaboratively to devise a structured drama that communicates an intended idea, perspective or meaning.
criteria: Student contributes to a devised drama that communicates an identifiable idea or perspective
Student can describe what the drama is about and one element choice they made to communicate it
Student demonstrates collaborative engagement — offering ideas and accepting others' contributions

width.minimum: Student contributes to devising a drama (with at least one other student) that has a clear beginning, development and ending, and communicates a recognisable idea.
width.typical: Students work in groups to devise sections of drama and then, working as a class, combine sections using a play-building process; they communicate their connection to Country/Place through Acknowledgement of Country (as appropriate); they shape improvisation to communicate their intentions as drama-makers.
wider: Students devise drama exploring issues and ideas, using empathy to consider multiple perspectives and challenge their own assumptions
Students devise drama based on a real or imagined 'miniature world', developing a complex fictional space with consistent roles, rules and relationships

modes.reason: Devising integrates all prior moves — identifying intent, using elements, collaborating. Scaffold with clear group roles and regular reflection stops ('Is the meaning clear? What element could you adjust?').

descriptors.title: Elements of drama in improvisation
descriptors.description: use the elements of drama to explore and develop ideas for dramatic action in improvisations and/or devised drama
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use elements of drama — role, place, situation, language, movement — in dramatic play and process drama (Y1-2). They can identify and use drama vocabulary and take on roles purposefully.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use the elements of drama to explore and develop ideas for dramatic action in improvisations and/or devised drama.
elaborations: experimenting with loudness/softness, pace and pitch of voices to create roles and situations
exploring roles using language choice, expressions and tone to heighten tension
improvising ways to connect short scenes through clapping, phrases or movement
developing spatial awareness — considering distance and movement to manipulate tension

nodes.label: Experimenting with voice as a dramatic tool
nodes.checkpoint: Students can experiment with vocal qualities — loudness, pace, pitch — to create and differentiate roles, situations and atmosphere.
criteria: Student makes at least one deliberate vocal choice (pace, pitch, or loudness) to create a character or atmosphere
Student can describe what their vocal choice was communicating
nodes.hinge_reason: Voice is a primary expressive tool in drama; students who default to a single register cannot effectively create distinct roles or atmospheres, limiting their ability to shape dramatic action in the devising strand.

width.minimum: Student makes at least one deliberate vocal choice (e.g. changes pace or pitch) to signal a character, situation, or emotional state.
width.typical: Students experiment with loudness/softness, pace and pitch of their voices when initiating and developing roles and situations; they explore how voice choices create time, place and character; they use language choices (word selection, tone) to heighten tension.
wider: Students compare how the same line of dialogue produces different dramatic effects when delivered with different vocal qualities
Students explore non-vocal sound (clapping, rhythmic patterns) as a transition tool between scenes

modes.reason: Vocal range develops through repeated guided practice — regular vocal warm-ups and focused short exercises where students try multiple voice qualities for the same role or situation.

nodes.label: Using movement and space in dramatic action
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use movement, stillness and spatial awareness to develop dramatic action and manipulate tension.
criteria: Student uses at least one spatial or movement choice that contributes to dramatic meaning
Student can explain what their movement choice was communicating in the drama

width.minimum: Student makes at least one spatial or movement choice (proximity, stillness, gesture) that contributes to the dramatic meaning.
width.typical: Students develop spatial awareness — considering how close/far apart they stand and how movement manipulates tension; they use facial expressions and movement to sustain role; they improvise ways to connect short scenes through movement or rhythmic transitions.
wider: Students experiment systematically with how proximity between characters communicates relationship and power
Students explore how stillness and silence function as dramatic elements, not simply as pauses

modes.reason: Build a movement vocabulary through structured exercises: exploring proximity, levels, tempo, stillness — students need a toolkit of spatial choices before they can select intentionally.

nodes.label: Combining elements to develop dramatic action
nodes.checkpoint: Students can combine elements of drama — voice, movement, language, space — to explore and develop ideas for dramatic action.
criteria: Student combines at least two elements of drama in a sustained improvisation or devised sequence
Student identifies at least two element choices they made and describes their effect on the drama

width.minimum: Student uses at least two elements in combination when developing a dramatic action sequence.
width.typical: Students combine voice, movement, language and space to develop roles, situations and tension; they use improvisation to generate ideas for devised drama; they explore how manipulating specific elements creates different effects and meanings.
wider: Students explore how language choice and movement combine to communicate status and power relationships in drama
Students use a specific element (e.g. silence, proximity) as a structural device to shape a complete improvised scene

modes.reason: Combining elements into coherent dramatic action is the integration move here; support students to reflect ('Which elements are you using? Is the effect what you intended?') after each improvisation.

descriptors.title: Drama across cultures, times and places
descriptors.description: explore where, why and how drama is created and/or performed across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore where, why and how people across cultures experience drama (Y1-2). They understand that drama communicates feelings, ideas and cultural knowledge for different communities.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore where, why and how drama is created and/or performed across cultures, times, places and other contexts.
elaborations: listening to actors talk about how they developed their character and what they found interesting
comparing audience and performer expectations in different cultural settings including Asia
reflecting on live or recorded performances asking questions about purpose and features
examining drama in their community and comparing it with drama from other cultures, times and places

nodes.label: Purpose and audience across contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the purpose of a drama — entertainment, cultural transmission, infotainment, community ritual — and describe what an audience needs to know to engage with it.
criteria: Student identifies a purpose for a specific drama from a given cultural context
Student describes at least one thing an audience needs to know to engage with that drama
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding purpose and audience is prerequisite to the analytical inquiry asked by the descriptor — 'how drama is created/performed' is only interpretable if students have a frame for 'why'; without it, observation stays at surface description.

width.minimum: Student identifies one purpose for a specific drama they have experienced or studied, and names one thing an audience needs to understand.
width.typical: Students listen to actors or makers discuss how they developed characters and what they found interesting about the imaginary world they created; they reflect on live or recorded performances asking what purpose the drama serves; they compare expectations and requirements of performers and audience in different cultural settings.
wider: Students compare a drama from Australia with one from a country or region in Asia, identifying similarities and differences in purpose and audience relationship
Students examine puppetry or physical theatre in their community and compare it with examples from other cultures, times or places

modes.reason: Use structured reflection questions before and after viewing drama: 'What is the purpose of this drama?', 'What does the audience need to know?', 'Why do you think people from this culture create drama for this purpose?'

nodes.label: Features and ideas across cultures, times and places
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify features and ideas in drama from diverse cultures, times and places, and consider how they might inform their own drama-making.
criteria: Student identifies at least one feature or idea in drama from a cultural or historical context different from their own
Student makes a connection between that feature and their own drama-making practice or ideas

width.minimum: Student identifies one feature or idea from a drama from another culture, time or place and considers how it might be used in their own work.
width.typical: Students reflect on drama performances and ask questions ('What features and ideas come from other cultures, times and places?', 'How could we use these in our drama?', 'Why do people from diverse cultures create drama for similar purposes?'); they share embodied responses — movement, gesture, language — to reflect on drama meaning.
wider: Students investigate a specific drama form from another culture or historical period in depth — exploring its conventions, purposes and how it has changed over time
Students investigate how drama from a country or region in Asia uses elements differently from Australian dramatic conventions and apply one insight in their own devising

modes.reason: Exposure to a range of drama contexts, times and cultures is the mechanism here; breadth of examples enables comparison and supports genuine understanding of drama's diversity.

descriptors.title: First Nations drama and country/place
descriptors.description: explore how First Nations Australians use drama to communicate their connection to, and responsibility for, Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored examples of drama created and/or performed by First Nations Australians and attended to how elements communicate cultural meaning (Y1-2). They understand that First Nations Australians use drama to share cultural knowledge.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how First Nations Australians use drama to communicate their connection to, and responsibility for, Country/Place.
elaborations: collecting and sharing information about First Nations drama for festivals or ceremonies communicating knowledge about Country/Place
exploring how First Nations Australians use drama to communicate knowledge and maintain unique ways of life
observing how elements of drama are used in First Nations drama to communicate connection to Country/Place
accessing drama by First Nations Australians exploring ways to live sustainably and respect the land
looking at performances representing the importance of Country/Place and Story as a starting point for talking about different ways of seeing the same place

nodes.label: Drama as expression of Country/Place — what and why
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe what it means for First Nations Australians to communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place through drama, and identify examples.
criteria: Student describes at least one way First Nations drama communicates connection to or responsibility for Country/Place
Student identifies a specific drama example (festival, ceremony, storytelling) in which this is expressed
nodes.hinge_reason: The concept of Country/Place as a living relationship — not just a place on a map — is foundational for understanding First Nations drama; without grasping this, students cannot read the elements of drama in the second node with cultural appropriateness.

width.minimum: Student describes one way First Nations drama communicates knowledge about or connection to Country/Place.
width.typical: Students collect and share information about drama created and performed by First Nations Australians for festivals, ceremonies or cultural occasions; they explore how First Nations Australians use drama to communicate knowledge about the local environment and to maintain unique ways of life.
wider: Students access drama created and/or performed by First Nations Australians and explore how it communicates ways to live sustainably and care for land, sea, sky or waterways
Students explore performances that represent the importance of Country/Place and Story as a starting point for discussing different ways of seeing the same place and telling stories

modes.reason: Use guided discussion and culturally authoritative resources to establish the concept of Country/Place before observing drama; ensure students understand this is about living relationship, not geography.

nodes.label: How elements of drama communicate Country/Place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can observe and describe how elements of drama are used in First Nations drama to communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place.
criteria: Student describes how at least one element of drama is used in a First Nations drama to communicate cultural meaning
Student demonstrates respect for cultural context in their description — attends to meaning, not just surface features

width.minimum: Student describes how at least one element of drama (movement, language, place) functions in a specific First Nations drama example to communicate cultural meaning.
width.typical: Students observe how elements of drama — place, language, movement — are used in First Nations drama that shares cultural narratives; they explore how drama communicates knowledge and consider how different ways of seeing the same place produce different stories.
wider: Students compare how the same Country/Place is represented through drama across different First Nations communities, exploring how cultural perspectives shape dramatic choices
Students investigate how First Nations drama performers use specific movement or language conventions tied to cultural knowledge of their country

modes.reason: Engage with drama from multiple First Nations communities and cultural contexts — diversity within First Nations Australia is significant and should not be flattened to a single representative example.

descriptors.title: Perform in informal settings
descriptors.description: perform improvised and/or devised drama in informal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can share drama in informal settings, considering audience perspective and reflecting on the experience (Y1-2). They can use elements of drama in dramatic play and simple performance.
descriptors.endpoint: Students perform improvised and/or devised drama in informal settings, demonstrating commitment to role and using voice, movement and language to sustain dramatic action.
elaborations: using voice, movement and language to sustain role and relationships when performing
demonstrating commitment to the reality of the drama — staying in role throughout
manipulating focus, tension, space and time to shape dramatic action when performing

nodes.label: Sustaining role through performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sustain role throughout a performance — including when not actively driving the dramatic action.
criteria: Student remains visibly in-role throughout a performance, including during moments of inactivity
Student's physical presence — posture, expression, attention — is consistent with the role
nodes.hinge_reason: Role-commitment is the foundation of performed drama; students who break role disrupt both the fictional world and audience engagement, collapsing the performance context and undermining the communicative work of the whole group.

width.minimum: Student remains 'in-role' (through posture, expression, or attention) during a performance, including during moments when other characters are the focus.
width.typical: Students demonstrate commitment to the reality/world of the drama; they stay 'in-role' throughout the performance even when not actively participating in the dramatic action; they use voice, movement and language to sustain role and relationships.
wider: Students rehearse specific moments where role-commitment is tested — e.g. reactions to another character's action — and discuss what staying in role communicates to the audience
Students experiment with how physical stillness and focused attention in an 'inactive' role moment contributes to the overall performance

modes.reason: Role-commitment develops through repeated short practice; use quick 'freeze-frame' exercises where students must hold role while the teacher or peers observe, building the habit of sustained presence.

nodes.label: Using voice, movement and focus to shape performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can manipulate focus, tension, space and time in their performance to shape dramatic action for an audience.
criteria: Student makes at least two performance choices (vocal and physical) that contribute to dramatic meaning
Student demonstrates manipulation of at least one dramatic variable (tension, focus, pace, space) in the performance
Student can describe a performance choice they made and explain what it was communicating

width.minimum: Student makes at least two performance choices (one vocal, one physical) that contribute to the drama's meaning and communication.
width.typical: Students vary facial expressions and movements to create roles and situations; they manipulate focus, tension, space and time to shape dramatic action; they use voice and movement in combination to communicate character relationships and dramatic situation.
wider: Students explore how changing one performance variable (e.g. deliberately slowing movement to heighten tension) transforms audience experience
Students take on contrasting roles in different performances, exploring how different character types require different vocal and physical approaches

modes.reason: Performance integrates role-commitment, element knowledge, and communicative intent. Post-performance reflection ('Did the audience experience what you intended? What would you change?') closes the loop.
Performing in multiple informal contexts — for a partner, a class, at assembly — builds adaptability and deepens understanding of audience relationship.

descriptors.title: Construct with media languages
descriptors.description: use media languages, media technologies and production processes to construct representations that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use media languages and technologies to construct representations that communicate identifiable ideas or stories. They can apply basic shot types and make deliberate compositional decisions. They have not yet worked with the full production process — pre-production, production, post-production — or communicated perspectives and meaning through multi-element works.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use media languages, media technologies and production processes to construct representations that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning.
elaborations: taking a series of photographs that show themselves and their friends as comic superheroes and villains through setting, costume and body language

creating a soundscape to accompany a moving image that includes Foley sounds and recorded sounds on a variety of devices to explore volume, layering and the use of voice to create a sense of environment

using learning from explorations of media arts works that communicate First Nations Australians' connection to and responsibility for Country/Place to devise media arts works that communicate their own connection to and responsibility for place
experimenting with the camera and framing the subject, using shot types, angles and lighting, and experimenting to apply text to still or moving images, such as credits in a title sequence
filming a short sequence that focuses on conflict by selecting camera angles, lighting and/or costume to convey meaning without dialogue
collaborating with others to make a small publication to explore ideas that are significant in their lives; for example, a zine or new website, using collaged images and texts and drawings

nodes.label: Media languages for perspective and meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how technical elements (shot type, angle, lighting, sound, text) communicate perspective and meaning — going beyond basic identification to explaining the communicative function.
criteria: Student can identify at least two technical elements in a media work
Student can explain how each element communicates a perspective or creates meaning for the audience
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how technical elements communicate perspective and meaning is the conceptual prerequisite for making deliberate production choices — without it, production decisions are aesthetic preferences rather than communicative strategies.

width.minimum: Identify two technical elements (e.g. shot angle and lighting) in an existing work and explain how each communicates a perspective or creates meaning for an audience.
width.typical: Analyse how technical elements (shot types, angles, lighting, text in title sequences, Foley sounds) communicate perspective and meaning in existing works; use Viewpoints questions to frame analysis; connect technical choices to intended audience response.
wider: Analyse a short film sequence that communicates conflict through camera angles, lighting and/or costume without dialogue — identifying how each technical choice communicates a perspective and discussing what would change if the choices were different
Investigate how a soundscape uses volume, layering and voice to create a sense of environment — comparing two soundscapes for the same scene and explaining what meaning each creates

modes.reason: Use Viewpoints questions explicitly: 'What images will I use and in what order?', 'What does this camera angle communicate about this character's power?' Students need to practise the reasoning chain from choice to communicative effect.

nodes.label: Production processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan and carry out a production using at least two stages of the production process (planning, capture, editing) — making deliberate decisions at each stage.
criteria: Student applies at least two stages of the production process when constructing a media work
Student makes and can explain at least one deliberate production decision at each stage

width.minimum: Use at least two production process stages (e.g. plan a shot list or storyboard, then capture footage; or capture footage and then edit/sequence) to produce a media element.
width.typical: Apply production process stages to construct a work — camera and framing decisions during capture, Foley sound creation, text application to images, editing and sequencing; use pre-production planning (storyboard, shot list) to guide production decisions.
wider: Create a soundscape using Foley sounds and recorded sounds (found objects, voice, recording technology) to accompany a moving image — applying production planning and experimenting with volume, layering and voice across multiple takes
Investigate and use digital or analog storyboarding as a pre-production tool — plan a short film, stop motion or comic strip, then rearrange the boards to change narrative meaning before producing

modes.reason: Production process fluency requires repeated practice — students who skip planning or who don't review and select media elements produce accidental rather than intentional representations. Invest in the full cycle, not just capture.

nodes.label: Representations communicate perspectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a complete representation — using media languages and production processes to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning for an audience.
criteria: Student produces a media arts work that communicates an identifiable idea, perspective or meaning
Student can explain at least two media language or production choices they made and how those choices serve the communicative intent

width.minimum: Produce one media arts work using deliberately chosen media languages and at least one production process, and explain how the choices communicate a perspective or meaning to the intended audience.
width.typical: Produce representations across two or more forms or contexts (photo sequence communicating emotion, short film communicating conflict, soundscape communicating place, collaborative zine); connect technical choices to communicative intent; reflect on whether the representation communicates the intended meaning.
wider: Create a short film that communicates connection to a place in the community — drawing on First Nations Australian media arts works about Country/Place for inspiration, and using camera, lighting and sound to convey feeling without dialogue

Create a comic book, photo series or zine that communicates the maker's perspective on an idea significant in their lives — using layout, image selection, text and visual elements deliberately to create meaning for a specific audience

modes.reason: This node integrates technical language understanding with production process skills — the produced work is evidence that both are operating together. Ensure students can articulate the connection between their choices and their communicative intent.

descriptors.strand: Media arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Shape ideas with media technologies
descriptors.description: develop media production skills by exploring ways of shaping ideas using media technologies, images, sounds, text and/or interactive elements
descriptors.knowledge: Students can capture and organise media elements and experiment with how changes affect meaning. They can apply basic production skills. They have not yet systematically explored how specific production techniques (suspense, genre conventions, Foley sound) shape meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop media production skills by exploring ways of shaping ideas using media technologies, images, sounds, text and/or interactive elements.
elaborations: experimenting with suspense to create meaning and sustain representations; for example, exploring the way colour, shot type and editing techniques are used to communicate film genre
investigating how the conventions of a news story or video game communicate meaning
exploring different ways of creating sounds when making a soundscape; for example, creating Foley sounds with available resources
exploring media technologies and languages when creating sound effects or images to convey a mood or main idea of a story
using Viewpoints to develop questions to respond to their experiences as they work, such as, "In what ways does the meaning of the image change when I manipulate the sound effects?"

nodes.label: Techniques that shape meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe at least two production techniques (e.g. suspense through editing, genre conventions, Foley sound creation) and explain how each shapes meaning.
criteria: Student can identify at least two production techniques in existing media works
Student can explain how each technique shapes meaning or audience experience
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding specific production techniques and their effects is the prerequisite for deliberately applying them — without this, exploration of media technologies is random rather than purposeful.

width.minimum: Identify one technique used in an existing media work (e.g. how colour and editing create suspense in a film genre clip) and explain how it shapes the audience's experience.
width.typical: Explore how colour, shot type and editing create suspense and genre meaning; investigate how news story conventions and video game conventions communicate differently from narrative; explore how sound effects and music change mood and meaning.
wider: Investigate how the conventions of a news story or video game communicate meaning — examining speech bubble text, headlines and framing choices to understand how form shapes audience expectations
Explore how colour, shot type and editing techniques signal film genre — comparing two clips from different genres and identifying the techniques that create genre recognition

modes.reason: Use Viewpoints questions to scaffold technique analysis: 'Where is the suspense happening in this work, and how do I know?' This builds transferable analytical skills.

nodes.label: Exploring and experimenting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can experiment with media technologies to apply and modify production techniques — using Viewpoints questions to evaluate what changes when techniques are altered.
criteria: Student experiments with at least one production technique using media technologies
Student uses Viewpoints questions or equivalent reflection to evaluate what changed and why

width.minimum: Experiment with at least one production technique (e.g. create Foley sounds using found objects, or modify the sound effects on an image sequence) and describe how the change affects the mood or meaning.
width.typical: Experiment across multiple techniques — Foley sound creation, storyboarding and rearranging sequences, zooming in/out, adding text and sound to images, reviewing and selecting captured images; use Viewpoints questions to evaluate experiments: 'In what ways does the meaning change when I manipulate the sound effects?'
wider: Create multiple soundscapes for the same image sequence using different materials and sound types (Foley, voice, recorded sounds) — comparing how each soundscape changes the mood and meaning, and selecting the most effective approach

Experiment with digital and analog storyboarding as a planning tool — create a storyboard for a short film or comic strip, rearrange the boards to create different narrative meanings, and test audience responses

modes.reason: Build students' repertoire of experimenting strategies — Foley, storyboard rearrangement, image review, sound-image combination. A broader repertoire means more informed production choices in later work.

descriptors.title: Media arts across cultures and times
descriptors.description: explore where, why and how media arts is created and/or distributed across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain why media arts works matter to communities and describe the role of media artists. They have explored media arts from their own and First Nations Australian communities. They have not yet explored media arts across historical periods or analysed representations and stereotypes across different social contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore where, why and how media arts is created and/or distributed across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts — comparing works made for different purposes and identifying how context shapes representation.
elaborations: sequencing images, sounds and/or text to clearly establish the beginning, middle and end of a story or event

identifying meaning and describing representations in media arts works from different social, cultural or historical contexts; for example, examining the different ways traditional stories are retold using media technologies or the use of stereotypes in advertising
comparing media arts works made for different purposes using appropriate language, and identifying features such as use of conventions in a variety of media types
using appropriate language to discuss the meaning of their own media arts works
investigating digital or analog storyboarding as a planning tool

nodes.label: Context shapes representation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how social, cultural or historical context shapes the representations and meanings in a media arts work.
criteria: Student can identify at least one way a media arts work's context shapes its representations or values
Student can use at least one piece of media arts language (e.g. 'representation', 'convention', 'stereotype') to describe what they found
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how context shapes representation is the conceptual foundation for media literacy at Y3-4 — without it, students read media works as neutral rather than constructed, which blocks more sophisticated analysis.

width.minimum: Examine one media arts work from a context different from their own (different time, culture or social context) and identify at least one way the context shapes the characters, stories or values in the work.
width.typical: Examine media arts works from different social, cultural and historical contexts; identify and describe representations, stereotypes and storytelling conventions; compare how the same topic (e.g. heroes, family) is represented differently across contexts; use appropriate media arts language.
wider: Investigate how traditional First Nations Australian stories are being retold using media technologies (animation, stop motion, green screen) — examining how media arts concepts (framing, sound, editing) serve cultural storytelling purposes different from mainstream media conventions

Compare how the same type of story (e.g. a superhero narrative) is told across different cultural or historical contexts — identifying what values, representations and conventions differ, and what this reveals about the contexts

modes.reason: Students need explicit scaffolding to move from 'this is what the work shows' to 'the context shaped this representation' — use structured comparison questions: 'Why would a filmmaker from this time/place represent it this way?'

nodes.label: Purpose, distribution and comparison
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare media arts works made for different purposes and identify features that serve those purposes — including how the same story might be told differently across media types.
criteria: Student can compare two media arts works made for different purposes
Student can identify at least two features that differ between them and explain why those differences serve the different purposes

width.minimum: Compare two media arts works made for different purposes (e.g. a news story and an advertisement) and identify at least two features that differ and explain why.
width.typical: Compare media arts works made for different purposes (entertainment, persuasion, information, cultural preservation) using appropriate language; investigate how conventions vary across media types; use language of media arts to discuss meaning; investigate storyboarding as a planning tool across different media forms.
wider: Compare how the same event or topic is represented across different media types (news report, advertisement, social media post, animated retelling) — identifying how purpose and platform shape representation and what a viewer might understand differently from each

Investigate how media arts works are distributed for different purposes and contexts (school intranet, community event, broadcasting, cultural festivals) — discussing how distribution context affects who the audience is and what the work communicates

modes.reason: Vary the comparison contexts — news, advertising, cultural storytelling, entertainment — to ensure students develop a broad understanding of how purpose shapes form, not just a narrow comparison of two similar works.

descriptors.title: First Nations media arts and country/place
descriptors.description: explore how First Nations Australians use media arts to communicate their connection to and responsibility for Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify media arts works produced by First Nations Australians and describe how visual, audio and interactive elements communicate cultural knowledge. They have not yet explored specifically how media arts communicates connection to and responsibility for Country/Place.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how First Nations Australians use media arts to communicate their connection to and responsibility for Country/Place.
elaborations: identifying meaning and describing representations in media arts works created and/or co-created by First Nations Australians, such as how traditional stories of First Nations Australians are being retold using media technologies
recognising, through media arts, how First Nations Australians' cultural expressions often contain and communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place

exploring First Nations Australians' use of media arts to express connection to and responsibility for Country/Place, such as communicating knowledge about the local seasons or using screen-based storytelling to maintain language and unique ways of life
exploring how First Nations Australians use media arts concepts to communicate their connection to and responsibility for Country/Place
collecting and sharing information about media arts works created and produced by First Nations Australians for occasions such as festivals or ceremonies
exploring how stories and ideas can communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place

exploring a media arts work that includes images, sound and/or text and communicates the diversity of First Nations Australians' cultures, such as an interactive map of First Nations Australian languages

nodes.label: Connection to Country/Place in media arts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how a First Nations Australian media arts work communicates connection to and responsibility for Country/Place — naming at least one specific media arts concept used (framing, language, sound, symbols).
criteria: Student can identify how a First Nations Australian media arts work communicates connection to Country/Place
Student can name at least one media arts concept (framing, language, sound, symbols) used to communicate that connection
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the specific connection between First Nations Australian media arts and Country/Place is the conceptual foundation for this standard — without it, exploration of specific elements and practices has no cultural grounding.

width.minimum: Explore one First Nations Australian media arts work that communicates connection to Country/Place and identify at least one media arts concept (framing, language, symbols, sound) used to communicate that connection.
width.typical: Explore First Nations Australian media arts works across forms that communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place — identifying how cultural expressions include: naming Country and Traditional Owners, acknowledging Ancestors, singing/speaking in language, communicating knowledge about seasons, land, sea, sky and waterways; recognise how screen-based storytelling maintains language and ways of life.
wider: Explore First Nations Australian media arts works created for ceremonial or festival contexts — collecting and reflecting on how the occasion, purpose and media arts choices communicate knowledge about Country/Place

Investigate how First Nations Australian media artists use screen-based storytelling to maintain language and unique ways of life — examining specific examples and discussing what would be at risk if these works were not made

modes.reason: Students need guided inquiry with community resources or accredited materials to connect observable media elements to their Country/Place significance — this is not interpretable from the text or images alone.

nodes.label: Diversity of First Nations media arts expression
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare how different First Nations Australian media arts works communicate connection to Country/Place — noting how different media arts concepts, languages and purposes produce different works.
criteria: Student can compare at least two First Nations Australian media arts works communicating connection to Country/Place
Student can describe at least one way each work uses media arts concepts differently, and explain what that difference communicates

width.minimum: Explore two different First Nations Australian media arts works communicating connection to Country/Place and describe one similarity and one difference in how they use media arts concepts.
width.typical: Collect and share information about First Nations Australian media arts works created for different occasions and purposes; compare how different media arts concepts (languages, symbols, icons) and forms communicate connection to Country/Place; explore the diversity of First Nations Australian cultures through media arts works.
wider: Explore an interactive map of First Nations Australian languages as a media arts work — investigating how media technologies and languages create a relationship with the viewer, and discussing how digital tools communicate the diversity of First Nations cultures

Compare how two First Nations Australian communities use media arts to communicate their distinct relationships to Country/Place — identifying what is shared and what is specific to each community's culture and story

modes.reason: Expose students to multiple First Nations Australian media arts works from different communities, forms and occasions — diversity is the point, not a single representative example.

descriptors.title: Share with responsible media practice
descriptors.description: share media arts works in informal settings considering responsible media practice
descriptors.knowledge: Students can share media arts works with audiences in informal settings and apply basic permission principles. They have not yet applied a full suite of responsible media practices (credits, formal permission workflows, audience and relationship considerations) when presenting.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share media arts works in informal settings considering responsible media practice — including permission, credits, and audience/relationship considerations.
elaborations: creating credits in a title sequence and selecting appropriate fonts, colour and length of display time to accompany screening of a series of moving images
seeking permission to take photos of class members; for example, documenting a school excursion for publication on the school intranet

considering media concepts, such as audience and relationships, when formatting and laying out a story, using available software and appropriate text conventions for a front-page news story or print advertisement

nodes.label: Responsible media practice in presentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and apply at least two responsible media practices when preparing to share a work — including one permission/credit consideration and one audience consideration.
criteria: Student can identify at least two responsible media practice requirements relevant to their sharing context
Student applies both requirements when sharing their work and can explain why each is needed
nodes.hinge_reason: Responsible media practice habits established here underpin all subsequent sharing and publication work — failure to establish the habit at Y3-4 creates compliance gaps in later years when stakes increase.

width.minimum: Identify and apply two responsible media practice requirements before sharing (e.g. create credits, obtain permission for photographs) — and explain why each is required.
width.typical: Apply responsible media practices across sharing contexts — creating credits for title sequences (font, colour, display time), seeking and acknowledging permission for photographs, considering audience and relationship when formatting a publication; apply media concepts of audience and relationships to layout decisions.
wider: Document a school excursion through photography — practising the full permission-to-publication workflow: seeking permission from class members, selecting and sequencing images, creating credits, and publishing to the school intranet
Develop and apply a class protocol for responsible sharing that addresses: individual permission, cultural material permission, credits, and platform-appropriate sharing

modes.reason: Responsible media practice is a procedural habit that requires repeated application across different contexts — not just conceptual understanding. Students need practice applying permission and credits workflows, not just knowing they exist.

nodes.label: Sharing for audience and purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share a media arts work in an informal setting — applying audience and relationship considerations to presentation decisions.
criteria: Student shares a media arts work in an informal setting applying at least one audience or relationship consideration
Student can explain at least one presentation decision (layout, format, credits, platform) in terms of its effect on the audience

width.minimum: Share one media arts work in an informal setting applying at least one media concept (audience or relationships) to at least one presentation decision (layout, format, timing, platform).
width.typical: Present media arts works in informal settings applying audience and relationship thinking; create title sequences with deliberate credits; format publications using appropriate text conventions; screen class-created moving image works; consider how the intended audience shapes presentation choices.
wider: Create a title sequence with credits for a class screening of moving image works — selecting fonts, colours and display timing deliberately, and reflecting on how these choices serve the audience experience

Format and lay out a front-page news story or print advertisement using available software — applying audience and relationship concepts to every layout decision and presenting the reasoning to the class

modes.reason: Audience and relationship thinking integrates responsible media practice with media language understanding — credits, layout and format choices are not just compliance but communicative decisions about how to treat an audience.

descriptors.title: Manipulate elements to communicate ideas
descriptors.description: manipulate elements of music to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning when composing and practising for performance
descriptors.knowledge: Students can select and combine elements of music when composing (AC9AMU2C01) and have practised documentation using signs, symbols and recordings. They can combine two elements for expressive effect and justify their selections. They have not yet manipulated elements strategically to communicate specific ideas, perspectives or meaning across a sustained composition.
descriptors.endpoint: Students manipulate elements of music to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning when composing and practising for performance, using notation, documentation or recording to capture their work.
elaborations: writing lyrics and/or melodies for songs, raps or chants and using formats such as graphic or staff notation or a lead-sheet or an audio recording to notate/document/record their work
using available technologies to create accompaniments; for example, improvising patterns and recording as a loop or using digital tools to notate/document music
improvising phrases of music on an instrument to practise known notes and rhythm patterns
learning songs and/or instrumental music associated with specific cultures
listening to live or recorded performances and gathering ideas they can use in their performance
manipulating the elements of music to express different characters or dramatic action when composing music for a screen-based work or to accompany drama
combining composed and improvised sections to create a complete work
working in pairs or groups to create ostinatos or accompaniments

nodes.label: Manipulating vs selecting elements
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand that manipulating elements means actively changing, shaping and controlling them throughout a composition — not just choosing them at the start.
criteria: Demonstrates at least one active manipulation of an element within a composition (not just its initial selection)
Can describe the effect of the manipulation on the music's mood or meaning
nodes.hinge_reason: The conceptual leap from 'selecting elements' (Y1-2) to 'manipulating elements' is the core of this standard. Students who remain at selection level — choosing elements but not actively shaping them throughout — cannot meet the descriptor's command term and cannot access AC9AMU6C01 which requires manipulating elements plus compositional devices.

width.minimum: Demonstrate one manipulation of a musical element during a composition (e.g. making a section get louder over time, or changing a melody's rhythm) and explain what effect the manipulation creates.
width.typical: Manipulate elements dynamically within compositions — varying dynamics across sections, extending or shortening rhythmic values, changing tempo for dramatic effect, altering articulation; describe how each manipulation shapes the music's meaning or mood.
wider: Compose a section where one element (e.g. dynamics) gradually changes across the whole section — describe what that arc communicates
Take a known song and deliberately manipulate two elements (e.g. tempo and articulation) to create a completely different mood — compare before and after

modes.reason: Make the distinction explicit: 'Selecting means choosing which elements to use. Manipulating means changing how an element behaves during the music — making it grow, shrink, shift, transform.' Use guided analysis of recordings to identify manipulations before students attempt them in their own compositions.

nodes.label: Communicating ideas through manipulation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can manipulate elements of music specifically to communicate an idea, perspective or meaning — e.g. expressing dramatic action, emotion or character.
criteria: Composes a piece with a stated communicative intention
Can identify which element manipulations serve that intention and explain how they do so
nodes.hinge_reason: Connecting element manipulation to communicative intent — rather than to aesthetic preference — is the critical move this standard makes. Without it, students compose music they like but cannot explain or justify in terms of ideas or meaning. AC9AMU6C01 explicitly requires communicating 'ideas, perspectives and/or meaning'; if this connection is not established at Y3-4, that requirement becomes inaccessible.

width.minimum: Compose a short piece where element manipulations serve a specific communicative intention (e.g. tension building, a character emerging, a story unfolding).
width.typical: Manipulate elements to express different characters or dramatic action in compositions for screen-based works or drama; write lyrics for songs that communicate ideas; combine composed and improvised sections that serve different communicative purposes (e.g. composed theme + improvised soundscape); work in pairs or groups on ostinatos or accompaniments that support a larger musical idea.
wider: Compose music to accompany a re-telling of a familiar story — map which manipulations correspond to which story events, and explain each choice
Learn and compose music associated with a specific cultural style — identify which element manipulations are characteristic of that style

modes.reason: Communicative purpose becomes clearer with more compositional contexts. Composing for drama, screen, songs and accompaniments each require different types of communicative manipulation — each context adds a new angle on how elements serve meaning.

nodes.label: Notation and documentation for practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use notation or documentation to capture their compositions and use this during rehearsal to practise and refine the work.
criteria: Documents a composition in at least one notation format with enough accuracy to use in rehearsal
Uses the documentation during rehearsal to maintain or refine the composition

width.minimum: Document a composition using at least one notation format (graphic, lead-sheet, staff, audio) and use the documentation during at least one rehearsal.
width.typical: Use multiple documentation formats depending on the composition type — lead-sheets for songs with lyrics, graphic notation for soundscapes, audio recordings for improvisations; use documentation to practise independently and in groups; revise documentation when the composition changes.
wider: Use a story-boarding app or digital template to document where music will be used in a media work — connect notation to the visual timeline
Compare two different notation formats for the same piece (e.g. a graphic score and a lead-sheet) — discuss which is more useful for rehearsal and why

modes.reason: Students who only know one notation format default to it regardless of whether it suits the composition type. Building a repertoire of documentation formats (graphic, lead-sheet, audio recording, staff notation) gives students appropriate tools for different musical contexts.

descriptors.title: Develop skills for manipulating elements
descriptors.description: develop listening skills and skills for manipulating elements of music when singing and playing instruments
descriptors.knowledge: Students have developed listening skills for specific purposes and basic singing/instrumental technique (AC9AMU2D01). They can match pitch with developing accuracy and demonstrate correct technique for classroom instruments. They have not yet focused on manipulating elements deliberately to create and control intended effects.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop listening skills and skills for manipulating elements of music to create controlled expressive effects when singing and playing instruments.
elaborations: using speaking, singing, voice/vocalisation and movement to develop skills for singing/vocalisation
manipulating elements of music to create and control intended effects, using sounds from a range of sources
singing and playing learnt pitch and rhythm patterns and varying elements of music within them to create different effects
listening to the effects they create by manipulating elements of music in different ways
listening to diverse examples of music to explore how rhythm and pitch patterns, structures or timbres are used
practising reading staff, graphic and/or invented notation as they rehearse and perform
exploring options for representing sounds in a score

nodes.label: Manipulating elements during performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can manipulate at least one element of music (e.g. dynamics, tempo, articulation) during singing or playing to create a specific intended effect.
criteria: Demonstrates at least one deliberate element manipulation during singing or playing
Can describe the intended effect of the manipulation
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to execute deliberate element manipulations during performance — not just plan them in composition — is a separate skill that requires practice. Students who can plan manipulations but not execute them under performance conditions cannot achieve the descriptor's requirements. This also underpins AC9AMU6D01 which requires developing expressive facility and control.

width.minimum: Demonstrate one deliberate element manipulation during singing or playing (e.g. gradually getting louder, or changing articulation from smooth to detached) and describe the effect.
width.typical: Manipulate elements across a range of singing and instrumental contexts — varying dynamics in repeated sections for interest, using articulation to suit different lyrics, choosing instruments for specific mood effects, using melodic steps and jumps to suit different sections of a piece.
wider: Perform the same section twice with different element manipulations — compare the effects and discuss which better suits the music's intention
Focus on a single element (e.g. articulation) across three different pieces — how does manipulating the same element produce different effects in different musical contexts?

modes.reason: Element manipulation during performance requires the technique to be sufficiently automatic that it can be executed while simultaneously monitoring other aspects of performance. Repeated targeted practice — isolating one manipulation and drilling it across multiple repetitions before integrating — builds this automaticity.

nodes.label: Listening to evaluate and compare effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can listen to the effects they create by manipulating elements and evaluate which manipulations work better for the musical intention.
criteria: Can compare two versions of a musical passage and identify at least one difference in element manipulation
Can give a reason for preferring one version over the other in terms of the music's intended effect

width.minimum: Listen to two versions of a short piece (or two attempts at the same section) with different element manipulations; describe one difference and say which they prefer and why.
width.typical: Listen to and evaluate effects of element manipulation across multiple dimensions — compare how easy/difficult different manipulations are to perform accurately, ask 'What works and why', listen to diverse music examples to identify how others have used elements and compare with their own choices.
wider: Listen to diverse music examples and identify how rhythm, pitch and timbre are used — use these observations to inform choices in their own compositions or performances
Record two rehearsal attempts with different manipulations, listen back and write a brief comparison — practise the language of musical evaluation

modes.reason: Evaluative listening is a skill that needs scaffolding — students default to 'I liked it' without structure. Build evaluation language: 'What changed between the two versions?', 'Which version better communicates the mood?', 'How difficult was version two to perform accurately?' These questions develop the feedback loops that drive musical improvement.

nodes.label: Notation as a performance tool
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read from staff, graphic and/or invented notation during rehearsal and performance, using it to guide element manipulation decisions.
criteria: Can read from at least one notation type during rehearsal and follow its instructions
Can contribute to creating or refining a notation document to better capture intended manipulations

width.minimum: Read from at least one notation type during rehearsal; follow at least one element-related instruction in the notation (e.g. a dynamic marking or a tempo change).
