width.typical: Practise reading from staff, graphic and/or invented notation as an integral part of rehearsal and performance; invent a graphic score to represent specific sounds and use it in rehearsal; make adjustments to notation to ensure it is accurate and useful.
wider: Invent a graphic score to represent environmental or found sounds — refine it through rehearsal to ensure it accurately captures the intended manipulations
Compare reading from a graphic score vs a staff score for the same piece — discuss what information each type conveys and what each leaves out

modes.reason: Students at Y3-4 benefit from building a repertoire of notation types they can read fluently, not just one they have memorised. Graphic, staff and invented notation each have different uses and learning to switch between them prepares students for the range of documentation formats required in Y5-6 and beyond.

descriptors.title: Music across cultures, times and places
descriptors.description: explore where, why and how music is composed and/or performed across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored music from diverse cultural contexts and discussed preferences (AC9AMU2E01). They can identify where and how people experience music and connect personal preferences to contexts. They have not yet compared music across times and places for similar purposes, or examined audience/performer expectations across different settings.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore where, why and how music is composed and performed across cultures, times, places and other contexts, comparing purposes, notation formats, performance settings and audience expectations.
elaborations: exploring examples of music created for similar purposes across different times and/or places, such as music for dancing, songs that communicate messages, or narrative songs
examining the purpose for which music is used in their lives and community
comparing the expectations and requirements of performers and audiences in different performance settings
exploring ways of notating or documenting forms of music
exploring ways to make instruments from a range of materials

nodes.label: Music for similar purposes across different contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare music created for similar purposes across different cultural or historical contexts, identifying similarities and differences in how elements of music are used.
criteria: Can identify the purpose of two pieces of music from different cultural or historical contexts
Can describe at least one similarity and one difference in how elements of music are used

width.minimum: Listen to two pieces created for a similar purpose (e.g. two dance songs from different cultures) and identify one similarity and one difference in how they use elements of music.
width.typical: Explore music for similar purposes across multiple cultural and historical contexts — dance music, songs communicating identity or health messages, narrative songs; ask questions about rhythmic patterns, instruments and how elements serve the purpose; identify and clap characteristic rhythmic patterns.
wider: Compare music for similar purposes from two different historical periods — how has the instrumentation or style changed while the purpose remained the same?
Explore music from a cultural group in the local community — attend a performance or access a recording and respond by describing what you like, find interesting, or want to know more about

modes.reason: Comparative cross-cultural listening is the core task of this descriptor. Each new cultural or historical context adds evidence for both the diversity and the commonality of musical purpose — the pattern that music serves similar human needs in different ways across contexts is only visible with sufficient examples.

nodes.label: Performer and audience expectations in different settings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe different expectations for performers and audience members in at least two different performance settings.
criteria: Can describe audience and performer expectations in at least two different performance settings
Can give a reason why expectations differ between settings

width.minimum: Identify one setting where audience behaviour expectations differ from their classroom (e.g. a concert hall vs a rock concert vs a ceremonial performance) and describe what is expected.
width.typical: Compare performance and audience expectations across multiple settings — when is it acceptable to talk, dance or clap during a performance? What do different settings expect from performers and audiences? Connect these expectations to the purpose of the music.
wider: Investigate a specific performance setting (e.g. a formal concert, a community ceremony, a street performance) and research what is expected of performers and audiences
Compare expectations when experiencing music for ceremony (e.g. a Welcome to Country) with expectations at a school concert — discuss why they are different and why those differences matter

modes.reason: Setting-specific expectations are not intuitive to Y3-4 students. Explicit discussion of why different settings have different rules — connected to the music's purpose and cultural context — builds the social understanding of music performance that underpins respectful engagement with diverse musical traditions.

nodes.label: Notation and documentation across contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore different ways of notating or documenting music and explain how each type conveys information to performers.
criteria: Can identify two different notation formats and describe what each communicates
Can explain which format would be more useful for a specific type of music and why

width.minimum: Identify two different notation formats (e.g. graphic notation and a lead-sheet) and describe one thing each format communicates to performers.
width.typical: Explore multiple notation and documentation forms — graphic notation, lead-sheets (lyrics and chords), staff notation, visual images, music terminology; explain how each conveys different information; connect notation choice to the type of music being notated.
wider: Create instruments from recycled/repurposed materials and use them to create Foley sounds for a soundscape — document the soundscape using an invented notation format
Compare how a staff score and a graphic score represent the same musical ideas — discuss what each can and cannot show

modes.reason: Students who have encountered multiple notation formats are better equipped to select appropriate documentation tools in their own composition work. Each format type represents a different philosophy about what needs to be communicated to performers.

descriptors.title: First Nations music and country/place
descriptors.description: explore how First Nations Australians use music to communicate their connection to and responsibility for Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored diverse styles and instruments in First Nations Australian music and examined how music communicates messages about Country/Place (AC9AMU2E02). They can identify instruments and ask basic analytical questions. They have not yet focused on connection to and responsibility for Country/Place as the specific communicative purpose, or engaged with First Nations Australian community protocols for performance.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how First Nations Australians use music to communicate their connection to and responsibility for Country/Place, including listening expectations and protocols for different contexts.
elaborations: examining a diverse range of music composed and/or performed by First Nations Australians to communicate connection to, and responsibility for Country/Place
listening to and exploring music that shares feelings and ideas about the importance of Country/Place and Story for First Nations Australians
learning from First Nations Australians about how they use music to communicate their connection to, and responsibility for Country/Place, culture and people
learning from First Nations Australians about the expectations and requirements of performers and audiences experiencing music that communicates connection to Country/Place

nodes.label: Music communicating connection to Country/Place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe specific ways that First Nations Australian music communicates connection to Country/Place — including through lyrics, melody, rhythm and instrumentation.
criteria: Can describe at least one specific way a musical element communicates connection to Country/Place in a First Nations Australian piece
Can explain the concept of 'connection to Country/Place' in their own words
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that First Nations Australian music communicates specific relationships — connection and responsibility — rather than just emotion or aesthetic effect requires conceptual reframing of what music does. Students who engage with this music only as sonic experience miss the cultural knowledge it carries. This conceptual understanding underpins AC9AMU6E02's investigation of cultural continuity and revitalisation.

width.minimum: Listen to one piece of First Nations Australian music connected to Country/Place and identify at least one specific musical element that communicates that connection.
width.typical: Listen to a diverse range of First Nations Australian music communicating connection to Country/Place — songs with lyrics about Country/Place, music accompanying dances that communicate knowledge; discuss how specific elements (melody, rhythm, texture, instrumentation) serve the communicative purpose; compare different composers' and performers' approaches.
wider: Listen to and explore music that shares feelings about the importance of Country/Place and Story as a starting point for discussing how the same place might be seen and storied differently

Compare two First Nations Australian pieces from different regions or traditions that both connect to Country/Place — what is similar? What is different? What does this reveal about the diversity of connections to Country/Place?

modes.reason: The concept of 'responsibility for Country/Place' is culturally specific and may be unfamiliar to non-Indigenous students. Use guided questioning — 'What is the music telling us about this place?', 'What does responsibility for Country/Place mean?' — and, where possible, First Nations Australian voices (resources, interviews) to build genuine conceptual understanding rather than a surface-level encounter.

nodes.label: Learning from First Nations Australians
nodes.checkpoint: Students can engage with resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians (interviews, podcasts, performances) to learn directly about music and its connection to Country/Place.
criteria: Can identify at least one resource created or co-created by First Nations Australians used in learning
Can report at least one specific thing learned from that source (attributed to the source)

width.minimum: Engage with at least one resource created or co-created by a First Nations Australian person about their music; identify one thing learned directly from that source.
width.typical: Learn from First Nations Australians about how they use music to communicate connection to Country/Place, culture and people — using interviews, podcasts, performances and co-created resources; distinguish between what they have learned from First Nations sources and what they have inferred or assumed.
wider: Compare learning from a First Nations Australian artist's interview or podcast with listening to their music alone — what additional understanding does hearing directly from them add?
Research a First Nations Australian musician and prepare to share one key thing learned about how their music connects to Country/Place, using the artist's own words where possible

modes.reason: The source of knowledge matters in this descriptor. Students who only encounter First Nations Australian music through textbooks or teacher description do not develop the practice of seeking out First Nations Australian voices directly. Each encounter with a co-created or primary source resource builds this practice.

nodes.label: Performance protocols and audience responsibilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the expectations and responsibilities of performers and audiences when experiencing First Nations Australian music that communicates connection to Country/Place.
criteria: Can describe at least one protocol or expectation relevant to a First Nations Australian performance context
Can explain why that protocol exists in relation to the music's cultural significance

width.minimum: Identify at least one protocol or expectation relevant to a specific context of First Nations Australian music performance (e.g. a Welcome to Country).
width.typical: Learn about expectations and requirements for both performers and audiences in contexts where First Nations Australian music communicates connection to Country/Place — music for Welcome to Country, ceremonial music, community events; discuss why these expectations exist and what they protect.
wider: Compare the expectations for a Welcome to Country with those for a school concert — discuss why the responsibilities are different and why those differences are important
Investigate what it means to engage respectfully as an audience with culturally significant music — identify two or three specific behaviours and explain why each matters

modes.reason: Protocol knowledge integrates the conceptual understanding of connection to Country/Place with practical, respectful engagement. Students who understand why protocols exist are more likely to follow them authentically than those who follow rules without understanding their cultural basis.

descriptors.title: Perform learnt and composed music in informal settings
descriptors.description: sing and play music they have learnt and/or composed in informal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can sing and play in informal settings, follow agreed performance decisions, introduce performances and contribute to post-performance discussion (AC9AMU2P01). They can make basic staging decisions. They have not yet performed from notation in rehearsal/performance, used sound reinforcement technology, or iteratively refined a performance using recordings.
descriptors.endpoint: Students sing and play music they have learnt and/or composed in informal settings, using notation, staging plans, technology and feedback to prepare and introduce performances.
elaborations: performing music such as unison songs, rounds and instrumental music arranged for small ensembles
introducing performances by sharing information such as the intended purposes of their compositions
rehearsing and performing music using a range of technologies
planning how they will stage a performance and introduce their performances to audiences
reading from notation and/or documentation such as a lead-sheet, staff or graphic notation when practising and performing

nodes.label: Performing from notation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read from and follow notation or documentation (lead-sheet, staff or graphic notation) when practising and performing music.
criteria: Can navigate a notation document during rehearsal and find their place
Follows at least one specific instruction from the notation (e.g. a dynamic marking or repeat sign) during performance
nodes.hinge_reason: Performing from notation is a new performance skill at Y3-4 and the primary new technical demand of this standard relative to Y1-2. Students who cannot follow notation in performance cannot access the full range of repertoire available in Y5-6 and beyond, and cannot participate in ensemble contexts where notation is shared.

width.minimum: Read from at least one notation format during a rehearsal and apply at least one instruction from it during the performance.
width.typical: Read from a range of notation formats (lead-sheet, staff and graphic notation) across different repertoire; use notation to guide element manipulation decisions during rehearsal; revise notation when performance decisions change.
wider: Perform from a lead-sheet (lyrics and chords) for a song — navigate the notation in real time and discuss where reading helped and where it required additional preparation
Compare rehearsing from memory vs from notation for the same piece — what are the advantages and limitations of each?

modes.reason: Reading notation while simultaneously singing, playing and following group cues is a compound skill that requires the notation-reading component to be sufficiently automatic. Targeted practice of notation reading before full rehearsal integration — practise reading the notation first, then add the performance — reduces cognitive load.

nodes.label: Using technology in rehearsal and performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use rehearsal recordings and (with assistance) sound reinforcement to evaluate and improve their performances.
criteria: Records a rehearsal and identifies at least one specific thing to improve from the recording
Can describe the difference between how they thought they sounded and how they actually sounded

width.minimum: Make at least one recording of a rehearsal, listen back, and identify one specific thing to improve.
width.typical: Use rehearsal recordings systematically to evaluate performance and make documented adjustments; with assistance, apply basic sound reinforcement (PA, microphones, foldback) in a performance context and adjust to ensure the audience and performers can hear the music clearly.
wider: Record two rehearsals at different stages of preparation, listen back to both, and document what improved and what still needs work
Learn to set up and adjust basic PA equipment — practise the process before a performance so it is efficient and reliable on the day

modes.reason: Listening back to recordings requires students to listen as audience rather than as performers. Build a structured listening framework: 'Listen first for timing, then for balance, then for tone.' Without structure, students either hear only overall impression or listen only for their own part.

nodes.label: Planning and introducing a performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a performance presentation including staging and introduction, and share compositional intent and musical decisions with an audience.
criteria: Contributes to a performance plan that includes at least staging and introduction
Delivers or contributes to an introduction that communicates compositional intent or musical decisions to the audience

width.minimum: Plan a performance with at least one staging decision and one introduction element that communicates compositional intent or musical decisions to the audience.
width.typical: Plan and present performances — introducing using spoken, written or audio-visual formats; sharing compositional intent and how elements of music were used; making staging decisions for the performance space; documenting performance plans.
wider: Present a performance for a specific audience beyond the classroom (e.g. another class, a school assembly) — adapt the introduction format for that audience
Document the full performance plan (staging, introduction, notation, rehearsal notes) as a portfolio — use it to reflect on what worked and what to do differently

modes.reason: Performance planning integrates all elements of the standard — notation-guided rehearsal, technology use, staging decisions, introduction format — into a cohesive performance event. The teaching investment is in helping students see that a performance is planned and prepared, not just executed.

descriptors.title: Create artworks that communicate ideas and meaning
descriptors.description: use visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials to create artworks that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use visual conventions, processes and materials to create artworks with deliberate intent (AC9AVA2C01). They make choices about conventions and materials based on communicative purpose. They have not yet planned artworks in advance, used compositional strategies, or created works that communicate specific perspectives.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials to create artworks that communicate specific ideas, perspectives or meaning — making and explaining deliberate compositional choices.

nodes.label: Generating and selecting ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generate multiple ideas for an artwork, select one, and document their reason for the selection.
criteria: Generates at least two distinct ideas for an artwork
Selects one and gives a specific reason for the choice (not just 'I like it')
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot generate and evaluate ideas create from the first option that comes to mind. The selection habit is the prerequisite for intentional composition — without it, later nodes about communicating specific perspectives are undermined.

width.minimum: Generate at least two possible ideas for an artwork and choose one, giving a reason for the choice.
width.typical: Use mind-mapping, Viewpoints questions and brainstorming to generate multiple compositional ideas linked to a topic; evaluate options and select one; document reasons for selection.
wider: Generate ideas for an artwork inspired by a performance (dance, drama) — explore how to capture movement, gesture or emotion through visual means
Brainstorm how an illustrator's choices in a familiar text communicate perspective — generate and evaluate different ways to illustrate a specific moment

modes.reason: Students at this level need structured tools (mind-mapping, Viewpoints questions) to generate genuine options rather than defaulting to one idea immediately. The reasoning move — evaluating and choosing — requires explicit scaffolding.

nodes.label: Compositional strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply compositional strategies — foreground/background, scale, tone, arrangement — to organise their artwork deliberately.
criteria: Uses at least one compositional strategy in an artwork
Explains how that strategy affects the work's meaning or impact on the viewer
nodes.hinge_reason: Compositional skills are the craft that makes communicative intent readable to a viewer — students who cannot organise their work compositionally produce artworks that fail to communicate their intended meaning regardless of the quality of the idea.

width.minimum: Use at least one compositional strategy (e.g. foreground/background, scale, tone) in an artwork and explain how it affects the meaning.
width.typical: Apply compositional strategies including depth, foreground/middle/background, contrast, arrangement and scale; experiment with how compositional choices change meaning; document and explain choices.
wider: Explore frame-within-frame compositions — experiment with different sized frames to view the world and design compositions that use frames as portals
Investigate how artists from a specific cultural tradition use composition — explore how arrangement serves cultural meaning with guidance from culturally authoritative resources

modes.reason: Compositional techniques require practice to become fluent — students need to apply them across multiple works before the choices become natural rather than effortful. Single-exposure teaching at this level produces surface compliance, not genuine skill.

Applying compositional strategies in different contexts (landscape, figure, abstract, response to performance) reveals how the same technique works differently in each — broadening application builds genuine understanding of composition.

nodes.label: Creating to communicate a perspective
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create an artwork that communicates a specific idea, perspective or meaning — combining visual conventions, compositional choices and materials in service of the intent.
criteria: Creates an artwork that communicates a specific idea, perspective or meaning
Explains at least two visual choices (convention, composition, material) in terms of how they serve the communicative intent

width.minimum: Create an artwork that communicates one idea, perspective or meaning; explain how the visual choices serve that intent.
width.typical: Create artworks using combinations of visual conventions, processes and materials that communicate specific ideas and perspectives; make and explain deliberate choices; produce artworks that respond to a topic, cross-curricular theme or other arts form.
wider: Create an artwork inspired by a dance or drama — communicate the energy, emotion or narrative through abstract or representational visual means
Apply the compositional approach of an illustrator to communicate a specific perspective on a scene from a familiar text — compare your approach to other students' and to the original

Create an artwork that communicates your personal connection to a place — select visual conventions, symbols and colours that are meaningful to you, informed by reflection on your own cultural background

modes.reason: Students bring together idea generation, compositional strategy and material choice into a unified artwork that communicates a specific perspective. The integration move is: all choices serve the communicative intent.

descriptors.strand: Visual arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Experiment with visual conventions and materials
descriptors.description: experiment with a range of ways to use visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials
descriptors.knowledge: Students can experiment with materials and processes, reflect using Viewpoints questions, and use visual arts language to describe their discoveries (AC9AVA2D01). They have begun to use named visual conventions in their work. They have not yet investigated composition as a deliberate technique or documented their thinking formally.
descriptors.endpoint: Students experiment with a range of ways to use visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials, and document and reflect on what they discover.

nodes.label: Investigating composition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can observe and describe how artists use composition — space, balance, foreground/background, positive/negative space — in a range of artworks.
criteria: Identifies at least one compositional choice in an artwork (how space is used, what is emphasised)
Explains how that choice affects the meaning or experience of the work
nodes.hinge_reason: Composition is the structural knowledge that allows experimentation to become purposeful — students who cannot observe and name compositional choices in others' work cannot apply them deliberately in their own experimentation.

width.minimum: Examine one artwork and identify at least one compositional choice the artist made (e.g. how space is divided, where emphasis is placed).
width.typical: Examine diverse artworks to observe compositional choices; use transparent overlays or digital tools to trace dominant forms and spatial divisions; identify foreground/background, positive/negative space, and areas of emphasis.
wider: Use the compositional outline of an observed artwork as the basis for a new artwork — adapt the spatial structure while changing the subject matter or visual conventions
Compare compositional choices across artworks addressing the same theme — investigate how different compositional strategies serve different communicative purposes

modes.reason: Compositional analysis is not spontaneous — students need a systematic way to look (tracing overlays, Viewpoints questions) to move beyond surface description to naming specific structural choices.

nodes.label: Experimenting with materials and effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can experiment with combinations of materials and visual conventions to produce specific visual effects, working within limits and documenting discoveries.
criteria: Tries at least two ways of combining materials or conventions
Documents what was tried and what visual effect resulted

width.minimum: Try at least two ways of combining materials or conventions to produce a visual effect; document what was tried and what resulted.
width.typical: Experiment within limits (one set of materials, one visual convention focus) to explore what combinations produce; document with annotated visual records; use Viewpoints questions to reflect on effectiveness.
wider: Explore a tactile/texture board — collect, sort and categorise materials by texture; brainstorm adjectives; invent new colour names; reflect on how materials could be used in future artworks
Try multiple printmaking approaches — use different coloured inks, add pattern and texture progressively, cut and combine elements; document how complexity increases

modes.reason: Experimentation with a single material type develops narrow material knowledge. The range of explorations — texture, colour, printmaking, 3D, crosshatching — each reveals different properties that enrich future making choices.

nodes.label: Documenting and reflecting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use visual arts language to document and reflect on their experimentations — annotating what they tried, what worked, and what they would do differently.
criteria: Annotates at least one experiment with specific comments using visual arts language
Identifies at least one thing that could be explored or improved in future work

width.minimum: Annotate at least one experiment with at least two specific comments — what was tried, what worked or didn't, and what could be explored next.
width.typical: Document experimentations with annotations, arrows and Viewpoints questions; use visual arts language accurately; reflect on effectiveness and what could be explored further; create a record that communicates learning and thinking.
wider: Create a 'work-in-progress' presentation — use audio or video annotation to accompany visual experiments, explaining the thinking and learning as it developed
Explore visual conventions used in First Nations Australian artworks — with guidance from culturally authoritative resources, document what you notice using visual arts language

modes.reason: Documentation habits need to be established through repeated practice at this level — the habit of annotating discoveries (not just labelling) requires consistent expectation and practice across multiple experiments.

descriptors.title: Visual arts across cultures, times and places
descriptors.description: explore where, why and how visual arts are created and/or presented across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored artworks across cultures and communities and asked questions about artists and their practices (AC9AVA2E01). They can identify similarities and differences across cultural contexts. They have not yet examined how an artist's context (time, place, culture) shapes their approach, or compared artists addressing the same theme from different contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore where, why and how visual arts are created and presented across cultures, times and places, making connections and comparisons between artists and their contexts.

nodes.label: Observing artworks closely
nodes.checkpoint: Students can observe an artwork in detail — noticing materials, proportions, patterns and features they didn't see at first — and use questions to develop deeper understanding.
criteria: Shares at least two observations about an artwork — one immediately visible and one discovered through careful looking
Asks at least one question arising from close observation

width.minimum: Examine one artwork and share at least two observations — one noticed immediately and one discovered through careful looking.
width.typical: Examine artworks using close observation strategies; use Viewpoints questions to notice materials, patterns, proportions, colours and features; develop understanding through discussion.
wider: Categorise visual features and cultural works in the school environment (murals, memorials, displays) by purpose — social, decorative, functional, cultural, architectural
Compare how different artists represent the same subject or theme — identify what each emphasises and discuss why

modes.reason: Close observation requires technique — students need strategies for discovering what they missed initially (looking through half-shut eyes, considering texture, tracing compositional lines) rather than just looking again.

nodes.label: Artist context and approach
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate an artist's context — when, where and how they work — and explain how context shapes their artistic approach.
criteria: Identifies at least one aspect of an artist's context
Explains how that context connects to a specific choice in the artwork

width.minimum: Identify one aspect of an artist's context (where they live, when they worked, what influences them) and explain how it connects to one choice in the artwork.
width.typical: Investigate artists' practices using accounts created or co-created by the artist; use Viewpoints questions about studio, process, materials and engagement with galleries; connect context to specific artistic choices.
wider: Explore artists who work collaboratively — investigate why artists might choose to work as a team; compare a collaborative artwork with a solo work addressing the same theme
Compare how artists from different cultural contexts approach sustainability as a theme — identify how context shapes emphasis, material choices and visual conventions

modes.reason: Students who investigate only one artist's context develop limited understanding of how context shapes art. A range of artists — across time, place and culture — shows that the relationship between context and making is consistent but varied.

nodes.label: Comparing across cultures, times and places
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make connections and comparisons between artists working across cultures, times and places — identifying similarities and differences and explaining how context accounts for them.
criteria: Compares artworks from at least two different cultures, times or places
Identifies at least one similarity and one difference, and suggests how context might explain the difference

width.minimum: Compare two artworks from different cultures, times or places; identify one similarity and one difference and suggest how context might explain the difference.
width.typical: Make connections and comparisons across multiple artists and contexts; investigate how the same theme (sustainability, celebration, community) is approached differently; discuss how artworks develop social awareness; explore multiple perspectives on the same event.
wider: Compare artworks addressing sustainability from different cultural contexts — identify how land art, works using recycled materials, and representations of climate effects each reflect their makers' relationships to the environment
Explore artworks by First Nations Australian artists that represent connection to Country/Place — compare with artworks by non-First Nations artists representing the same landscapes

modes.reason: Comparative analysis draws on close observation skills and context understanding to produce a higher-order claim: that differences between artworks reflect differences in context, not just differences in style.

descriptors.title: First Nations visual arts and country/place
descriptors.description: explore how First Nations Australians use visual arts to communicate their connection to and responsibility for Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored artworks by First Nations Australians, identified visual conventions and observed how Country/Place is central to First Nations art-making (AC9AVA2E02). They understand that place is connected to identity. They have not yet explored the concept of responsibility for Country/Place, or examined how visual arts communicate this responsibility.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how First Nations Australians use visual arts to communicate their connection to and responsibility for Country/Place.

nodes.label: Responsibility for Country/Place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that First Nations Australian visual arts communicate not only connection to Country/Place but also responsibility for caring for it.
criteria: Identifies at least one way a First Nations Australian artwork communicates responsibility or care for Country/Place
Distinguishes between connection (belonging to a place) and responsibility (caring for a place)
nodes.hinge_reason: The shift from connection to responsibility is the conceptual advance in this descriptor over Y1-2 — students who understand only connection miss the relational and ethical dimension that gives First Nations visual arts their full meaning at this level.

width.minimum: Look at one First Nations Australian artwork and identify at least one way it communicates responsibility or care for Country/Place (not only connection).
width.typical: Access accounts by contemporary First Nations Australian artists about their ideas concerning Country/Place; use Viewpoints questions to investigate what the works communicate about responsibility; discuss spiritual and intellectual connections to land, sea, sky and waterways.
wider: Explore visual arts that share cultural accounts of Country/Place — investigate how specific visual conventions, symbols and patterns communicate responsibility for specific places
Examine artworks addressing the diversity of First Nations Nations — investigate how distinct communities communicate their relationships to their own Country/Place

modes.reason: Responsibility for Country/Place is an unfamiliar concept for most students. Explicit discussion with targeted prompts is needed before students can identify it in artworks — the concept must be introduced before artworks can demonstrate it.

nodes.label: Symbols, stories and cultural identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine symbols and emblems important to First Nations Australians and understand their importance to identity and culture, engaging with people of cultural authority.
criteria: Examines at least one symbol or emblem important to a First Nations Australian community
Explains what it communicates about identity or cultural connection, using information from culturally authoritative sources

width.minimum: Examine at least one symbol or emblem important to First Nations Australians and explain what it communicates about identity or culture.
width.typical: Examine a diverse range of symbols and emblems; engage with accounts from people with cultural authority about their importance; explore artworks addressing cultural identity; connect visual conventions to specific cultural meanings.
wider: Explore visual conventions, symbols or patterns with representatives of a First Nations Australian community, or through resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians — document what you learn about how the visual conventions carry cultural meaning
Compare place-based symbols across different First Nations communities — investigate how different communities use visual conventions to communicate their specific relationships to their Country

modes.reason: Students who examine symbols from only one First Nations community risk homogenising First Nations culture. Engaging with diverse communities and their distinct symbols builds respect for cultural specificity.

nodes.label: Personal connections and visual arts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on their own cultural connections and consider how visual arts can communicate personal connection to place.
criteria: Identifies at least one personal cultural connection to a place
Reflects on how First Nations Australian approaches to communicating place connection compare with how they would communicate their own

width.minimum: Identify at least one personal connection to a place (family, community, landscape) and one visual way to represent it.
width.typical: Map personal cultural connections — place, language, family customs, values — and use Viewpoints questions to plan an artwork that communicates connection to place; reflect on how First Nations Australian approaches to this question compare with your own.
wider: Create an artwork that communicates your personal connection to place using visual conventions meaningful to you — reflect on similarities and differences between your approach and approaches used by First Nations Australian artists
Investigate stories connected to local Country/Place — explore how knowledge of place history enriches the visual arts made in and about a place

modes.reason: This node brings together the conceptual understanding of Country/Place responsibility and the personal making dimension — students connect what they have learned about First Nations Australian visual arts to their own relationship with place.

descriptors.title: Share and display artworks in informal settings
descriptors.description: share and/or display artworks and/or visual arts practice in informal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can share artworks in informal settings, choosing audience and format and explaining their work (AC9AVA2P01). They have basic experience of multiple sharing contexts. They have not yet selected documentation of a process to share, curated a display, or produced an artist statement.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share and/or display artworks and visual arts practice in informal settings, selecting documentation and making decisions about appropriate audiences and presentation formats.

nodes.label: Selecting and arranging for display
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select examples from their visual arts practice and arrange them to communicate the development of their ideas.
criteria: Selects at least two examples from their practice to form a display
Arranges them in a way that shows development — can explain what the arrangement communicates

width.minimum: Select at least two examples from their practice (experiments, in-progress work, final artwork) and arrange them to show how ideas developed.
width.typical: Select a range of documentation (experiments, compositional approaches, reflections, final artwork) and arrange in a visual display; explain the sequence and what it shows about the development of ideas.
wider: Trial two different arrangements of the same artworks — compare which communicates the development of ideas more clearly and explain why
Arrange a physical wall display and then consider what would need to change to share the same works on a digital platform

modes.reason: Curation — selecting and arranging to communicate — is a new skill at this level. Students need to understand that arrangement communicates meaning, not just that display looks tidy. Structured questions ('What does this arrangement say about how your ideas grew?') support the curatorial reasoning.

nodes.label: Producing an artist statement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce a written or spoken artist statement that explains the ideas, themes and meanings in their artwork.
criteria: Produces a spoken or written artist statement
The statement explains an idea, theme or meaning — not only what the artwork shows

width.minimum: Produce a spoken or written artist statement that explains one idea or meaning in their artwork.
width.typical: Discuss and document ideas, themes and meanings; produce written or spoken artist statements; explore multimedia formats for combining artwork with statement.
wider: Create a multimedia artist statement — combine photographs of the making process with spoken explanation of ideas and decisions
Identify and explain your own and another artist's choices in art-making — use the comparison to sharpen your explanation of your own choices

modes.reason: Artist statements require repeated practice to develop from superficial description ('I painted a sunset') to genuine explanation of intent ('I used orange and red to communicate the feeling of heat fading'). Consolidation across multiple artworks builds depth.

nodes.label: Choosing audience and format
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make deliberate decisions about appropriate audiences for their work and choose presentation formats suited to each context.
criteria: Identifies at least one appropriate audience for a sharing context and gives a reason
Makes at least one format choice (display, digital, folio, verbal) suited to that audience

width.minimum: Identify an appropriate audience for one artwork and explain why that audience is suitable.
width.typical: Choose appropriate audiences and formats across multiple sharing contexts — folio, peer circle, digital platform, physical display, school community exhibition; explain how format choices serve the audience and purpose.
wider: Plan a class exhibition for a specific audience (younger students, families, community) — make decisions about layout, labels, accessibility and purpose
Adapt an existing physical display for a digital sharing context — consider what changes and what can be preserved

modes.reason: Students bring together their curatorial skills, artist statement capability and audience awareness to make a complete sharing decision — who, how and in what context the work is best shared.

descriptors.title: Manipulate elements and devices
descriptors.description: manipulate the elements of dance and/or choreographic devices to choreograph dances that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use elements of dance to choreograph dance that communicates ideas, perspectives and/or meaning (Y3-4). They can structure dances with beginning-middle-end, generate and combine movement material, and use choreographic intent to guide decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students manipulate the elements of dance and/or choreographic devices to choreograph dances that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning.
elaborations: exploring character and mood by experimenting with elements, developing narrative dance
devising movement possibilities and selecting, combining, arranging and refining; using some movements in repeating sections that alternate with contrasting sections
creating dance that focuses on technical and expressive skills
creating dance that explores a theme or issue such as sustainability

nodes.label: Choreographic devices as tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and intentionally use choreographic devices — such as repetition, contrast, unison — to shape how their dance communicates.
criteria: Student can name at least one choreographic device used in their dance
Student can explain what effect that device creates in their dance
nodes.hinge_reason: Choreographic devices are the compositional vocabulary of Y7-8 and Y9-10 Creating strand work. Students who have not internalised devices as intentional tools will approach composition as movement arrangement rather than structural craft.

width.minimum: Using at least one choreographic device (e.g. repetition or contrast) intentionally in a movement sequence — can name the device and explain its effect.
width.typical: Exploring and applying choreographic devices: repetition, contrast, unison; using a repeating section that alternates with contrasting sections; structuring a dance using devices to create sections; exploring how devices change the audience experience.
wider: Investigate how choreographic devices are used in a dance they are studying or have experienced — applying the same device in their own work
Experiment with combining multiple devices in a single dance — examining how layered device use deepens communicative effect

modes.reason: Devices need naming and analysis before they become tools. Use examples from dances students have experienced — 'this section repeats, and here's what that does' — before expecting intentional application.

nodes.label: Generating material through manipulation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can manipulate elements of dance and choreographic devices to generate and develop movement material — exploring multiple possibilities before selecting.
criteria: Student generates at least three distinct movement possibilities from one starting point
Student can explain why they selected the movements they used (connects to communicative intent)

width.minimum: Generating at least three movement variations from one starting movement using element manipulation (space, time, dynamics, relationship); selecting among them for a choreographic purpose.
width.typical: Exploring stimuli and other dances to devise movement possibilities (different ways to jump/land, roll/stand, spiral to ground); selecting, combining, arranging and refining; experimenting with characters and mood through element manipulation; exploring technical-expressive focus (control, coordination, balance).
wider: Use positive and negative space as a choreographic consideration — exploring how spatial relationships between dancers change meaning
Develop movement material from a theme or issue (sustainability, identity) — using element manipulation to represent ideas abstractly

modes.reason: Students at this level should be developing choreographic range — the habit of generating many possibilities before committing. Reward exploration over early closure.

nodes.label: Structuring a complete dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can structure a dance using choreographic devices that communicate a clear idea, perspective or meaning — with technical and expressive skill considerations integrated.
criteria: Student produces a dance that uses at least one choreographic device to structure communication of an idea
Student can identify how technical-expressive skill choices contribute to the dance's communicative effect
Student can describe what their dance communicates and explain at least one structural decision
nodes.hinge_reason: Producing a complete structured dance using devices — not just movement arranged in order — is the capability milestone of this standard. Without this, students enter Y7-8 without the compositional experience to work with more complex structural forms (binary, ternary, narrative) and genre-specific techniques.

width.minimum: A structured dance using at least one device; clear communicative intent; attention to at least one technical-expressive skill (control, coordination, balance).
width.typical: Creating structured dances: narrative dances retelling a story, dances exploring themes or issues; using choreographic devices to create sections; focusing on technical and expressive skills; reflecting on and refining using Viewpoints questions ('How is the body used to represent the story?', 'How can space communicate meaning?').
wider: Create a dance using production elements (music, costume, props) to enhance communication of the theme or idea
Choreograph a dance that explores a sustainability or social issue — using device choices to structure an argument or narrative arc

modes.reason: Structuring integrates device knowledge (N1), generated material (N2), and technical-expressive attention into a communicative whole. Use Viewpoints questions throughout the process — not just at the end.

descriptors.title: Technical and expressive skills
descriptors.description: develop and practise technical and expressive skills using safe dance practice and the elements of dance
descriptors.knowledge: Students can experiment with and practise skills for moving safely and expressively (Y3-4). They demonstrate habitual safe practice and can use elements to communicate ideas through movement.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop and practise technical and expressive skills using safe dance practice and the elements of dance.
elaborations: improvising new movement to communicate ideas in response to stimulus
developing technical and expressive skills to refine execution of fundamental movements
developing expressive skills of focus, clarity of movement, confidence and facial expression/character
exploring an element of dance; experimenting with shapes and positive/negative space, contrasting dynamics

nodes.label: Developing technical skill range
nodes.checkpoint: Students can refine technical execution of fundamental movements — improving control, coordination, accuracy and expressive quality across a range of movement types.
criteria: Student can demonstrate improved technical quality in a target movement following sustained practice
Student applies safe dance practice consistently across all technical skill development activities

width.minimum: Refining technical execution of at least three movement types (e.g. galloping, jumping, rolling, spinning) — demonstrating improvement over time in at least one.
width.typical: Developing technical and expressive skills in fundamental movements: galloping, jumping, sliding, rolling, slithering, spinning, shrinking, exploding, collapsing; developing focus, clarity, confidence and facial expression/character; applying safe dance practice throughout.
wider: Choose one technically demanding movement as a sustained practice focus — setting specific quality targets and tracking improvement across sessions
Explore how the same movement (e.g. jumping) is executed differently in different dance styles — developing style-awareness alongside technical skill

modes.reason: Technical skill development requires deliberate, repeated practice with targeted feedback. Students benefit from sustained focus on specific movements rather than constant variety.

nodes.label: Expressive skills and communicative clarity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use expressive skills — focus, clarity of movement, confidence, facial expression — to communicate ideas through performance.
criteria: Student uses at least two expressive skills in a performance — visible to an observer
Student can explain how each expressive skill serves the communicative intention of the dance
nodes.hinge_reason: Expressive skill in performance is the bridge between technical execution and communicative impact. Students without expressive skill development will produce technically competent but communicatively flat performance — this limits their work in Y7-8 Performing strand where technical and expressive integration is foregrounded.

width.minimum: Demonstrating at least two expressive skills in a movement sequence — can name each and explain its communicative function.
width.typical: Developing expressive skills of focus, clarity of movement, confidence and facial expression/character; improvising new movement in response to stimuli to practise communicative expressiveness; exploring element of dance choices (positive/negative space, contrasting dynamics) to develop expressive range.
wider: Use video self-review to identify expressive skill strengths and development areas — setting specific goals for a subsequent performance
Explore how contrasting expressive skill choices (e.g. confident vs hesitant, focused vs distracted) change what a movement communicates

modes.reason: Expressive performance integrates technical skill (N1) with communicative intent and audience awareness. Frame expressiveness as a skill that can be practised and refined — not a personality trait.

descriptors.title: Elements of dance communicate meaning
descriptors.description: explore ways that the elements of dance are combined to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in dance across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore where, why and how dance is choreographed and/or performed across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts (Y3-4). They can compare dances and identify purpose and meaning using Viewpoints questions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore ways that the elements of dance are combined to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in dance across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts.
elaborations: exploring how dances use elements and choreographic devices such as repetition, unison, contrast
seeking feedback about how audience interpreted the dance's movements
discussing purpose of movements, elements, production elements and technical/expressive skills and their effect on mood
asking Viewpoints questions to explore similarities and differences across choreographers
exploring how dance communicates cultural traditions; considering dances from Asia

nodes.label: Reading element use in observed dances
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe how elements of dance and choreographic devices are combined in dances they experience — connecting element choices to communicative effect.
criteria: Student can describe how at least two elements combine in an observed dance to create a specific communicative effect
Student connects at least one element choice to the mood, meaning or audience relationship in the dance
nodes.hinge_reason: Reading element combinations as communicative — not just aesthetic — is the analytical move that distinguishes appreciation from analysis. Students who cannot yet do this will engage with dances at a descriptive surface level in Y7-8 investigating work.

width.minimum: Identifying how at least two elements of dance are used together in one observed dance — and describing the communicative effect of those choices.
width.typical: Exploring how dances use elements and choreographic devices (repetition, unison, contrast); discussing purpose of movements, elements, production elements, technical and expressive skills and their effect on mood and audience relationship; using Viewpoints to explore similarities and differences across choreographers and contexts.
wider: Explore how dance communicates cultural traditions — examining a dance from a country or region in Asia and asking how it reflects cultural ways of being
Investigate how elements of dance in a specific dance style (e.g. hip hop, contemporary, classical) reflect the cultural or historical context of that style

modes.reason: Element-to-meaning reading requires an explicit interpretive move — students need Viewpoints questions with analytical scaffolding: 'How does the use of slow dynamics here change the mood?', 'What does the unison say about the relationship between dancers?'

nodes.label: Comparing element use across cultural contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare how elements of dance are combined across different cultural and temporal contexts — identifying how context shapes element use.
criteria: Student can compare element use in two dances from different cultural or temporal contexts
Student offers a culturally contextualised explanation for at least one difference observed

width.minimum: Comparing element use in two dances from different cultural or temporal contexts — identifying at least one difference in how elements are combined and suggesting why.
width.typical: Exploring similarities and differences in how choreographers use elements across genres, styles, cultures and times; using Viewpoints to develop questions about how main ideas are communicated; seeking feedback about how audience perceived choreographic intent; considering how cultural traditions shape element use.
wider: Investigate how dance-on-screen (film, music video) uses production elements alongside dance elements — examining how the combination changes what is communicated
Explore how a dance from a country or region in Asia uses elements in ways that differ from familiar Western dance styles — discussing what this reveals about cultural values and aesthetics

modes.reason: Genuine comparison requires genuine diversity of examples. Students who have encountered only one or two cultural dance contexts cannot make meaningful comparative observations.

descriptors.title: First Nations dance and culture
descriptors.description: explore the ways that First Nations Australians use dance to continue and revitalise cultures
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore how First Nations Australians use dance to communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place (Y3-4). They can identify element use in First Nations dance and understand the cultural purposes of specific dance occasions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore the ways that First Nations Australians use dance to continue and revitalise cultures.
elaborations: exploring how and why cultural expressions are critical for sharing, continuing or revitalising cultures
investigating how meaning and purpose are communicated in dance at community events
experiencing how First Nations Australians' stories and ideas communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place
using Viewpoints to develop questions and build understanding about First Nations dance
exploring how narrative dances maintain culture — knowledge about sustainable practices or place stories

nodes.label: Dance as cultural continuation and revitalisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why cultural expressions including dance are critical for sharing, continuing and revitalising First Nations Australian cultures.
criteria: Student can explain what it means for First Nations Australians to use dance to continue or revitalise their culture
Student can describe at least one specific example of dance serving this purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding dance as a vehicle for cultural continuation and revitalisation — not merely performance — is the conceptual shift required for meaningful engagement with the more complex issues of cultural diversity, ICIP rights and identity in Y7-8.

width.minimum: Describing at least one way that dance helps First Nations Australians continue or revitalise a cultural practice — using a specific example.
width.typical: Exploring, using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians, how and why cultural expressions are critical for sharing, continuing and revitalising cultures; investigating how meaning and purpose are communicated in dance at community events; experiencing how First Nations Australians' stories and ideas communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place.
wider: Explore how narrative dances maintain culture — examining specific examples of dances that communicate knowledge about sustainable approaches or place-naming stories
Investigate how community events use dance to communicate cultural knowledge to the broader community — noting what knowledge is shared and with whom

modes.reason: Revitalisation is a concept that requires contextualisation — students need to understand what cultural continuity means and why it matters before they can appreciate dance's role. Use resources created by First Nations Australians and guided discussion to build this understanding.

nodes.label: Investigating meaning and purpose in First Nations dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how meaning and purpose are communicated in specific First Nations Australian dance works — using Viewpoints questions to deepen inquiry.
criteria: Student uses Viewpoints questions to investigate how meaning is communicated in a First Nations Australian dance
Student can explain what the dance communicates about culture, knowledge or connection to Country/Place

width.minimum: Observing one First Nations Australian dance work and using at least two Viewpoints questions to investigate how meaning is communicated.
width.typical: Investigating how meaning and purpose are communicated in dances performed at community events or via resources created/co-created by First Nations Australians; using Viewpoints questions to build understanding ('What do I already know?', 'What do I need to learn?', 'What questions would I ask the dancers?'); exploring how dances communicate sustainable practices for caring for land, sea, sky.
wider: Compare how two different First Nations Australian dance practices communicate cultural knowledge — noting what is shared versus what is community-specific
Develop and pursue an inquiry question about a First Nations Australian dance practice — following protocols and using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians

modes.reason: Students' capacity to investigate First Nations dance meaningfully deepens with exposure to multiple examples from diverse communities. Breadth here prevents reductive single-example conclusions.

descriptors.title: Perform with technical skills
descriptors.description: practise and perform dances using technical and expressive skills in informal and/or formal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can practise and perform dances in informal settings (Y3-4). They use expressive skills (projection, focus) and can communicate intent to an audience and reflect on performance.
descriptors.endpoint: Students practise and perform dances using technical and expressive skills in informal and/or formal settings.
elaborations: rehearsing and performing with awareness of body capabilities and applying technical and expressive skills
using specific technical and expressive skills to communicate ideas, perspectives and meaning
presenting using production elements — music, costumes, props — appropriate to the context
using Viewpoints to reflect on performance — space, energy, relationship between dancers and audience

nodes.label: Technical and expressive skill in rehearsal
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply technical and expressive skills in rehearsal — working within their body capabilities and improving quality across multiple attempts.
criteria: Student can identify at least one technical and one expressive skill they are working on in rehearsal
Student shows improvement in a target skill across multiple rehearsal sessions

width.minimum: Rehearsing a dance with awareness of technical skill application (e.g. landing alignment, balance) and at least one expressive skill — able to identify what they are working to improve.
width.typical: Rehearsing learned and/or self-choreographed dances with awareness of body capabilities; applying technical and expressive skills; creating tension through slow controlled movements with neutral facial expression; using Viewpoints questions to reflect on spatial placement, focus, musicality, clarity.
wider: Use video to review rehearsal — identifying specific technical and expressive skill development areas and setting targeted goals
Rehearse across multiple sessions with a documented improvement focus — tracking change in a performance journal or checklist

modes.reason: Rehearsal skill — the capacity to use repetition productively and target improvements — is itself a learnable practice. Students benefit from explicit rehearsal strategy instruction alongside content.

nodes.label: Performing for audiences in varied settings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform dances in informal and/or formal settings — using technical and expressive skills and appropriate production elements to communicate ideas to an audience.
criteria: Student performs a dance using at least two identifiable technical-expressive skills
Student can use at least one production element purposefully in performance
Student can reflect on their performance using a Viewpoints question — identifying one strength and one area for development
nodes.hinge_reason: Performance in varied settings — including formal contexts — is the experiential foundation for the more demanding performance requirements of Y7-8. Students who have only ever performed in highly informal single-class settings lack the performance confidence and audience awareness that formal contexts require.

width.minimum: Performing one dance in an informal or formal setting using at least two technical-expressive skills; using at least one production element where appropriate.
width.typical: Performing in informal and/or formal settings: using specific technical and expressive skills to communicate ideas, perspectives or meaning; using production elements (music, costumes, props) to enhance different contexts; performing with cultural community representatives using traditional music where appropriate; using Viewpoints questions to reflect on performance.
wider: Perform a dance for an audience beyond the class — a school assembly, community event, or online platform — adapting performance presence for the context
Perform a dance using traditional music when presenting with representatives of the cultural group from the community — following relevant cultural protocols

modes.reason: Performance integrates rehearsal skill (N1), technical-expressive skill, and production element choices into a communicative event. The audience relationship is the critical new element at this node — frame performance as communication, not demonstration.

descriptors.title: Develop characters and dramatic action
descriptors.description: develop characters and situations, and shape and sustain dramatic action to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in improvised, devised and/or scripted forms
descriptors.knowledge: Students can improvise and devise drama using elements of drama to communicate ideas and meaning (Y3-4). They can shape improvisations using voice, movement and language, and devise drama collaboratively with communicative intent.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop characters and situations, and shape and sustain dramatic action to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in improvised, devised and/or scripted forms.
elaborations: exploring physical, fictional or emotional spaces to create characters
varying voice using projection, dynamics, pace, pause and pitch to communicate character intentions
rehearsing, interacting and negotiating with others to interpret scripts and create characters
devising drama based on research about a school/community project for cultural awareness or debate
working collaboratively to devise drama for a school ritual or gathering
using Viewpoints to ask questions when exploring character

nodes.label: Developing character
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a character with consistent physical, vocal and relational qualities, distinguishable from their own default behaviour.
criteria: Student creates a character distinguishable from their own default through at least two consistent choices (voice and physical)
Student sustains character across a scene including during reactions to others
Student can describe the character's perspective or intention
nodes.hinge_reason: Consistent character development is the anchor for sustaining dramatic action; if characters collapse under pressure (breaking in and out of role or losing character consistency), the dramatic action cannot be sustained across longer or more complex forms — particularly in scripted drama.

width.minimum: Student creates and sustains one character across a short scene, making at least two distinct characterisation choices (voice and physicality).
width.typical: Students explore physical, fictional or emotional spaces to create characters; they vary voice (projection, dynamics, pace, pause, pitch) and use movement and gesture to communicate characters' intentions; they rehearse and negotiate with others to interpret scripts and create characters and their relationships.
wider: Students use empathy to develop characters from different perspectives, considering situations from multiple characters' viewpoints and challenging stereotypes
Students develop a 'new scene' to include in a dramatic re-telling of a known narrative, creating a character who was not in the original

modes.reason: Character consistency develops through rehearsal and deliberate practice; students need repeated opportunities to 'inhabit' a character across different scenarios before they can sustain it through a full drama.

Developing characters across different contexts — improvised, scripted, empathy-based, culturally situated — builds transferable characterisation skills and prevents students from defaulting to a single character type.

nodes.label: Shaping dramatic action across forms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can shape dramatic action — developing situation, tension and resolution — across improvised, devised and/or scripted forms.
criteria: Student shapes a dramatic sequence with a recognisable dramatic arc (beginning, complication, resolution)
Student demonstrates sustained dramatic action across a complete piece in at least one form
Student can articulate what idea, perspective or meaning the drama is communicating

width.minimum: Student shapes a dramatic sequence with an identifiable beginning, complication and resolution across one form.
width.typical: Students shape and sustain dramatic action across improvised, devised and/or scripted drama; they use rehearsal, interaction and negotiation with others; they use props, costumes and available technologies (light, sound, multimedia) as dramatic symbols; they develop drama for school rituals or community events with a specific purpose.
wider: Students devise drama based on research about a school or local community project, using drama to present different perspectives in a debate or issue
Students explore how a devised drama for a specific community audience (e.g. school assembly, cultural ceremony) requires adapting form and content to purpose
Students use Viewpoints to frame questions about their own drama: 'How did the performers use elements effectively?', 'What was the purpose?'

modes.reason: Shaping sustained dramatic action across forms is the integration point — character, situation, tension, purpose and audience awareness all converge. Structured reflection and feedback during rehearsal is the key scaffold.

descriptors.title: Combine elements to communicate
descriptors.description: explore ways to combine the elements of drama to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in improvisations, devised drama and/or scripted drama
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use elements of drama — voice, movement, language, space — in combination to develop dramatic action in improvisations and devised drama (Y3-4). They can make deliberate element choices and describe their effect.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore ways to combine elements of drama to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in improvisations, devised drama and/or scripted drama.
elaborations: experimenting with empathy to develop characters, considering situations from different perspectives and challenging stereotypes
imagining and developing a 'new scene' to include in a dramatic re-telling of a known narrative
using Viewpoints to ask questions about cultures and element use
using improvisation or process drama to compare ways improvised and scripted drama create characters
imagining being in the time/place of a historical event and considering why people made certain decisions

nodes.label: Using empathy and perspective to develop combination choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use empathy to explore how combining elements differently communicates different perspectives and challenges stereotypes.
criteria: Student makes at least one element combination choice informed by a specific character perspective
Student can explain how their combination choice communicates that character's viewpoint or intention
nodes.hinge_reason: Empathy-informed element choice is what distinguishes purposeful dramatic crafting from mechanical application of techniques; without this, combinations may be technically correct but lack communicative power — particularly critical in scripted drama where character interior is essential.

width.minimum: Student makes at least one element combination choice that is informed by a character perspective other than their own default.
width.typical: Students experiment with empathy when combining elements in improvised and scripted drama; they consider situations from multiple characters' perspectives; they use Viewpoints to explore how cultures shape element use ('How are relationships, language and symbols shaped by cultures?').
wider: Students imagine themselves in the time/place of a historical event, considering why participants made particular decisions, and explore this through deliberate element combinations
Students explore how the same dramatic situation produces different element-combination choices for characters from different cultural backgrounds

modes.reason: Use structured empathy activities before script or devising work — 'hot-seating', role-on-the-wall, or perspective-taking exercises — to give students the interior perspective that informs element choices.

nodes.label: Combining elements across forms — improvised, devised and scripted
nodes.checkpoint: Students can combine elements of drama purposefully across improvised, devised and scripted forms, evaluating which combinations communicate most effectively.
criteria: Student combines elements of drama purposefully in at least two different forms
Student evaluates the effectiveness of a specific element combination and suggests an alternative

width.minimum: Student compares how element combinations produce different effects in at least two different dramatic forms.
width.typical: Students use improvisation or process drama to compare how improvised and scripted drama create characters and action; they explore how elements combine differently across forms; they consider how cultural understandings shape meaning through element combinations.
wider: Students evaluate drama they experience in live performance, identifying specific element combinations, and consider how to apply those techniques in their own work
Students explore drama from another culture or historical period and investigate how element combinations reflect that culture's dramatic conventions

modes.reason: Exploring element combinations across multiple forms and cultural contexts builds the flexible, transferable skill of combining intentionally rather than habitually.

descriptors.title: Elements combine to communicate meaning
descriptors.description: explore ways that the elements of drama are combined to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in drama across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore where, why and how drama is created across cultures, times and places; they can identify features from other drama contexts and connect them to their own practice (Y3-4).
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore ways that elements of drama are combined to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in drama across cultures, times, places and other contexts.
elaborations: exploring how drama is used within communities to maintain, continue and revitalise culture
identifying and discussing element use using Viewpoints questions
exploring drama from other places and times and discussing how it might contribute to their own drama and how cultural understandings shape meaning

nodes.label: Identifying how elements combine in specific drama
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe how specific elements of drama are combined in a drama work to communicate ideas or meaning.
criteria: Student identifies at least two elements in combination in a specific drama and describes what each communicates
Student can connect an element combination choice to a communicative intention or cultural context
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot identify and describe specific element combinations in a drama they observe, they cannot make the cross-cultural comparison the descriptor requires; 'across cultures' demands a precise enough analytical lens to identify what varies.
